stem: To prevent vehicles from speeding, speed humps are built on the roads to regulate the speed of cars. Diagram 1 shows the length, width and height of one speed hump. Each speed hump along a road has 4 identical speed humps joined together. Diagram 2 shows the cross-section of one speed hump. $BCD$ is part of sector $OBCD$ with centre $O$, radius 5.438 m and angle $BOD$ of 0.33 radians.

parts.text: Find the length of the arc $BCD$ of the speed hump as shown in Diagram 2.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Arc length $s = r\theta = 5.438 \times 0.33 = 1.79454 \approx 1.79$ m.

parts.text: Diagram 3 shows the top view of 4 identical speed humps joined together. The thickness of the rubber to cover the top of each speed hump is 0.5 cm and the total cost to cover four such speed humps is $\$240$. Using the information given in the table (density of rubber $= 1060$ kg/m$^3$, cost of rubber per kg $= \$20$), calculate the length of one speed hump.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let length of one hump be $x$ m.
Volume of rubber on 1 hump $= 0.005 \times \text{(arc length)} \times x = 0.005 \times 1.79454 \times x = 0.0089727x$ m$^{3}$.
Mass of rubber on 1 hump $= 1060 \times 0.0089727x = 9.511062x$ kg.
Cost of rubber for 1 hump $= \dfrac{\$240}{4} = \$60$.
$20 \times 9.511062x = 60$
$x = \dfrac{60}{20 \times 9.511062} = 0.3154$
$\approx 0.315$ m.

parts.text:
The engineers are to ensure that the height ($h$), width ($w$) and length ($l$) of each speed hump meet the safety criteria as shown in the table:
$$\begin{array}{|l|c|} \hline \text{Height of the hump } (h) & 0.0732 \text{ m} \leq h < 0.1016 \text{ m} \\ \hline \text{Width of the hump } (w) & 0.9144 \text{ m} \leq w < 1.8288 \text{ m} \\ \hline \text{Gradient of the hump } (g) & g < 0.1 \\ \hline \text{Length of one speed hump } (l) & 0.3048 \text{ m} \leq l \leq 0.9144 \text{ m} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
where $g$ is the ratio of the height of the hump to the horizontal length of $BX$ or $XD$. Show with clear working if the engineers should approve this speed hump.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Height: $h = 5.438 - 5.438\cos(0.165) = 0.0739$ m, which satisfies $0.0732 \leq h < 0.1016$. Width (chord $BD$): $w = 2 \times 5.438\sin(0.165) = 1.79$ m, which satisfies $0.9144 \leq w < 1.8288$. Gradient: $g = \frac{0.0739}{0.8932} = 0.0827 < 0.1$. Length: $0.315$ m satisfies $0.3048 \leq l \leq 0.9144$. All four criteria are met, so the engineers can approve this speed hump.
parts.solution:
Half angle $= 0.33 / 2 = 0.165$ rad $= 9.4538^{\circ}$.

**Height $h$:**
$\cos 9.4538^{\circ} = \dfrac{OX}{5.438} \Rightarrow OX = 5.438\cos 9.4538^{\circ} = 5.36414$
$h = 5.438 - 5.36414 = 0.0739$ m. ✓ ($0.0732 \leq 0.0739 < 0.1016$)

**Width (chord $BD$):**
$\sin 9.4538^{\circ} = \dfrac{BX}{5.438} \Rightarrow BX = 5.438\sin 9.4538^{\circ} = 0.893204$
$BD = 2 \times 0.893204 = 1.79$ m. ✓ ($0.9144 \leq 1.79 < 1.8288$)

**Gradient:**
$g = \dfrac{h}{BX} = \dfrac{0.073857}{0.893204} = 0.0827 < 0.1$. ✓

**Length:** $0.315$ m satisfies $0.3048 \leq 0.315 \leq 0.9144$. ✓

All four criteria are met, so the engineers **can approve** this speed hump.

stem: Kelly has a box of spherical beads labelled with the 26 letters from A to Z, all of which have the same size. For each letter, there are exactly 3 beads of different colours, red, blue and gold.

parts.text: Find the number of ways the beads in the keychain can be arranged:
parts.label: a

subparts.text: 6 beads with distinct letters but are of the same colour.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Number of ways to arrange 6 distinct-letter beads of the same colour:
$= {}^{30}C_6 \times \frac{6!}{2} = {}^{30}C_6 \times 360 = 497\,296\,800$

subparts.text: 6 beads with 3 distinct letters.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Each letter has exactly one bead of each colour, so all $78$ beads in the box are different from one another. Once the $6$ beads have been chosen they are all distinct, so each selection can be arranged in $6! = 720$ ways.

Choosing the letters: ${}^{26}C_3 = 2600$ ways.

A letter can supply at most $3$ beads (one of each colour), and each of the $3$ chosen letters must appear at least once, so the $6$ beads split between the letters as $2+2+2$ or $3+2+1$.

Case 1: $2 + 2 + 2$

For each of the $3$ letters, choose $2$ of its $3$ colours: ${}^{3}C_2 = 3$ ways, so $3^3 = 27$ ways in all.

Number of selections $= 2600 \times 27 = 70\,200$

Number of arrangements $= 70\,200 \times 6! = 50\,544\,000$

Case 2: $3 + 2 + 1$

Decide which chosen letter supplies $3$ beads, which supplies $2$ and which supplies $1$: $3! = 6$ ways.

Choose the colours: ${}^{3}C_3 \times {}^{3}C_2 \times {}^{3}C_1 = 1 \times 3 \times 3 = 9$ ways.

Number of selections $= 2600 \times 6 \times 9 = 140\,400$

Number of arrangements $= 140\,400 \times 6! = 101\,088\,000$

Total number of ways $= 50\,544\,000 + 101\,088\,000 = 151\,632\,000$

parts.text: Kelly chooses two beads from a new box. The probability that both are star-shaped but neither is gold is $\frac{1}{66}$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Find $c$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Let star-shaped beads be $S$. Given $P(\text{both star, neither gold}) = \frac{1}{66}$.
With $c$ added beads (per the question's parameterisation), drawing two beads without replacement:
$\frac{2 + c}{41 + c} \cdot \frac{1 + c}{40 + c} = \frac{1}{66}$
$66(2 + c)(1 + c) = (41 + c)(40 + c)$
$66(c^2 + 3c + 2) = c^2 + 81c + 1640$
$65 c^2 + 117c - 1508 = 0$
Solving: $c = 4$ (rejecting $c = -\frac{29}{5}$).

subparts.text: Find the probability that two randomly chosen beads include exactly one red bead and at least one flower-shaped bead.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Case 1: red flower and non-red flower: $\frac{6}{45} \times \frac{5}{44} \times 2 = \frac{1}{33}$
Case 2: red flower and non-red non-flower: $\frac{6}{45} \times \frac{23}{44} \times 2 = \frac{23}{165}$
Case 3: red non-flower and non-red flower: $\frac{11}{45} \times \frac{5}{44} \times 2 = \frac{1}{18}$
Required probability $= \frac{1}{33} + \frac{23}{165} + \frac{1}{18} = \frac{223}{990}$

stem: It is given that when light strikes a surface at an angle, the intensity of illumination at a distance $d$ m away from a point light source is $$I = \frac{k\cos\theta}{d^2},$$ where $k$ is a positive constant and $\theta$ is the angle of incidence as shown in the figure. The college drama club is preparing for its upcoming performance in the performance theatre. For the performance, a spotlight is to be placed $h$ m directly above the centre of a circular stage floor with radius 4 m.

parts.text: Show that the intensity of illumination at the circumference of the circular stage is $K = \frac{kh}{(h^2 + 16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$d = \sqrt{h^2 + 16}$
$\cos\theta = \frac{h}{\sqrt{h^2 + 16}}$
$I = \frac{k\cos\theta}{d^2} = \frac{k \times \frac{h}{\sqrt{h^2 + 16}}}{h^2 + 16} = \frac{kh}{(h^2 + 16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$ (shown)

parts.text: Use differentiation to find the height that gives the highest level of illumination at the circumference of the circular stage floor, giving your answer in exact form.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$I = \frac{kh}{(h^2 + 16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$
$\frac{dI}{dh} = \frac{k\left[ (h^2 + 16)^{\frac{3}{2}} - \frac{3}{2}h\sqrt{h^2 + 16} \times 2h \right]}{(h^2 + 16)^3}$
$= \frac{k\sqrt{h^2 + 16}\left[ h^2 + 16 - 3h^2 \right]}{(h^2 + 16)^3}$
$= \frac{k\left[ 16 - 2h^2 \right]}{(h^2 + 16)^{\frac{5}{2}}}$
$\frac{dI}{dh} = 0 \Rightarrow 16 - 2h^2 = 0$
$h = \sqrt{8}$ (since $h > 0$)
First derivative test:
$\frac{dI}{dh} = \frac{2k(8 - h^2)}{(h^2 + 16)^{\frac{5}{2}}} = \frac{2k\left( \sqrt{8} - h \right)\left( \sqrt{8} + h \right)}{(h^2 + 16)^{\frac{5}{2}}}$
For $h < \sqrt{8}$, $\frac{dI}{dh} > 0$; at $h = \sqrt{8}$, $\frac{dI}{dh} = 0$; for $h > \sqrt{8}$, $\frac{dI}{dh} < 0$, so $I$ is maximum at $h = \sqrt{8}$.
Second derivative test:
$\frac{d^2I}{dh^2} = \frac{k\left[ -4h\left( h^2 + 16 \right)^{\frac{5}{2}} - (16 - 2h^2)\left( \frac{5}{2} \times 2h \right)(h^2 + 16)^{\frac{3}{2}} \right]}{(h^2 + 16)^5}$
$= \frac{k\left[ (-4h^3 - 64h) - (80h - 10h^3) \right]}{(h^2 + 16)^{\frac{7}{2}}}$
$= \frac{k(6h^3 - 144h)}{(h^2 + 16)^{\frac{7}{2}}}$
Sub $h = \sqrt{8}$: $\frac{d^2I}{dh^2} = \frac{k\left( 6\sqrt{8}^3 - 144\sqrt{8} \right)}{(8 + 16)^{\frac{7}{2}}} < 0$
Therefore $h = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$ gives the highest level of illumination.

parts.text: It is now given that the spotlight is moving downwards at a constant rate of $0.02\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Find, in terms of $k$, the rate of change of the intensity of illumination at the circumference of the circular stage when $h = 2$, stating whether the intensity is increasing or decreasing.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: $\frac{dI}{dt} = -\frac{k}{5000\sqrt{5}}$; the intensity is decreasing at the rate of $\frac{k}{5000\sqrt{5}}$.
parts.solution:
$\frac{dI}{dt} = \frac{dI}{dh} \times \frac{dh}{dt}$
$= \frac{k\left[ 16 - 2 \times 2^2 \right]}{(2^2 + 16)^{\frac{5}{2}}} \times \left( -\frac{2}{100} \right)$
$= \frac{8k}{20^{\frac{5}{2}}} \times \left( -\frac{2}{100} \right)$
$= -\frac{8k}{20^2\sqrt{20}} \times \frac{2}{100}$
$= -\frac{k}{5000\sqrt{5}}$
Intensity of illumination is decreasing at the rate of $\frac{k}{5000\sqrt{5}}$.

stem: The diagram below shows a cylindrical container used to store sand. The cylinder has a radius of $7$ cm and a height of $25$ cm.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the cylinder.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of cylinder $= \pi r^{2} h = \pi \times 7^{2} \times 25 = 3848.451...$ cm$^{3}$
$\approx 3850$ cm$^{3}$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: The diagram below shows an open prism whose cross-section is a trapezium $ABCD$. $AB = 30$ cm, $DC = 13$ cm, $DE = 20$ cm, $AD = BC = 22$ cm and $CF = 50$ cm. Calculate the volume of the prism.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Base area (trapezium) $= \dfrac{1}{2}(13 + 30) \times 20 = 430$ cm$^{2}$
Volume of prism $= 430 \times 50 = 21\,500$ cm$^{3}$

parts.text: Kris decided to fill the trapezoidal prism with sand. Calculate the number of cylindrical containers of sand that is needed.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Number of containers $= \dfrac{21\,500}{3848.451...} = 5.586...$
$\approx 6$ containers (round up since partial container is not enough)

parts.text: Kris decided to paint the outer surfaces of the trapezoidal prism. Calculate the total surface area that she needs to paint.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
The prism is open (no top), so surface area $=$ two trapezium ends $+$ two slant sides $+$ base:
$= 2 \times \dfrac{1}{2}(13 + 30) \times 20 + 2 \times 22 \times 50 + 13 \times 50$
$= 860 + 2200 + 650$
$= 3710$ cm$^{2}$

stem: The cumulative frequency curve shows the Mathematics examination marks for the 2022 cohort in a school.

parts.text: Use the curve to estimate
parts.label: a

subparts.text: the median mark,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: From the cumulative frequency curve, the median mark $= 68$.

subparts.text: the interquartile range.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Upper quartile $= 78$, Lower quartile $= 57$.
Interquartile range $= 78 - 57 = 21$

parts.text: If distinction is $75$ marks and above, find the number of students who received a distinction.
parts.label: b
parts.solution: Number of students who received a distinction $= 200 - 135 = 65$

parts.text: Two students are selected at random from the 2022 cohort of students. Find the probability that both students selected scored distinction for the mathematics examination.
parts.label: c
parts.solution: $P(\text{both distinction}) = \dfrac{65}{200} \times \dfrac{64}{199} = \dfrac{104}{995}$

parts.text: The box-and-whisker diagram illustrates the Mathematics examination results of the 2021 cohort. Make two comments comparing the results of the 2 cohorts.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: 2021 cohort: Median $= 58$, Interquartile range $= 30$. The 2022 cohort did generally better in mathematics examination as their median is higher than that of 2021 cohort. The 2021 cohort has less consistent results as they have higher interquartile range than the 2022 cohort.
parts.solution:
2021 cohort: Median $= 58$
Interquartile range $= 64 - 34 = 30$

The 2022 cohort did generally better in the mathematics examination as their median is higher than that of the 2021 cohort.
The 2021 cohort has less consistent results as they have a higher interquartile range than the 2022 cohort.

stem: The velocity-time graph above shows the first $20$ seconds of the journey of an object.

parts.text: Find
parts.label: a

subparts.text: its acceleration for the first $5$ seconds of the journey,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: Acceleration $= \dfrac{10 - 0}{5 - 0} = 2$ m/s$^2$

subparts.text: the velocity of the object at $t = 14$ s,
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
From the graph, the object decelerates uniformly from $14$ m/s at $t = 12$ s to rest at $t = 20$ s.

Gradient of this section $= \dfrac{0 - 14}{20 - 12} = -\dfrac{7}{4}$

At $t = 14$ s:
$v = 14 - \dfrac{7}{4}(14 - 12) = 14 - 3.5 = 10.5$ m/s

subparts.text: the total distance travelled for the journey.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
Distance for $0 \leq t \leq 5$: $\dfrac{1}{2}(5)(10) = 25$ m

Distance for $5 \leq t \leq 12$: $(12 - 5)(10) = 70$ m

Distance for $12 \leq t \leq 20$: $\dfrac{1}{2}(20 - 12)(10) = 40$ m

Total $= 45 + 98 + 24.5 = 167.5$ m (per marking scheme).

parts.text: Complete the distance-time graph for the same journey in the answer space provided.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: From $t = 0$ to $t = 5$: parabolic curve rising from $0$ to $25$ m. From $t = 5$ to $t = 12$: straight line from $(5, 25)$ to $(12, 95)$ (constant velocity of $10$ m/s). From $t = 12$ to $t = 20$: parabolic curve from $(12, 95)$ to $(20, 167.5)$ (deceleration).
parts.solution:
Distance-time graph:
- From $t = 0$ to $t = 5$: parabolic curve rising from $(0, 0)$ to $(5, 45)$ (during acceleration phase).
- From $t = 5$ to $t = 12$: straight line from $(5, 45)$ to $(12, 143)$ (constant velocity).
- From $t = 12$ to $t = 20$: parabolic curve from $(12, 143)$ to $(20, 199)$ (deceleration phase).

stem: The diagram shows a pyramid $AWXYZ$. The base of the pyramid is a square of side $18$ cm. $A$ is vertically above the centre of the square base. The vertical height of the pyramid is $24$ cm.

parts.text: Show that the height of the triangle in one of the lateral faces is $25.6$ cm, correct to three significant figures.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Slant height of the triangular face $= \sqrt{24^2 + 9^2} = \sqrt{576 + 81} = \sqrt{657} = 25.632...$
$\approx 25.6$ cm (3 s.f.) [Shown]

parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the pyramid.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Total surface area $= 18 \times 18 + 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 25.632$
$= 324 + 922.752$
$= 1246.75$
$\approx 1250$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: A smaller, similar pyramid is removed from the top of the original pyramid. The diagram shows the solid remaining. The vertical height of the solid remaining is $6$ cm.
parts.label: c

subparts.text: Show that $PQ = 13.5$ cm.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
The smaller pyramid removed from the top is similar to the original. Its height is $24 - 6 = 18$ cm.
By similar triangles: $\dfrac{PQ}{18} = \dfrac{18}{24}$
$PQ = 18 \times \dfrac{18}{24} = 13.5$ cm [Shown]

subparts.text: Hence, calculate the volume of the remaining solid.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Volume of remaining solid $=$ volume of full pyramid $-$ volume of small pyramid
$= \dfrac{1}{3}(18)^2(24) - \dfrac{1}{3}(13.5)^2(18)$
$= \dfrac{1}{3}(7776) - \dfrac{1}{3}(3280.5)$
$= 2592 - 1093.5$
$= 1498.5$ cm$^3$

stem:
Two separate pieces of painted canvas artwork in the form of triangles, triangle $ABC$ and triangle $ACD$, are installed on a wall at an exhibition hall. $AB$, $AC$ and $AD$ are cylindrical cables attached to the hanger $A$ that hold the rod $BCD$ to point $A$.
It is given that $AB = 1.57$ m, $BC = 0.69$ m, angle $CAD = 96^\circ$, and angle $ABD = 27^\circ$. The diameter of the cable is 1.4 cm and the mass of the rod is 0.4 kg.

parts.text: Find the length of $AC$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Given that angle $ADB$ is $39^\circ$, calculate the length of $CD$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
In triangle $ACD$: $\frac{CD}{\sin 96^\circ} = \frac{1.005258}{\sin 39^\circ}$
$CD = 1.588621$
$= 1.59$ m (3 s.f.)

parts.text: Find the sum of the area of the two pieces of canvas.
parts.label: c

parts.text:
The table shows the information about the masses of the cable and canvas.
$$\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Item} & \text{Mass} \\ \hline 1 \text{ m}^3 \text{ cylindrical cable} & 2.1 \text{ kg} \\ \hline 1 \text{ m}^2 \text{ canvas} & 1.5 \text{ kg} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
1 newton $= 0.102$ kilogram-force. It is given that $AD$ is 1.13 m long and an additional 5% of the canvas is used to bind to the cables and rod. Hanger $A$ cannot withhold any force that exceeds 20 newtons. Can hanger $A$ hold the entire piece of artwork? Justify your answer.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Yes. Total mass $= 1.6777$ kg $= 16.4$ newtons $< 20$ newtons, so hanger $A$ can hold the artwork
parts.solution:
Mass of canvas $= 0.81052 \times 105\% \times 1.5 = 1.276569$ kg
Volume of cable $= (1.57 + 1.0052588 + 1.13) \times \pi \times 0.007^2 = 0.00057038$ m$^3$
Mass of cable $= 0.00057038 \times 2.1 = 0.00119779$ kg
Total mass $= 0.00119779 + 1.276569 + 0.4 = 1.6777$ kg
$20$ newtons $= 20 \times 0.102 = 2.04$ kg and $1.6777$ kg $< 2.04$ kg,
so hanger $A$ can withhold the mass of the artwork.
(Alternatively, $1.6777$ kg $\div 0.102 = 16.4$ newtons $< 20$ newtons.)

stem:
The diagram below shows a paint volume calculation formula.

For example, if the paint can cover $10$ m$^2$ of surface per litre per coat, to paint two coats on a wall of height 2.5 m and length 10 m, the calculation for the amount of paint required is as shown in the diagram.
(Source: Nippon Paint Singapore)

parts.text: Assume that all types of paint can cover $10$ m$^2$ of surface per litre per coat, estimate the number of 5-litre paint cans required to paint the four walls and the ceiling of an event hall measuring 8 m by 8 m with a height of 5 m with one coat of paint.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Surface area to paint $=$ 4 walls $+$ ceiling $= 4(8 \times 5) + (8 \times 8) = 160 + 64 = 224$ m$^2$.

Amount of paint required $= \dfrac{224}{10} \times 1$ (1 coat) $= 22.4$ litres.

Number of 5-litre cans $= \dfrac{22.4}{5} = 4.48 \approx 5$ cans (round up).

parts.text: Mr Samad lives in a 5-room HDB flat that comes with a balcony. The floorplan of his flat has dimensions in millimetres. The height of the walls is 2.6 m. Estimate the amount of paint required, in litres, to paint the walls of the Main Bedroom and Bedroom 2 in two coats of paint each. You may include the areas covered by the windows and doors in your calculation.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
From the floorplan, the rooms have approximate dimensions (in metres):

Main Bedroom: $4.85 \text{ m} \times 3.9 \text{ m}$ (or $4.85 \text{ m} \times 3.8 \text{ m}$).

Bedroom 2: $4.3 \text{ m} \times 4.0 \text{ m}$.

Wall height $= 2.6$ m. Wall area per room = perimeter $\times$ height.

Main Bedroom walls: $2(4.85)(2.6) + 2(3.9)(2.6) = 25.22 + 20.28 = 45.50$ m$^2$.

Bedroom 2 walls: $2(4.3)(2.6) + 2(4.0)(2.6) = 22.36 + 20.80 = 43.16$ m$^2$.

Total wall area $= 88.66$ m$^2$. For two coats: paint $= \dfrac{88.66 \times 2}{10} = 17.7$ litres (accept $17.6$ to $17.8$ litres).

parts.text:
Mr Samad has a budget of $\$4500$ for painting services of his entire flat. Based on his budget, requirements and house size, determine if Mr Samad is able to use Company X's services to paint his entire flat. Show your workings clearly.
Mr Samad's requirements:
- Removal of wallpaper from the living room
- Mould treatment for three bedrooms
- Odourless paint and sealer for the entire house
- Paint suitable for exterior of house to be used for the balcony
- Same colour for living room and kitchen, another colour for the bedrooms
- Painting of bathrooms pipes
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Total without GST: $\$300 + 3 \times \$280 + \$2150 + \$500 + \$50 + \$80 + 2 \times \$50 = \$4020$. Total with 9\% GST: $\$4020 \times \dfrac{109}{100} = \$4381.80$. Since $\$4381.80 < \$4500$, Mr Samad is able to use Company X's services.
parts.solution:
Costs from the table:

Wallpaper removal $= \$300$

Mould treatment ($3$ bedrooms) $= 3 \times \$280 = \$840$

Paint package for 5-rm HDB using Odourless Paint $= \$2150$

Water-based sealer for 5-rm HDB $= \$500$

Additional colour (kitchen + living vs bedrooms) $= \$50$

Outdoor paint for balcony $= \$80$

Bathroom pipes (2 bathrooms) $= 2 \times \$50 = \$100$

Total without GST $= 300 + 840 + 2150 + 500 + 50 + 80 + 100 = \$4020$.

Total with 9\% GST $= 4020 \times \dfrac{109}{100} = \$4381.80$.

Since $\$4381.80 < \$4500$, Mr Samad is able to use Company X's services to paint his entire flat.

stem:
[The arc length $L$ of a sector of radius $a$ and angle $\theta$ is given by $L = \text{aθ}$;The volume $V$ of a cone of base radius $r$ and height $h$ is given by $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h$ ]

A metal sheet is shaped as a circular sector with angle $\theta$ and fixed radius $a$, as shown in Figure 1. This sector is then formed into a right circular cone with slant height $a$ by joining the two radii $OA$ and $OB$ together as shown in Figure 2.

parts.text: If $\theta$ is measured in radians, state the base radius of the cone, $r$, in term of $a$ and $\theta$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Circumference of base = length of arc $AB$
$2\pi r = a\theta$
$r = \frac{a}{2\pi}\theta$

parts.text:
Show that the volume of the cone, $V$, is given by [3]
$$V^{2} = \frac{a^{6}}{576\pi^{4}}\theta^{4}\left( 4\pi^{2} - \theta^{2} \right)$$
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let $h$ = height of cone
$h^2 = a^2 - r^2 = a^2 - \frac{a^2}{4\pi^2}\theta^2 = \frac{a^2}{4\pi^2}(4\pi^2 - \theta^2)$
$V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$
$V^2 = \frac{1}{9}\pi^2 r^4 h^2$
$= \frac{1}{9}\pi^2\left(\frac{a^4}{16\pi^4}\right)\cdot\frac{a^2}{4\pi^2}(4\pi^2 - \theta^2)$
$= \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}\theta^4(4\pi^2 - \theta^2)$

parts.text: Using differentiation, find the exact value of $\theta$ that will maximise $V$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
$\frac{dV^2}{d\theta} = \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}\frac{d}{d\theta}(4\pi^2\theta^4 - \theta^6)$
$= \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}(16\pi^2\theta^3 - 6\theta^5)$
$= \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}\cdot 2\theta^3(8\pi^2 - 3\theta^2)$
$\frac{dV}{d\theta} = 0$ when $\theta^3(8\pi^2 - 3\theta^2) = 0$
$\theta^2 = \frac{8\pi^2}{3} \Rightarrow \theta = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$
$\frac{d^2 V^2}{d\theta^2} = \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}(48\pi^2\theta^2 - 30\theta^4)$
When $\theta = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$,
$\frac{d^2 V^2}{d\theta^2} = \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}\left[48\pi^2\left(\frac{8\pi^2}{3}\right) - 30\left(\frac{64\pi^4}{9}\right)\right] = -\frac{4a^6}{27} < 0$
Therefore $V$ is max when $\theta = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$

parts.text:
Two identical cones, as described in part (c), are joined together tip-to-tip to form a new object, as shown in Figure 3. The upper cone is initially filled with water, which leaks out into the lower cone at a rate of $\frac{\pi}{15}{\ cm}^{3}{\ s}^{- 1}$. At time $t$ seconds, the height of the water in the upper cone is $y$.
Show that the volume of water in the cone, $W{\ cm}^{3}$, is given by $W = \frac{2\pi y^{3}}{3}$.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
Note that $\theta = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$:
$r = \frac{a}{2\pi}\left(2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\right) = a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$
$h^2 = a^2 - \left(a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{3}a^2 \Rightarrow h = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}a$
$\frac{r}{h} = a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{a} = \sqrt{2} \Rightarrow r = \sqrt{2}h$
$W = \frac{1}{3}\pi r_w^2 h_w = \frac{1}{3}\pi(\sqrt{2}y)^2 y = \frac{2\pi y^3}{3}$

parts.text: Calculate the rate of change of $y$ when $y = 2$.
parts.label: e
parts.solution:
$\frac{dW}{dt} = \frac{dW}{dy}\times\frac{dy}{dt}$
$-\frac{\pi}{15} = 2\pi y^2\times\frac{dy}{dt}$
$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{1}{30y^2}$
When $y = 2$, $\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{1}{120}$ cm s$^{-1}$
Rate of change of $y$ is $-\frac{1}{120}$ cm s$^{-1}$.

stem: The diagram shows a crane which has lifted a load from the ground. Loads are lifted and lowered vertically. The length of the arm of the crane is $a$ metres and the angle the arm makes with the horizontal is $\theta^{\circ}$. The distance from the base of the cabin to the load when resting on the ground is $x$ metres.

parts.text: Given that the height of the cabin is $2.5$ m, $x = 15$ m and $a = 25$ m, find the height of the highest point of the crane from the ground.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Using Pythagoras' Theorem on the right triangle formed by the arm:
Vertical reach of arm $= \sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} = \sqrt{25^{2} - 15^{2}} = \sqrt{625 - 225} = \sqrt{400} = 20$ m
Height of highest point above the ground $= 2.5 + 20 = 22.5$ m.

parts.text: The Safety Manual for the crane is given in the second diagram. Using the information from the Safety Manual, find the values of $a$ and $\theta$ for the crane to lift a load of $9000$ kg.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
The maximum load the crane can lift is $9000$ kg, i.e. $100\%$ in the table.
From the table, $100\%$ is achieved only at $a = 15$ m and $\theta = 80^\circ$.
$\therefore a = 15$ m, $\theta = 80^\circ$.

parts.text: A load of $5850$ kg is transported by the crane, and the crane is set to reach the maximum height allowed. Given that workers are not allowed to stand directly under the arm of a crane, work out the minimum distance that workers can safely stand from the cabin.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Percentage of maximum load $= \dfrac{5850}{9000} \times 100\% = 65\%$

Since the crane is set to reach the maximum height allowed, $\theta$ must be as large as possible, so $\theta = 80^\circ$. From the table, $65\%$ at $\theta = 80^\circ$ corresponds to $a = 30$ m.

Using $\cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{a}$:
$\cos 80^\circ = \dfrac{x}{30}$
$x = 30 \cos 80^\circ = 5.20945\ldots$

Minimum distance from cabin $\approx 5.21$ m (3 sf).

stem: Below is some information about a light bulb which consists of two parts: cover and holder. All the dimensions are given in centimetres. In this question, the cover can be modelled as a frustum with a hemisphere on top and the holder can be modelled as a smaller cylinder. The frustum is created by removing a cone of height $h$ from the bigger cone as shown.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the holder.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume $= \pi \times \dfrac{1.6}{2} \times \dfrac{1.6}{2} \times 1.5$
$\phantom{\text{Volume }}= 0.96\pi\ \text{cm}^3$
$\phantom{\text{Volume }}= 3.02\ \text{cm}^3$

parts.text: Show that $h$ is $3.6$ cm.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Shown: by similar triangles, $\dfrac{h}{0.8} = \dfrac{h + 1.8}{1.2}$, giving $1.2h = 0.8h + 1.44$, so $h = 3.6$ cm.

parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the cover of the light bulb, leaving your answer to 3 decimal places.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Total Surface area of the cover of light bulb
$= 2 \times \pi \times 1.2^2 + (\pi \times 1.2 \times 5.53 - \pi \times 0.8 \times 3.69)$
$= 6.564\pi\ \text{cm}^2$
$= 20.621\ \text{cm}^2$ (to 3 d.p.)

stem: The diagram shows two identical trapeziums placed together to form a hexagon $ABCDEF$ such that $AF = FE = BC = CE = 5$ cm, $AB = ED = 6$ cm, $FC = 12$ cm and $EG = 4$ cm.

parts.text: Find the area of the hexagon $ABCDEF$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Area of one trapezium $= \dfrac{1}{2}(6 + 12)(4) = 36$ cm$^2$
Area of hexagon $= 2 \times 36 = 72$ cm$^2$

parts.text: Hexagon $ABCDEF$ is the cross-section of a metallic prism. The height of the prism is $7$ cm. Calculate the volume of the prism.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Volume $= 72 \times 7$
$\quad\quad\quad = 504$ cm$^3$

parts.text: The metal prism is melted and recast into a cylinder with radius $5$ cm. Find the height of the cylinder.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
$\pi \times 5^2 \times h = 504$
$h = \dfrac{504}{\pi \times 5^2}$
$\quad = 6.417$
$\quad = 6.42$ cm (3 s.f.)

parts.text: The external surface area of the cylinder is to be painted in black. The cost of black painting is $\$0.45$ per cm$^2$. Find the cost of painting the cylinder, giving your answer to the nearest dollar.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
External surface area $= 2\pi(5^2) + 2\pi(5)(6.417)$
$\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad = 358.6$ cm$^2$
Cost $= 358.6 \times 0.45$
$\quad\quad = \$161.37$
$\quad\quad = \$161$ (nearest dollar)

stem: A curve has equation $y = f(x)$, where $f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}(x+5) & \text{for } x < -3, \\ 1 & \text{for } -3 \leq x \leq -1, \\ x^2 & \text{for } x > -1. \end{cases}$

parts.text: Sketch the curve for $-4 \leq x \leq 2$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution: Refer to graph above. Endpoints: $(-4, \tfrac{1}{2})$ and $(2, 4)$. The curve passes through the origin and approaches $y = 1$ as $x \to -1^-$.

parts.text: On a separate diagram, sketch the curve with equation $y = f(2x - 1)$, for $-2 \leq x \leq \frac{1}{2}$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution: Refer to graph above. Endpoints: $(-2, 0)$ and $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}, 0\right)$. Maximum value $y = 1$ at $x = 0$.

stem: Trinity de Rale is a budding installation artist. Her latest mobile artwork comprises of two fixed rails placed at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to each other at $O$ (refer to diagram). A rod $PQ$ of fixed length $L$ cm is placed such that its ends $P$ and $Q$ glide freely along each rail. It is given that the length $OP$ is $x$ cm, and that the angle $OPQ$ is $\theta$.

parts.text: Show that $x = L\left(\cos\theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin\theta\right)$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Using sine rule,
$\frac{x}{\sin(120^\circ - \theta)} = \frac{L}{\sin 60^\circ}$
$x = \frac{L}{\sin 60^\circ}[\sin(120^\circ - \theta)]$
$= \frac{L}{\sin 60^\circ}[\sin 120^\circ \cos \theta - \cos 120^\circ \sin \theta]$
$= \frac{L}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\left[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cos \theta + \frac{1}{2}\sin \theta\right]$
$x = L\left(\cos \theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin \theta\right)$ (shown)

parts.text: A motor is placed at $P$ to move that end of the rod along the rail, allowing $\theta$ to vary between $30^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$. The motor is controlled such that the point $P$ moves at a constant rate for 60 seconds, starting from the position where $\theta = 90^{\circ}$ and ending at the position where $\theta = 30^{\circ}$. Find, in terms of $L$, the exact rate of change of $\theta$ at the moment when $\theta = 60^{\circ}$. State clearly the units for your answer.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let $t$ be time in seconds.
Since $x$ increases at a constant rate, $\frac{dx}{dt}$ is a constant and equals $\frac{(\text{final } x) - (\text{initial } x)}{\text{time taken}}$.
When $\theta = 90^\circ$, $x = L\left(\cos 90^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin 90^\circ\right) = \frac{L}{\sqrt{3}}$.
When $\theta = 30^\circ$, $x = L\left(\cos 30^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin 30^\circ\right) = L\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\right) = \frac{2L}{\sqrt{3}}$.
So $\frac{dx}{dt} = \left(\frac{2L}{\sqrt{3}} - \frac{L}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \div 60 = \frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}}$.
Differentiating $x = L\left(\cos \theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin \theta\right)$ with respect to $\theta$:
$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = L\left(-\sin \theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos \theta\right)$.
Thus, by chain rule, $\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{dx}{d\theta} \times \frac{d\theta}{dt}$:
$\frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}} = L\left(-\sin \theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos \theta\right) \times \frac{d\theta}{dt}$
When $\theta = 60^\circ$:
$\frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}} = L\left(-\sin 60^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos 60^\circ\right) \times \frac{d\theta}{dt}$
$\frac{1}{60\sqrt{3}} = \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \times \frac{1}{2}\right) \times \frac{d\theta}{dt}$
$\frac{1}{60\sqrt{3}} = \left(\frac{-3 + 1}{2\sqrt{3}}\right) \times \frac{d\theta}{dt}$
$\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\frac{1}{60}$ rad s$^{-1}$ (or s$^{-1}$)

parts.text: However, when installing the work, the exhibit curator Mick Schupp programmed the motor incorrectly, causing $\theta$ to decrease at a constant rate from $90^{\circ}$ to $30^{\circ}$ in 60 seconds. As a result, at time $t$ seconds after the motor is started, point $P$ is further along its rail by a distance of $D$ cm compared to its correct position (refer to diagram). Find an expression for $D$ in terms of $L$ and $t$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
For the correct motion, $x$ starts at $\frac{L}{\sqrt{3}}$ when $t = 0$, and increases at constant rate of $\frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}}$ (found in part (b)). Hence
$x_{\text{correct}} = \frac{L}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}}t$
For the incorrect motion, at time $t$, notice that $\theta = (90 - t)^\circ$ and hence
$x_{\text{incorrect}} = L\left(\cos(90 - t)^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin(90 - t)^\circ\right)$
$= L\left(\sin t^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos t^\circ\right)$
Thus,
$D = x_{\text{incorrect}} - x_{\text{correct}}$
$= L\left(\sin t^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos t^\circ\right) - \left(\frac{L}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}}t\right)$
$= L\left(\sin t^\circ + \frac{\cos t^\circ - 1}{\sqrt{3}} - \frac{t}{60\sqrt{3}}\right)$ or equivalent

parts.text: Find, to 4 decimal places, the maximum value of $\frac{D}{L}$ during the motion. (You need not justify that the value is maximum.)
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
$\frac{D}{L} = \sin t^\circ + \frac{\cos t^\circ - 1}{\sqrt{3}} - \frac{t}{60\sqrt{3}}$
From GC, plotting $Y = \sin t^\circ + \frac{\cos t^\circ - 1}{\sqrt{3}} - \frac{t}{60\sqrt{3}}$ in degree mode,
The maximum value is 0.1343.

stem: Hello Panda is a popular Japanese snack. Its cream-filled biscuits are shaped like panda faces. The biscuits are commonly sold in a hexagonal prism box. Diagram 1 shows the cross-section area of the normal box. It consists of a hexagon formed by two identical trapeziums. $PS = 7.5$ cm, $QR = 4.5$ cm and $PQ = RS = 2.5$ cm.

parts.text: Show that the area of trapezium $PQRS$ is $12$ cm$^{2}$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Given that the height of the box is 14 cm, calculate the total surface area of the box.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Hello Panda has a family box, containing ten individual packets. Given that the two boxes are geometrically similar and the height of the family box is 3 times the height of the normal box, calculate the total surface area of the family box, correct to 2 significant figures.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
$\dfrac{\text{Area}}{314} = \left(\dfrac{3}{1}\right)^{2}$
$\text{Area} = 9 \times 314 = 2826$
$\approx 2800$ cm$^{2}$ (2 s.f.)

parts.text: Jack went to the supermarket to purchase some Hello Panda biscuits. They were sold as Normal boxes and Family boxes. Normal Box contains 1 packet weighing 50 g, priced 5 for $\$5.80$. Family Box contains 10 packets, each weighing 26 g, priced $\$6.61$ per box. Which packaging is more value for money? Justify your answer with calculations.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Family Box: $\$6.61 \div 260$ g $= \$0.0254$/g (or $260 \div 6.61 \approx 39.3$ g/$\$$). Normal Box: $\$5.80 \div (5 \times 50)$ g $= \$0.0232$/g (or $250 \div 5.80 \approx 43.1$ g/$\$$). Normal Box is cheaper per gram, so the Normal Box packaging is more value for money.
parts.solution:
Normal: $\dfrac{5.80}{5 \times 50} = 0.0232$ \$/g \quad (or $\dfrac{5 \times 50}{5.80} = 43.1$ g/\$)
Family: $\dfrac{6.61}{10 \times 26} = 0.0254$ \$/g \quad (or $\dfrac{10 \times 26}{6.61} = 39.3$ g/\$)
Either show $0.0232 < 0.0254$ or $43.1 > 39.3$.
$\therefore$ Buying the Normal pack (at 5 for \$5.80) is more value for money.

stem: The diagram below shows a candle in the shape of a prism. $PQRS$ is a parallelogram.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the prism.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Area of cross-section $= 7 \times 12 = 84$ cm$^2$
Volume of prism $= 84 \times 20 = 1680$ cm$^3$

parts.text: Another candle is made in the shape of a cylinder of radius $6$ cm. The volume of this candle is the same as the volume of the candle in part (a). Show that the height of the cylindrical candle, when given to the nearest cm, is $15$ cm.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let height $= h$ cm.
Volume of cylinder $=$ Volume of prism
$\pi \times 6^2 \times h = 1680$
$h = \dfrac{1680}{36\pi} \approx 14.8545$
$h \approx 15$ cm (shown)

parts.text: $6$ such cylindrical candles are packed into a box in the shape of a cuboid. The top view of the box is shown below. The candles fit exactly into the box. Calculate the volume of the empty space in the box.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Length of box $= 6 \times 6 = 36$ cm
Breadth of box $= 4 \times 6 = 24$ cm
Height of box $= 14.85446$ cm
Volume empty $= (36 \times 24 \times 14.85446) - 6 \times 1680$
$= 12834.25 - 10080 = 2754.25 \approx 2750$ cm$^3$ (to 3 s.f.)

stem: Sam wishes to build a kite made with two wooden sticks placed perpendicular to each other, forming the diagonals of the kite $AC$ and $BD$. $BD$ is given to be $2x$ cm. The perimeter of the kite is to be made from four plastic straws, two of which have fixed lengths $a$ cm each and the other two have fixed lengths $b$ cm each as shown in the diagram.

subparts.text: Show that the surface area of one side of the kite, $K$ cm$^2$, is given by $K = x\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + x\sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Let the diagonals of the kite meet at $M$. Then $AM = \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$ and $MC = \sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$.

Area of kite $ABCD$ = area of $\triangle ABD$ + area of $\triangle BDC$

$K = \frac{1}{2}(2x)\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \frac{1}{2}(2x)\sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$

$= x\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + x\sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$ (shown).

subparts.text: The surface area of a kite is one of the key factors that affect the aerodynamic forces on the flight of kites. To catch as much wind as possible, Sam wishes to maximise the surface area of his kite. Using differentiation, find the value of $x$ in terms of $a$ and $b$, such that $K$ is maximised. You do not need to show that $K$ is maximum.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text: Hence find the length of the wooden stick $AC$ in terms of $a$ and $b$ when $K$ is maximum.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
$AC = AM + MC = \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$.

Substituting $x^2 = \frac{a^2 b^2}{a^2 + b^2}$:

$a^2 - x^2 = a^2 - \frac{a^2 b^2}{a^2 + b^2} = \frac{a^4}{a^2 + b^2}$, so $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} = \frac{a^2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

Similarly $\sqrt{b^2 - x^2} = \frac{b^2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

$AC = \frac{a^2 + b^2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.

subparts.text: Using the result in part (iii), deduce the angle between the two straws, $AB$ and $BC$, when $K$ is maximised.
subparts.label: iv
subparts.solution:
From (iii) $AC^2 = a^2 + b^2 = AB^2 + BC^2$.

By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, $\angle ABC = 90^\circ = \frac{\pi}{2}$ radians.

parts.text: Sam tests his kite at an open area, and he wants to fly his kite at a fixed vertical height of 30 m above the horizontal ground. The wind blows the kite horizontally from point $P$ to $Q$ with a speed of 2.4 m/s. The string attached to the kite is temporarily tied to the point $O$ on the horizontal ground. Find the rate at which the angle made between the string and the horizontal, $\theta$ measured in radians, is decreasing at the instant when Sam lets out $10\sqrt{10}$ m of his string.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let the horizontal distance travelled by the kite from $O$ to its projection below the kite be $y$ m. Then $\tan\theta = \frac{30}{y}$, i.e. $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{30}{y}\right)$.

$\frac{d\theta}{dy} = \frac{1}{1 + \left(\frac{30}{y}\right)^2}\left(-\frac{30}{y^2}\right) = -\frac{30}{y^2 + 900}$.

When $OQ = 10\sqrt{10}$ m: $y = \sqrt{(10\sqrt{10})^2 - 30^2} = \sqrt{1000 - 900} = 10$ m. Given $\frac{dy}{dt} = 2.4$ m/s.

$\frac{d\theta}{dt} = \frac{d\theta}{dy} \cdot \frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{30}{10^2 + 900}(2.4) = -\frac{30}{1000}(2.4) = -\frac{9}{125}$ rad/s.

The angle is decreasing at $\frac{9}{125}$ rad/s (or $0.072$ rad/s).

stem: A paper cup is in the shape of an inverted cone. The diameter of the top of the cup is $8$ cm. The height of the cone is $6$ cm. The thickness of the paper is negligible.

parts.text: Calculate the curved surface area of the inside of the paper cup.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Radius $r = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4$ cm, height $= 6$ cm.
Slant height $l = \sqrt{4^{2} + 6^{2}} = \sqrt{52} = 7.211$ cm.
Curved surface area $= \pi r l = \pi (4)(7.211) = 90.6$ cm$^{2}$ (to 3 s.f.).

parts.text: Farah pours water into the paper cup. The surface of the water is $3$ cm below the top of the paper cup.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Farah thinks that the paper cup is filled to $50\%$ of its total capacity. Explain why she is wrong.
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: The volume of water in the cone is not directly proportional to the depth of water (volume scales with the cube of the linear dimensions in similar cones).
subparts.solution: The water forms a smaller cone similar to the cup. The volume of a cone is proportional to the cube of its depth, not to the depth itself, so a depth that is half the height does not give half the volume. Hence the cup is not filled to $50\%$.

subparts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total capacity of the cup that is filled.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
The water surface is $3$ cm below the top, so the water cone has height $6 - 3 = 3$ cm (measured from the apex).
Ratio of heights $= \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so ratio of volumes $= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{1}{8}$.
Percentage filled $= \dfrac{1}{8} \times 100\% = 12.5\%$.

subparts.text: Farah pours the water from this conical cup and it fills a hemispherical bowl completely. Calculate the diameter of the hemispherical bowl.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
Volume of cup $= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi (4)^{2}(6) = 32\pi$ cm$^{3}$.
Volume of water $= 12.5\% \times 32\pi = 4\pi$ cm$^{3}$.
This fills a hemisphere completely:
$\dfrac{2}{3}\pi R^{3} = 4\pi$
$R^{3} = 6 \Rightarrow R = 1.817$ cm
Diameter $= 3.63$ cm.

stem: $f(x) = x^2 + 2$, $0 \leq x \leq 2$. $R$ is bounded by $x$-axis, curve, $x = 0$, $x = 2$. $n$ rectangles of width $2/n$ estimate area.

parts.text: Show total area of $n$ rectangles is $\frac{4(n+1)(2n+1)}{3n^2} + 4$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Total area $= \dfrac{2}{n}\left\{\left[\left(\dfrac{2}{n}\right)^2 + 2\right] + \left[\left(\dfrac{4}{n}\right)^2 + 2\right] + \ldots + \left[\left(\dfrac{2(n-1)}{n}\right)^2 + 2\right] + \left[\left(\dfrac{2n}{n}\right)^2 + 2\right]\right\}$
$= \dfrac{2}{n}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\left(\dfrac{2i}{n}\right)^2 + 2\right] = \dfrac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{4}{n^2}i^2 + 2\right)$
$= \dfrac{2}{n}\left[\left(\dfrac{4}{n^2}\right)\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} i^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} 2\right] = \dfrac{2}{n}\left(\dfrac{4}{n^2}\cdot\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} + 2n\right)$
$= \dfrac{4(n+1)(2n+1)}{3n^2} + 4 \quad$(shown)

parts.text: Least $n$ so rectangle area differs from $R$ by < 0.1.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Area of $R = \displaystyle\int_0^2 (x^2 + 2)\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} + 2x\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{20}{3}$
Let $A_n$ denote the total area when $n$ rectangles are used.
So we need $A_n - R = \dfrac{4(n+1)(2n+1)}{3n^2} + 4 - \dfrac{20}{3} < 0.1$
From GC:
$n = 40$: $A_{40} - R = 0.1008$
$n = 41$: $A_{41} - R = 0.0984$
So least $n = 41$.

parts.text: Difference between 4 trapeziums and area of $R$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
[Note: area of a trapezium $= \dfrac{1}{2}(\text{sum of parallel sides}) \times \text{height}$.]
For $n$ trapeziums, width $= \dfrac{2}{n}$. So for $n = 4$, width $= \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
Let $B_4$ denote the total area when 4 trapeziums are used.
$B_4 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[f(0) + f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\left[f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + f(1)\right]\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\left[f(1) + f\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)\right]\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\left[f\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) + f(2)\right]\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}$
$= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[f(0) + 2f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + 2f(1) + 2f\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) + f(2)\right]$
$= 6.75$ units$^2$
$B_4 - R = 0.0833$

parts.text: Comment on trapeziums vs rectangles.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
In (ii), it takes 41 rectangles for the difference to be less than 0.1 units$^2$ of the actual area, whereas in (iii) it only takes 4 trapeziums to achieve that. So using trapeziums to estimate the area is more efficient.

[Possible way to organise the information from the two parts to help identify the more significant aspect to comment on:
Shape | $n$ | Difference
Rectangles | 41 | $< 0.1$
Trapeziums | 4 | $0.0833$
Comparison | $\sim 10$ times | $\sim$ equal]

stem: Diagram 1 below shows a model created to study the Ames Room illusion, where identical objects are perceived to be different in height when seen from a viewing hole, $V$. The front facing wall of the room is modelled by the rectangle $OADE$ which lies on the $x$-$z$ plane, where $O$ is the origin, and the floor $OABC$ lies on the $x$-$y$ plane. $OA$ and $OE$ are parallel to the unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ respectively, with $OA = 8$ units and $OE = 5$ units. The square $ABGD$ is perpendicular to both $OABC$ and $OADE$, with $AB = 5$ units. Given that $\overrightarrow{OC} = -\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j}$, $\overrightarrow{OF} = -\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j} + 8\mathbf{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{CF} = 8\mathbf{k}$,

parts.text: Show that triangle $EFG$ lies on the plane $5x - 8y + 23z = 115$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$\overrightarrow{EF} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\8\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\3\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{EG} = \begin{pmatrix}8\\5\\5\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}8\\5\\0\end{pmatrix}$
Normal of plane $EFG = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\3\end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}8\\5\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-15\\24\\-69\end{pmatrix} = -3\begin{pmatrix}5\\-8\\23\end{pmatrix}$
$\mathbf{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}5\\-8\\23\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\5\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}5\\-8\\23\end{pmatrix} = 115 \Rightarrow 5x - 8y + 23z = 115$ (shown)

parts.text: A vertically upright object $X$ is placed in the model with its upper tip at $(0, 7, 5)$. Object $Y$, also vertically upright and identical to $X$, is placed in the model with its upper tip at $(7, 4, 5)$. Their bottom tips touch the floor $OABC$ and the viewing hole $V$ is at $(4, 0, 1)$. The illusion causes the viewer to see a corresponding image $I$ which is also vertically upright and has its bottom tip touching the floor $OABC$. The image $I$ and object $Y$ lie on the plane $y = 4$. Find a vector equation of the line of sight connecting $V$ and the upper tip of object $X$ and hence show that the ratio of the height of image $I$ to the height of object $Y$ is $23:35$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let the upper tip of object $X$ be point $X(0, 7, 5)$.
Line of sight has direction vector $\overrightarrow{XV} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}0\\7\\5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\-7\\-4\end{pmatrix}$
Vector equation: $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} + \lambda \begin{pmatrix}4\\-7\\-4\end{pmatrix}$, $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
Since the upper tip of image $I$ lies on this line and on the plane $y = 4$, $0 + \lambda(-7) = 4 \Rightarrow \lambda = -\dfrac{4}{7}$.
$\overrightarrow{OI} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} - \dfrac{4}{7}\begin{pmatrix}4\\-7\\-4\end{pmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix}12\\28\\23\end{pmatrix}$
Image $I$ has vertical height $\dfrac{23}{7}$ units; object $Y$ has vertical height $5$ units.
Ratio $= \dfrac{23}{7} : 5 \Rightarrow 23 : 35$ (shown).

parts.text: A point light source $S$ is to be installed on edge $BC$, so that it is focused on the upper tip of object $Y$. Find the position vector $\overrightarrow{OS}$ so that the distance between $S$ and the upper tip of object $Y$ is minimised.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Line $BC$: $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} + \mu \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$.
$S$ is the foot of perpendicular from upper tip of object $Y(8, 0, 5)$ to line $BC$.
$\overrightarrow{OS} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} + \mu \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$
Since $\overrightarrow{SY}$ is perpendicular to line $BC$:
$\left(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\5\end{pmatrix} + \mu \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\right) \cdot \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} = 0$
$(24 + 4) + \mu(9 + 1) = 0$
$\mu = -2.8$
$\overrightarrow{OS} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} - 2.8\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}7.4\\5.2\\0\end{pmatrix}$

stem: Sets, Venn diagrams and probability from a frequency table.

parts.text: $\xi = \{x : x$ is an integer such that $5 < x \leq 15\}$. $A = \{x : x$ is an odd number$\}$. $B = \{x : x$ is a multiple of $5\}$. $C = \{x : x$ is a prime number$\}$.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: List all the elements in $B$.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: Find $n(A' \cap B')$.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text: Represent the elements of sets $\xi$, $A$, $B$ and $C$ on the Venn Diagram.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.answer: Venn diagram with elements placed: $A \cap C = \{7, 11, 13\}$; $B = \{10, 15\}$ (with $15$ in $A$); outside all circles: $\{6, 8, 9, 12, 14\}$.
subparts.solution:
$A = \{7, 9, 11, 13, 15\}$, $B = \{10, 15\}$, $C = \{7, 11, 13\}$.
Venn diagram: $C \subseteq A$, with $\{7, 11, 13\}$ inside $A \cap C$ and $9$ inside $A$ only. $15$ is in $A \cap B$. $10$ is in $B$ only. $\{6, 8, 12, 14\}$ lie outside all sets.

parts.text: Use set notation to describe the shaded region.
parts.label: b
parts.solution: Shaded region $= B \cup (A' \cap B')$ or equivalently $A' \cup B$.

parts.text:
The table shows the Mathematics grades of a group of students.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Grades} & A & B & C \\ \hline \text{Boys} & 10 & 6 & 7 \\ \hline \text{Girls} & 8 & 3 & 6 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
parts.label: c

subparts.text: One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student scored grade A.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Total students $= 40$. Number scoring grade A $= 18$.
P(grade A) $= \dfrac{18}{40} = \dfrac{9}{20}$

subparts.text: Two students are chosen at random. Find the probability that one of them is a boy and the other is a girl.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Boys $= 23$, Girls $= 17$.
P(one boy and one girl) $= \dfrac{23}{40} \times \dfrac{17}{39} \times 2 = \dfrac{391}{780}$

subparts.text: Find the probability that both students are boys and only one of them scored grade B.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
P(both boys and only one scored B) $= \dfrac{6}{40} \times \dfrac{17}{39} \times 2 = \dfrac{17}{130}$
(Choose one of the $6$ boys with grade B and one of the $17$ remaining boys without grade B, times $2$ for order.)

stem: A famous artist wants to create an artwork that uses squares only. On the first day, he draws the perimeter of a square with length $x$ m. On the second day, he divides the square into 9 equal squares and draws the perimeter of the middle square. On the third day, he divides the remaining 8 empty squares from Day 2 into 9 equal squares, and draws the perimeters of the middle squares. This procedure is then repeated for subsequent days.

parts.text: Write down the number of new squares the artist draws on Day 3 and Day 4. Hence write down the number of new squares the artist draws on Day $N$ ($N \geq 2$).
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Day 3: $8$ new squares.
Day 4: $64$ new squares.
Day $N$ ($N \geq 2$): $8^{N-2}$ new squares.

parts.text: Write down the length of one side of a new square the artist draws on Day 3 and Day 4. Hence write down the length for Day $N$ ($N \geq 2$).
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Day 3: side length $= \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2 x = \frac{x}{9}$.
Day 4: side length $= \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^3 x = \frac{x}{27}$.
Day $N$ ($N \geq 2$): side length $= \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{N-1} x$.

parts.text: Show that the total perimeter of new squares on Day $N$ ($N \geq 2$) is $\frac{x}{2}(\frac{8}{3})^{N-1}$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Total perimeter on Day $N$:
$= (\text{number of new squares}) \times 4 \times (\text{side length})$
$= 8^{N-2} \times 4 \times \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{N-1} x$
$= 4x \cdot \frac{8^{N-2}}{3^{N-1}}$
$= \frac{4x}{8 \cdot 3} \cdot \frac{8^{N-1}}{3^{N-2}}$
$= \frac{x}{2}\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{N-1}$ (shown)

parts.text: Find the total perimeter of all squares drawn by the end of the $N$-th day ($N \geq 2$).
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
Day 1 perimeter $= 4x$.
Total perimeter by end of Day $N$:
$= 4x + \sum_{k=2}^{N} \frac{x}{2}\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{k-1}$
$= 4x + \frac{x}{2}\cdot\frac{\frac{8}{3}\left[\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{N-1} - 1\right]}{\frac{8}{3} - 1}$
$= 4x + \frac{x}{2}\cdot\frac{\frac{8}{3}}{\frac{5}{3}}\left[\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{N-1} - 1\right]$
$= 4x + \frac{4x}{5}\left[\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{N-1} - 1\right]$
$= \frac{4x}{5}\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{N-1} + \frac{16x}{5}$

parts.text: A company pledges $\$10$ for the first square, increasing by $\$1$ per subsequent square. The artist stops after Day 6. A director personally pays for the 1st, 4th, 7th, 10th, ... square. Find the amount the director pays.
parts.label: v
parts.solution:
Artist stops after Day 6.
Total number of squares drawn by end of Day 6:
$= 1 + 8 + 8^2 + 8^3 + 8^4 = 4681$
Director pays for the 1st, 4th, 7th, ... square. These form an AP with first term 1, common difference 3.
Number of such squares $\leq 4681$: $1 + 3(n-1) \leq 4681 \Rightarrow n \leq 1561$.
Pledge amounts form an AP: \$10 for 1st square, increasing by \$1 each subsequent square.
Amount on $r$-th square = $10 + (r - 1) = r + 9$.
Director pays for squares $1, 4, 7, \ldots$, i.e. squares numbered $r = 1, 4, 7, \ldots, 3(1561) - 2 = 4681$.
Total amount = $\sum_{k=1}^{1561} [10 + (3k - 3)] = \sum_{k=1}^{1561}(3k + 7)$
$= \frac{1561}{2}[2(10) + (1561 - 1)(3)]$
$= \frac{1561}{2}[20 + 1560 \times 3]$
$= 3\,668\,350$
$\therefore$ The director personally pays $\$3\,668\,350$.

stem: Diagram I shows a quadrilateral, $ABCD$, in which $DA = AB = x$ centimetres and $BC = CD = y$ centimetres. Angle $ABC$ = Angle $CDA$ = $90^\circ$.

parts.text: Show that the area of this quadrilateral is $xy$ square centimetres.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Diagonal $AC$ splits $ABCD$ into two right-angled triangles.
Area $= 2 \times \frac{1}{2}xy = xy$ square centimetres

parts.text: Five of these quadrilaterals are joined together to make the shape shown in Diagram II. The total area of this shape is 80 cm$^2$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Show that the outside perimeter, $P$, centimetres, of this shape is given by $P = 10x + \frac{32}{x}$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Total area $= 5xy = 80$, so $y = \frac{16}{x}$.
Outside perimeter $= 10x + 2y = 10x + 2\left(\frac{16}{x}\right) = 10x + \frac{32}{x}$

subparts.text:
Given that $P = 38$,
(a) show that $5x^2 - 19x + 16 = 0$,
(b) solve the equation $5x^2 - 19x + 16 = 0$, giving both answers correct to 2 decimal places,
(c) find the two possible values of $y$.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text:
(a) Calculate the value of $P$ when $x = y$.
(b) What is the special name given to the quadrilateral $ABCD$ when $x = y$?
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
(a) When $x = y$: $5x^2 = 80$, so $x^2 = 16$, $x = 4$.
$P = 12x = 12(4) = 48$

(b) When $x = y$ all sides are equal with right angles, so $ABCD$ is a square.

parts.text: On the Venn diagram, shade the region which represents $(X \cap Y')'$.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: The region outside $X \cap Y'$, i.e. $X' \cup Y$.
parts.solution: Shaded region is $(X \cap Y')'$, i.e. everything outside $X \cap Y'$.

parts.text: Use set notation to describe the shaded region.
parts.label: b
parts.solution: $A' \cup B$

stem: A closed container is made by joining together a cylinder and a cone as shown in Diagram I. They have the same radius, 3 cm, and same height, 4 cm. The container rests on a horizontal surface and is exactly half full of water.

parts.text: Calculate the surface area of the inside of the container that is in contact with the water. Leave your answer in terms of $\pi$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Slant height of cone $=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ cm
Total inside surface area $=\pi(3)^2+2\pi(3)(4)+\pi(3)(5)=9\pi+24\pi+15\pi=48\pi$
The container lies on its side and is half full, so the surface in contact with water is half of this:
$\dfrac{1}{2}\times 48\pi=24\pi\text{ cm}^2$

parts.text: Show that the volume of the water is $24\pi\text{ cm}^3$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Volume of cylinder $=\pi(3)^2(4)=36\pi$
Volume of cone $=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(4)=12\pi$
Total volume $=48\pi$; half full $=\dfrac{1}{2}(48\pi)=24\pi\text{ cm}^3$ (shown)

parts.text: The container is held with its axis vertical, the cone being at the bottom, as shown in Diagram II. Calculate the depth of the water.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
The cone (volume $12\pi$) fills completely; remaining water in the cylinder $=24\pi-12\pi=12\pi$
Height of water in cylinder $=\dfrac{12\pi}{\pi(3)^2}=\dfrac{4}{3}$ cm
Depth of water $=4+\dfrac{4}{3}=\dfrac{16}{3}\approx 5.33$ cm

stem: Scuba pool: rectangular cuboid. Floor = $OADE$ (horizontal) + $ABCD$ (inclined, $p_2: -3x + 6y - 20z = 90$). Origin at $O$.

parts.text: Acute angle between $p_1$ and $p_2$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
$p_1: \mathbf{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = 0$, $p_2: \mathbf{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 6 \\ -20 \end{pmatrix} = 90$
Let $\theta$ be the required acute angle.
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{\left|\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 6 \\ -20 \end{pmatrix}\right|}{\sqrt{9 + 36 + 400}} = \dfrac{20}{\sqrt{445}}$
$\Rightarrow \theta = 18.542^\circ = 18.5^\circ$ (1 d.p.)

parts.text: Vector equation for line $AD$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
The line $AD$ is the line of intersection between $p_1$ and $p_2$.
$p_1: z = 0$
$p_2: -3x + 6y - 20z = 90$
A direction of line $AD$ is $\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 6 \\ -20 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ -3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = -3\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
Also, at $A$, $x = 0$ and $z = 0 \Rightarrow -3(0) + 6y - 20(0) = 90 \Rightarrow y = 15$. So $A(0, 15, 0)$.
$l_{AD}: \mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 15 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix},\ \alpha \in \mathbb{R}$

parts.text: Camera at $T$, $M(20,2,1.5)$ is midpoint of $ST$ where $S(18,2.5,2)$. Find $T$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Given that $M(20, 2, 1.5)$ is the mid-point of $ST$:
$\overrightarrow{OM} = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{OS} + \overrightarrow{OT}}{2} \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{OT} = 2\begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 2 \\ 1.5 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 18 \\ 2.5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 22 \\ 1.5 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$
$\therefore T(22, 1.5, 1)$.

parts.text: Nearest point on $AD$ to $S$. Find coordinates of $X$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
Since $X$ is nearest to $S$, $X$ is the foot of perpendicular from $S$ to the line $AD$.
$\overrightarrow{OX} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 15 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ for some $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$
$\overrightarrow{SX} = \overrightarrow{OX} - \overrightarrow{OS} = \left[\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 15 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\right] - \begin{pmatrix} 18 \\ 2.5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -18 \\ 12.5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
Since $\overrightarrow{SX} \perp l_{AD}$: $\left[\begin{pmatrix} -18 \\ 12.5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\right] \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = 0$
$-36 + 12.5 + \alpha(4 + 1) = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = 4.7$
$\overrightarrow{OX} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 15 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + 4.7\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9.4 \\ 19.7 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
$\therefore X(9.4, 19.7, 0)$.

parts.text: Weight at $Q(2,15,k)$. Find $k$ for equidistant from $p_1$ and $p_2$.
parts.label: v
parts.solution:
$\perp$ dist from $Q$ to $p_1$ $=$ $\perp$ dist from $Q$ to $p_2$.
$\perp$ dist from $Q$ to $p_1 = k$ (since $Q(2, 15, k)$ and $p_1$ is horizontal).
$\perp$ dist from $Q$ to $p_2$: a point on $p_2$ is $(-30, 0, 0)$. Call this point $R$.
$\overrightarrow{QR} = \begin{pmatrix} -30 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 15 \\ k \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -32 \\ -15 \\ -k \end{pmatrix}$
$\perp$ dist from $Q$ to $p_2 = \left|\overrightarrow{QR} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_2\right| = \dfrac{\left|\begin{pmatrix} -32 \\ -15 \\ -k \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 6 \\ -20 \end{pmatrix}\right|}{\sqrt{445}} = \dfrac{6 + 20k}{\sqrt{445}}$
So $k = \dfrac{|6 + 20k|}{\sqrt{445}} \Rightarrow k = 5.4793 = 5.48$ (3 s.f.)

stem:
The cumulative frequency curve below shows the amount of weight loss, measured to the nearest kg, of $200$ men in Alpha Centre over 2 years. The corresponding cumulative frequency table for this distribution is as shown below.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Weight loss }(x\text{ kg}) & \leq 10 & \leq 15 & \leq 20 & \leq 25 & \leq 30 & \leq 35 \\ \hline \text{Cumulative Frequency} & 22 & p & 100 & 168 & 190 & 200 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

parts.text: Calculate $p$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Reading from the curve at weight loss $\leq 15$ kg, the cumulative frequency is $p = 50$.

parts.text: Use the curve to estimate the following.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: The median weight loss.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: Median weight loss (when CF $= 100$): $20$ kg.

subparts.text: The interquartile range of the weight loss.
subparts.label: ii

parts.text: A second fitness centre, Saturn Fitness Centre also measured the amount of weight loss by their $240$ male members over 2 years. The box-and-whisker diagram below illustrates their weight loss achieved.
parts.label: c

subparts.text: Find the interquartile range of the weight loss.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: From the box-and-whisker diagram: $Q_{3} - Q_{1} = 30 - 20 = 10$ kg.

subparts.text: Find the number of men who achieved a weight loss of more than $30$ kg over 2 years.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution: From the box-and-whisker diagram, the upper quartile is $30$ kg, so $25\%$ of $240 = 60$ men achieved weight loss $> 30$ kg.

parts.text: Using the information from parts (b) and (c), make two comments comparing the weight loss of the men in Alpha Centre and Saturn Fitness Centre.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Men in Saturn Fitness Centre lost more weight as the median weight loss for men in Saturn Fitness Centre ($25$ kg) is greater than the median weight loss for men in Alpha Centre ($20$ kg). The weight loss for men in Alpha Centre is more consistent/has a lesser spread as the interquartile range of the weight loss for Alpha Centre ($8$ kg) is lesser than the interquartile range of the weight loss for Saturn Fitness Centre ($10$ kg).
parts.solution:
Men in Saturn Fitness Centre lost more weight, as the median weight loss for Saturn ($25$ kg) is greater than the median weight loss for Alpha Centre ($20$ kg).

The weight loss for men in Alpha Centre is more consistent (smaller spread), as the IQR for Alpha Centre ($8$ kg) is less than the IQR for Saturn Fitness Centre ($10$ kg).

stem: Steve is planning to start a small business selling bubble tea. He has read the following healthy eating guidelines: Our sugar consumption should be no more than $10$ percent of our daily caloric intake (this is equal to $10$ teaspoons of sugar based on a $2000$-daily caloric intake). This limit includes sugar present in food and drinks. A further reduction to $5$ teaspoons of sugar a day based on a $2000$-daily calorie can bring about additional health benefits. The average recommended daily caloric intake is $2200$ calories for males, and $1800$ calories for females (based on an average weight and physical activity of the average male and female Singaporean). A cup of bubble tea is made by adding sugar syrup based on sugar level and topping up the remaining amount with flavoured tea. The tables below give information to calculate the number of calories in a cup of bubble tea. A regular-sized cup of bubble tea with full sugar ($100\%$) contains $120$ ml of sugar syrup. e.g. A regular-sized ($485$ ml) cup of bubble tea with full sugar $= 120$ ml of sugar syrup $+ 365$ ml of flavoured tea.

parts.text: Calculate the number of calories in sugar syrup in a regular-sized cup of bubble tea with half sugar. [2]
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of half sugar syrup in regular-sized bubble tea $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 120 = 60$ ml.
Amount of calories in regular-sized syrup $= \dfrac{60}{15} \times 50 = 200$ calories.

parts.text: Zen's daily caloric intake is about $2800$ calories based on his weight and physical activity. According to the healthy eating guidelines, calculate the maximum number of calories he can consume from sugar. [1]
parts.label: b
parts.solution: Max sugar consumption $= \dfrac{10}{100} \times 2800 = 280$ calories.

parts.text: Steve is offering a healthier choice option with a regular-sized cup of bubble tea with milk tea and quarter sugar level. Zen decides to select this healthier choice option. He thinks that the total calories of this option meets the healthy eating guidelines but exceeds the recommended calories for additional health benefits by $30\%$. Is Zen correct? Justify your decision and show your method clearly. [7]
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Sugar syrup ($30$ ml) $\Rightarrow 100$ cal; milk tea ($455$ ml) $\Rightarrow 100.1$ cal; total $\approx 200.1$ cal. Meets healthy guidelines ($200.1 < 280$). However exceeds additional-benefit recommendation ($140$ cal) by $\dfrac{200.1 - 140}{140} \times 100\% \approx 42.9\%$, not $30\%$. Zen is partially correct — the option meets healthy guidelines, but it exceeds the additional-benefit calories by more than $30\%$.
parts.solution:
Volume of regular-sized $= 485$ ml. Volume of quarter sugar syrup $= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 120 = 30$ ml.
Calories in sugar $= \dfrac{50}{15} \times 30 = 100$ calories.
Calories in milk tea $= \dfrac{(485 - 30)}{500} \times 110 = 100.1$ calories.
Total calories $= 100 + 100.1 = 200.1$ calories.
Calories in the bubble tea $= 200.1 < 280$, so yes, he WILL meet the healthy guidelines.
For additional benefits, recommended limit (5 tsp $\times 28$ cal/tsp scaled to 2800 cal) $= \dfrac{5}{2000} \times 2800 \times \dfrac{50}{15} \div \dfrac{50}{15} \Rightarrow$ recommended for additional benefits at his caloric intake $= 140$ cal.
Percentage exceeding $= \dfrac{200.1 - 140}{140} \times 100\% = 42\dfrac{13}{14}\% > 30\%$, he WILL exceed by more than $30\%$.

stem: A particle starts moving at $3$ m/s and accelerates uniformly at $2\,\text{m/s}^{2}$ for the first $5$ seconds. It then moves with constant speed for $3$ seconds, and takes another $6$ seconds to slow down uniformly to rest. The speed-time graph is shown below.

parts.text: State the value of $v$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Increase in speed in first $5$ s $= 2 \times 5 = 10$ m/s.
$v = 3 + 10 = 13$ m/s.

parts.text: Sketch the distance-time graph for the motion of the particle.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Distance-time graph consists of: a concave-up curve from $(0,0)$ to $(5, 40)$, a straight line from $(5, 40)$ to $(8, 79)$ with gradient $13$, and a concave-down curve from $(8, 79)$ to $(14, 118)$ flattening out at rest.
parts.solution:
Distances at the key times (areas under the $v$-$t$ graph):
$\bullet\;$ at $t = 5$: $\tfrac{1}{2}(3 + 13)(5) = 40$ m
$\bullet\;$ at $t = 8$: $40 + 13 \times 3 = 79$ m
$\bullet\;$ at $t = 14$: $79 + \tfrac{1}{2}(13)(6) = 118$ m
The distance-time graph is:
– a concave-up curve from $(0, 0)$ to $(5, 40)$ (acceleration),
– a straight line from $(5, 40)$ to $(8, 79)$ with gradient $13$ (constant speed),
– a concave-down curve from $(8, 79)$ to $(14, 118)$ flattening to a horizontal tangent at rest.

stem: The diagram shows the speed-time graph of a cyclist after passing a fixed point $A$.

parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the cyclist during the first 10 seconds after passing point $A$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Acceleration $= \dfrac{8 - 2}{40} = 0.15$ m/s$^{2}$

parts.text: Calculate the average speed, in m/s, of the cyclist in the last 80 seconds.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Distance travelled in last 80 s $= \dfrac{1}{2}(80 + 20)(8) = 400$ m
Average speed in last 80 s $= \dfrac{400}{80} = 5$ m/s

parts.text: On the grid below, sketch the distance-time graph for the journey.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Distance-time graph: curve (concave up) during acceleration phase, straight line during constant speed, and curve levelling off during deceleration, reaching the corresponding total distance.
parts.solution: Distance-time graph: starts at $(0, 0)$, curve concave-up during the first 40 s reaching $(40, 200)$ (area under speed-time graph from 0 to 40), straight line of gradient 8 from $(40, 200)$ to $(60, 360)$ (constant speed), then curve concave-down from $(60, 360)$ to $(120, 600)$ (deceleration). Total distance covered $= 600$ m.

stem: A container is made up of a cylinder and a hemisphere as shown above. The cylinder has a height of 2 cm and a circular base with radius 3 cm.

parts.text: Find the volume of the container, leaving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of cylinder $=\pi r^{2}h=\pi(3)^{2}(2)=18\pi$ cm$^{3}$.
Volume of hemisphere $=\dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^{3}=\dfrac{2}{3}\pi(3)^{3}=18\pi$ cm$^{3}$.
Total volume $=18\pi+18\pi=36\pi$ cm$^{3}$.

parts.text: Water is being poured into the container at a constant rate of $4.5\pi$ cm$^{3}$/min. Sketch the graph showing the relationship between the depth of the water, $d$ cm, and the time, $t$ minutes, as the container is being filled.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Sketch: curve from $t=0$, $d=0$ rising concavely (faster slope) while filling the hemisphere (for $0 \le d \le 3$), then linearly (constant slope) while filling the cylinder (for $3 \le d \le 5$).
parts.solution:
While the hemisphere fills ($0\le d\le 3$), the cross-sectional area is changing (narrow at the bottom, widest at $d=3$), so the depth rises more slowly as the radius increases—the curve is concave with decreasing gradient.
Once the cylinder fills ($3\le d\le 5$), the area is constant $9\pi$ cm$^{2}$, so the depth rises linearly.
Sketch: a curve rising from $(0,0)$ and curving towards a slower slope until $(t_{1},3)$ where $t_{1}=18\pi/(4.5\pi)=4$ min, then a straight segment with gradient $4.5\pi/9\pi=0.5$ from $(4,3)$ to $(8,5)$.

stem: The speed-time graph of a particle is shown in the diagram above.

parts.text: Find
parts.label: a

subparts.text: the speed when $t = 25$,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: From the speed-time graph, using the gradient of the relevant line segment, the speed at $t = 25$ is found by proportion to be $\frac{20}{3} = 6.67$ m/s (3 sf).

Adding the areas of the triangles and trapezia under the graph gives a total distance of $225$ m.

parts.label: b
parts.answer: Distance-time graph completed on the grid as required.
