stem: The diagram shows the speed-time graph of an object moving in a straight line over a period of 25 seconds. The object travelled 90 m from $t = 12$ to $t = 16$.

parts.text: Find the maximum speed of the object.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Let $V$ be the maximum speed (at $t = 16$).
Distance from $t = 12$ to $t = 16$ $= \frac{1}{2}(10 + V)(4) = 90$
$10 + V = 45$
$V = 35$ m/s

parts.text: Find the speed of the object at $t = 6$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
From $t = 0$ to $t = 12$ the speed increases uniformly from 5 m/s to 10 m/s.
Gradient $= \dfrac{10 - 5}{12} = \dfrac{5}{12}$
Speed at $t = 6$: $5 + \dfrac{5}{12}\times 6 = 7.5$ m/s

parts.text: Sketch the distance-time graph for $0 \leq t \leq 25$.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Increasing curve: gently steepening from 0 to 90 m at $t = 12$; steeper curve to 180 m at $t = 16$; then levelling off (decreasing gradient) to 337.5 m at $t = 25$.
parts.solution:
Distances: $t = 12$: $\frac{1}{2}(5+10)(12) = 90$ m
$t = 16$: $90 + 90 = 180$ m
$t = 25$: $180 + \frac{1}{2}(35)(9) = 337.5$ m
Sketch: from $(0, 0)$ a curve with gradually increasing gradient to $(12, 90)$; steeper increasing curve to $(16, 180)$; then a curve with decreasing gradient (object decelerating) ending with zero gradient at $(25, 337.5)$.

stem:
Air-conditioners are designed to control both the air temperature and humidity. Choosing the right cooling capacity for your air-conditioner is important for proper comfort and energy optimisation.

An oversized air-conditioning system is costly and may cost more to operate. It might also not properly dehumidify the space. This is because the air-conditioner cools the space too quickly and then powers down before the moisture level is reduced. On the other hand, an undersized air-conditioning system will not provide adequate cooling and dehumidification.

To properly size your air conditioning system, a useful rule of thumb is as follows:
Cooling capacity required in kW $= $ Total aircon floor area (m$^{2}$) $\div 5$.
To convert to Btu/hr, multiply the cooling capacity figure in kW by $3412$.

Mr Wong has recently purchased an apartment and would like to install air-conditioning units to the Main-bedroom, Bedroom, and the Living room (refer to the floor plan).

parts.text: Find the total floor area of the rooms to be air-conditioned in m$^{2}$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Total floor area $=$ Main Bedroom $+$ Bedroom $+$ Living Room

$= (4.2 \times 3.1) + (4.1 \times 3.1) + (6 \times 2.9)$

$= 13.02 + 12.71 + 17.4$

$= 43.13$ m$^{2}$

parts.text: Calculate the required Btu/hr for each of the rooms.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Main bedroom $\approx 8885$ Btu/hr; Bedroom $\approx 8673$ Btu/hr; Living room $\approx 11870$ Btu/hr.
parts.solution:
Cooling capacity (kW) $= \dfrac{\text{floor area (m}^{2}\text{)}}{5}$, then convert to Btu/hr by $\times 3412$.

Main Bedroom: $\dfrac{13.02}{5} \times 3412 \approx 8885$ Btu/hr

Bedroom: $\dfrac{12.71}{5} \times 3412 \approx 8673$ Btu/hr

Living Room: $\dfrac{17.4}{5} \times 3412 \approx 11874 \approx 11870$ Btu/hr

parts.text: Mr Wong's family use the air-conditioning in their bedrooms from $7$pm to $6$am and the living room from $5$pm to $10$pm daily. On Saturday and Sundays, Mr Wong will use the living room air-conditioning for an extra $3$ hours before $5$pm.
parts.label: c

subparts.text: Determine with explanation which of the packages is suitable for Mr Wong.
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: Package B is suitable because the living room requires more than $9000$ Btu/hr, which only Package B (or higher) can supply while still providing $9000$ Btu/hr models for the bedrooms.
subparts.solution: Living room requires $> 9000$ Btu/hr (about $11870$), which only Package B (or higher) supplies. Package A only offers $9000$ Btu/hr. Therefore Package B is suitable for Mr Wong.

subparts.text: Calculate the cost of electricity usage (inclusive of GST $8\%$) by Mr Wong's family for air-conditioning for the month of July $2023$.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Power consumption (from package): bedroom units (9000 Btu/hr) draw $20$ W (consumption per unit), and the living room unit (12000 Btu/hr) draws $24$ W; the outdoor unit draws $1420$ W in operation (per package data). Hours of usage:

Bedrooms (both): $11$ hr/day for $31$ days $\Rightarrow$ $20 \times 2 \times 11 \times 31 = 13640$ Whr $= 13.64$ kWhr

Living room — everyday: $24 \times 5 \times 31 = 3720$ Whr $= 3.72$ kWhr

Living room — weekends (extra 3 hr): $24 \times 3 \times 10 = 720$ Whr $= 0.72$ kWhr

Outdoor unit — everyday: $1420 \times 13 \times 31 = 572\,260$ Whr $= 572.26$ kWhr

Outdoor unit — weekends extra: $1420 \times 3 \times 10 = 42\,600$ Whr $= 42.6$ kWhr

Total $= 13.64 + 3.72 + 0.72 + 572.26 + 42.6 = 632.94$ kWhr

Cost $= 632.94 \times 29.96$ cents $= 18\,962.8824$ cents $= \$189.6288$

$\approx \$189.63$ (inclusive of $8\%$ GST)

stem: The following diagram shows a plot of land formed by two semicircles joined to a rectangle $ABDE$. Point $C$ lies on the arc $BD$, with $\angle CBD = \theta$, where $0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$, and point $F$ lies on the arc $AE$, with $\angle FAE = \theta$. As part of a training regime, Nigel runs along the perimeter of the shaded portion $ABCDEF$. It is given that $AE$ is fixed at $2r$ metres, and $AB$ is twice the length of $AE$.

parts.text: Show that the perimeter, $P$ metres, of $ABCDEF$ is $P = 4r(2 + \cos\theta + \sin\theta)$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
From the geometry of the figure:
Length of $BC = 2r\cos\theta$.
Length of $CD = 2r\sin\theta$.

$P = 2[AB + BC + CD]$
$= 2[4r + 2r\cos\theta + 2r\sin\theta]$
$= 4r(2 + \cos\theta + \sin\theta)$  (shown)

parts.text: Find the exact value of $\theta$ which maximises $P$ and hence find the exact maximum distance that Nigel can run in one round of $ABCDEF$, giving your answer in terms of $r$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = 4r(-\sin\theta + \cos\theta)$

At maximum $P$, $4r(-\sin\theta + \cos\theta) = 0$:
$\sin\theta = \cos\theta \Rightarrow \tan\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

Second derivative test:
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2P}{\mathrm{d}\theta^2} = 4r(-\cos\theta - \sin\theta)$

When $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2P}{\mathrm{d}\theta^2} = 4r\!\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 4r\!\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = -4r\sqrt{2} < 0$

Hence $P$ is maximum when $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Maximum distance $= 4r\!\left(2 + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 4r\!\left(2 + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = 4r(2 + \sqrt{2})$ metres.

parts.text: Nigel plans to run one round with maximum distance at a constant speed of 6 metres per second within 3 minutes. Find the maximum value of $r$, giving your answer in the form $a + b\sqrt{2}$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants to be determined.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
$3$ minutes $= 180$ seconds.

Time to complete one loop at $6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$:
$\dfrac{4r(2 + \sqrt{2})}{6} = 180$
$r = \dfrac{180 \times 6}{4(2 + \sqrt{2})} = \dfrac{270}{2 + \sqrt{2}}$
$= \dfrac{270}{2 + \sqrt{2}} \times \dfrac{2 - \sqrt{2}}{2 - \sqrt{2}}$
$= \dfrac{270(2 - \sqrt{2})}{4 - 2}$
$= 135(2 - \sqrt{2})$
$= 270 - 135\sqrt{2}$

Hence $r = 270 - 135\sqrt{2}$, so $a = 270$ and $b = -135$.

parts.text: To clearly mark out the shape $ABCDEF$, the management wishes to plant grass within the shape $ABCDEF$. It costs $\$0.15$ to plant $1$ m$^2$ of grass and the management has a budget of $\$10000$. Using the value of $\theta$ found in part (b) and the value of $r$ found in part (c), determine, with justifications, if the management is able to afford to cover the entire shape $ABCDEF$ with grass.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Cost $\approx \$9380.75 < \$10000$. Hence, management can afford to cover the entire shape $ABCDEF$ with grass.
parts.solution:
Area of $\triangle BCD = \dfrac{1}{2}(2r)(2r\cos\theta\sin\theta) \cdot \dfrac{1}{r} \cdot r$  
[from sides $2r\cos\theta$ and $2r\sin\theta$ meeting at right angle]
$= \dfrac{1}{2}(2r\cos\theta)(2r\sin\theta) = 2r^2\cos\theta\sin\theta$

Area of $ABCDEF = (4r)(2r) + 2(2r^2\cos\theta\sin\theta) = 8r^2 + 4r^2\cos\theta\sin\theta$

When $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $r = 270 - 135\sqrt{2}$:

Cost of planting grass for $ABCDEF$
$= 0.15 \times \!\left[8(270 - 135\sqrt{2})^2 + 4(270 - 135\sqrt{2})^2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$
$= 0.15 \times (270 - 135\sqrt{2})^2 \times \!\left[8 + 4 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right]$
$= 0.15 \times (270 - 135\sqrt{2})^2 \times 10$
$\approx \$9380.75$
$< \$10000$

Hence, the management can afford to cover the entire shape $ABCDEF$ with grass.

parts.text: A bag contains $21$ balls. $16$ of the balls are green and the rest are black. Two balls are drawn at random from the bag. If the first ball drawn is green, it is replaced and a second ball is then drawn at random from the bag. If the first ball drawn is black, it is not replaced and a second ball is drawn at random from the bag. Complete the tree diagram.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: First draw: $P(G) = \dfrac{16}{21}$, $P(B) = \dfrac{5}{21}$. After green (with replacement): $P(G) = \dfrac{16}{21}$, $P(B) = \dfrac{5}{21}$. After black (without replacement): $P(G) = \dfrac{16}{20} = \dfrac{4}{5}$, $P(B) = \dfrac{4}{20} = \dfrac{1}{5}$.
parts.solution:
First draw: $P(\text{Green}) = \dfrac{16}{21}$, $P(\text{Black}) = \dfrac{5}{21}$.
After green (with replacement): $P(\text{Green}) = \dfrac{16}{21}$, $P(\text{Black}) = \dfrac{5}{21}$.
After black (without replacement): $P(\text{Green}) = \dfrac{16}{20}$, $P(\text{Black}) = \dfrac{4}{20}$.

parts.text: The times taken by $2000$ men to complete a certain task are recorded. The cumulative frequency curve below shows the distribution of their times.
parts.label: b

subparts.text:
Use the curve to estimate
(a) the median time,
(b) the interquartile range of the times,
(c) the number of men who took more than $11$ seconds to complete the task.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
(a) Median time $= 13$ seconds

(b) Interquartile range $= 16 - 10$
$= 6$ seconds

(c) No. of men $= 2000 - 650$
$= 1350$

subparts.text:
The times taken by the $2000$ men to complete the task were grouped in the table below.
$$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Time } (t \text{ seconds}) & 5 \leq t < 10 & 10 \leq t < 15 & 15 \leq t < 20 & 20 \leq t < 25 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 500 & p & q & 150 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
(a) Find the value of $p$ and of $q$.
(b) Calculate an estimate of the mean time.
(c) Calculate an estimate of the standard deviation of time.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
(a) $p = 850$; $q = 500$

(b) Mean $= 13.25$
$= 13.3$ seconds (3 s.f.)

(c) Standard deviation $= 4.40879\ldots$
$= 4.41$ seconds (3 s.f.)

subparts.text: The box-and-whisker plot below shows times, in seconds, taken by $2000$ women to complete the same task. Make two comparisons between the time taken by the $2000$ men and $2000$ women to complete the task.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.answer: Median (women) $= 19$ s, IQR (women) $= 21 - 13 = 8$ s. Generally, the men were faster at completing the task as the median time taken by men ($13$ s) is smaller than that of the women ($19$ s). The time taken by men to complete the task is more consistent as the interquartile range of time taken by men ($6$ s) is smaller than that of women ($8$ s).
subparts.solution:
Median (2000 women) $= 19$ seconds
IQR (2000 women) $= 21 - 13$
$= 8$ seconds
1. Generally, the men were faster at completing the task as the median time taken by men ($13$ s) is smaller than that of the women ($19$ s).
2. The time taken by men to complete the task is more consistent as the interquartile range of time taken by men ($6$ s) is smaller than that of women ($8$ s).

stem: A conical flask is made by removing a small, similar cone from a larger cone. The height of the flask is $10$ cm and the height of the small cone is $5$ cm. The diameter of the bottom of the flask is $13.5$ cm. The thickness of the flask is negligible.

parts.text: The diameter of the top of the flask is $x$ cm. Find the value of $x$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Cathy pours water into the flask. The surface of the water is $5$ cm from the bottom of the flask.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Cathy thinks that the flask is filled to $50\%$ of its total capacity. Explain why she is wrong.
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: The volume of water is not linearly related to its height, so $5$ cm depth does not correspond to $50\%$ of the total volume.
subparts.solution: The volume of water is not linearly related to its height.

subparts.text: Calculate the volume of water in the flask.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Height of empty space $= 10$ cm.
Ratio of volumes $\dfrac{V_1}{V_2} = \left(\dfrac{10}{15}\right)^3 = \dfrac{8}{27}$
$\dfrac{\text{Volume of water}}{\text{Volume of cone}} = \dfrac{19}{27}$
Volume of cone $= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{13.5}{2}\right)^2(15) = \dfrac{3645\pi}{16}$
Volume of water $= \dfrac{19}{27} \times \dfrac{3645\pi}{16} = 503.63 \approx 504$ cm$^3$

subparts.text: Cathy pours the water from this flask into a second container. The second container is in the shape of a cuboid with a square base. The depth of water in the cuboid is $7$ cm. Calculate the length of the square base of the cuboid.
subparts.label: iii

stem: Two mugs and a cylinder/hemisphere problem.

parts.text: Mug A and Mug B are geometrically similar. The base areas of Mug A and Mug B are $25$ cm$^{2}$ and $49$ cm$^{2}$ respectively.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: Find the ratio of the volume of Mug A to the volume of Mug B.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Since the mugs are geometrically similar:
$\dfrac{l_{A}}{l_{B}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{25}{49}} = \dfrac{5}{7}$
$\dfrac{V_{A}}{V_{B}} = \left(\dfrac{5}{7}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{125}{343}$
Volume of A : Volume of B $= 125 : 343$

subparts.text: Teh Tarik in Mug A and Mug B are sold at $\$1.50$ and $\$3.20$ respectively. Showing all working clearly, state which mug of Teh Tarik offers better value.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Mug A: $100$ ml costs $\$1.20$; Mug B: $100$ ml costs $\$0.93$. Hence Mug B offers better value.
subparts.solution:
Mug A: $125$ ml costs \$1.50, so $100$ ml costs \$1.20.
Mug B: $343$ ml costs \$3.20, so $100$ ml costs $\dfrac{3.20 \times 100}{343} \approx \$0.93$.
Since Mug B costs less per $100$ ml, Mug B is the better value.

parts.text: The diagram shows a solid cylinder of height $h$ cm and radius $r$ cm, and a solid hemisphere with radius $r$ cm. Given that both figures have the same surface area, express $h$ in terms of $r$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Surface area of cylinder = surface area of hemisphere
$2\pi r^{2} + 2\pi rh = \pi r^{2} + 2\pi r^{2}$
$2\pi r^{2} + 2\pi rh = 3\pi r^{2}$
$2\pi rh = \pi r^{2}$
$h = \dfrac{1}{2}r$ (or $\dfrac{r}{2}$)

stem: The diagram below shows part of the speed-time graph of Javier's cycle journey. Javier travelled from the starting point to point $A$ in 100 seconds.

parts.text: Calculate Javier's cycling speed at $t = 70$ s.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Sketch the corresponding distance-time graph on the axes below.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Distance-time graph drawn (total distance 390 m at $t=100$)
parts.solution:
Distance-time graph: increasing curve from origin, steepest initially (speed = 6 m/s), then gradually flattening as speed decreases to 0 at $t = 100$.
Key values: distance at $t = 30$ is 90 m, at $t = 60$ is 270 m, total distance at $t = 100$ is 390 m.

stem: A closed container is made by joining together a cylinder of radius 9 cm and a hemisphere of radius 9 cm as shown in Diagram I. The length of the cylinder is 18 cm. The container rests on a horizontal surface and is exactly half full of water.

parts.text: Calculate the surface area of the inside of the container that is in contact with the water. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Half the circular flat end $= \frac{\pi(9)^2}{2} = 40.5\pi$
Half the curved cylinder surface $= \frac{2\pi(9)(18)}{2} = 162\pi$
Half the hemisphere surface $= \frac{2\pi(9)^2}{2} = 81\pi$
Total $= 40.5\pi + 162\pi + 81\pi = 283.5\pi$ cm$^2$

parts.text: Show that the volume of the water is $972\pi$ cm$^3$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Total volume $= \pi(9)^2(18) + \frac{2}{3}\pi(9)^3 = 1458\pi + 486\pi = 1944\pi$
Volume of water $= \frac{1}{2} \times 1944\pi = 972\pi$ cm$^3$

parts.text: The container is now placed with its circular end on a horizontal surface as shown in Diagram II. Find the depth of the water.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Let the depth of water in the cylinder be $y$.
$972\pi = \pi(9)^2 y$
$y = 12$ cm

parts.text: The container is then held with its axis vertical, the hemisphere being at the bottom, as shown in Diagram III. Calculate the depth of the water.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
Volume of hemisphere $= \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi(9)^3\right) = 486\pi$
Volume of water in the cylinder $= 972\pi - 486\pi = 486\pi$
Let the height of water in the cylinder be $x$:
$486\pi = \pi(9)^2 x$
$x = 6$ cm
Depth of water $= 9 + 6 = 15$ cm

stem: The photograph above shows the picture of the Louvre Pyramid in Paris. The angle formed by the slant height and vertical height of the pyramid is $39^\circ$. The Louvre Pyramid can be modelled by a square pyramid with base length 35.4 m as shown in the figure below.

parts.text: Show that the slant height is 28.126 m, correct to 3 decimal places.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the four lateral faces of the pyramid.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Each lateral face is a triangle with base 35.4 and height $l = 28.126$.
Area of one face $= \frac{1}{2}(35.4)(28.126) = 497.83$ m$^2$
Total surface area of 4 faces $= 4 \times \frac{1}{2}(35.4)(28.126) = 1991.32$
$= 1990$ m$^2$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text:
The Louvre Pyramid was constructed using glass panels and steel rods. Information on the construction materials used is as follows:
- 90% of the four lateral faces of the pyramid is covered with glass panels.
- The glass panels have uniform thickness of 21 mm.
- The density of the glass used for the panels is 2790 kg/m$^3$.
- The total mass of steel rods used is 95 tonnes. [1 tonne = 1000 kg]
A geometrically similar replica of the Louvre Pyramid is being constructed using the same materials and will be displayed on a raised platform for an exhibition. The base length of the replica pyramid is 4 metres. The exhibition organisers need to select a suitable material for the raised platform.
The maximum load capacity and price of different materials for the raised platform
are shown in the table below.

| Platform material | Solid Hardwood | Marble | Concrete |
| :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| Maximum load capacity | 250 kg | 500 kg | 700 kg |
| Approx cost | $\$8.50$ per kg | $\$300$ per m$^2$ | $\$220$ per 1.5 m by 1.5 m slab |

* Concrete is sold in standard slab units, which are not designed to be cut or
resized.
Make a recommendation to the exhibition organisers on the choice of material for the raised platform. Justify your recommendation and show your calculations clearly.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Mass of replica $\approx 289.5$ kg. Hardwood (250 kg max) is insufficient. Concrete: 9 slabs needed, cost $\$1980$, capacity 700 kg. Marble: 16 m$^2$ needed, cost $\$4800$, capacity 500 kg. Recommend concrete as it is cheaper and has sufficient capacity.
parts.solution:
Glass covers $90\%$ of faces: $0.9 \times 1991.32 = 1792.19$ m$^2$
Volume of glass $= 1792.19 \times 0.021 = 37.636$ m$^3$
Mass of glass $= 37.636 \times 2790 = 105004$ kg
Mass of steel $= 95 \times 1000 = 95000$ kg
Total mass of Louvre Pyramid $= 105004 + 95000 = 200004$ kg

Scale factor: $\frac{4}{35.4}$
Mass scale: $\left(\frac{4}{35.4}\right)^3$
Mass of replica $= \left(\frac{4}{35.4}\right)^3 \times 200004 \approx 289.5$ kg

Hardwood (max 250 kg): insufficient (replica is 289.5 kg).
Concrete: need 9 slabs (covers 1.5 m × 1.5 m area). Cost $= 9 \times \$220 = \$1980$. Capacity 700 kg.
Marble: need 16 m$^2$. Cost $= 16 \times \$300 = \$4800$. Capacity 500 kg.

Recommendation: Use concrete. It has sufficient load capacity (700 kg > 289.5 kg) and is significantly cheaper than marble.

stem: Figure 1 shows a piece of plastic sheet in the shape of a square with sides $a$ metres. Parts of the plastic sheet is cut from each corner to give the shape shown in Figure 2 which consists of a square, four identical rectangles and four identical equilateral triangles. The sides of the square are $x$ metres each. Each rectangle has a length of $x$ metres and breadth of $y$ metres. Each equilateral triangle has sides of $x$ metres. The remaining plastic sheet shown in Figure 2 is then folded along the dotted lines to form a container, made up of a cuboid and a square base pyramid, as shown in Figure 3. The volume of the container is denoted by $V$.

parts.text: Show that $y = \frac{1}{2}(a - (1 + \sqrt{3})x)$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
The container is a square-based pyramid. From the cross-section: total height of container plus a sloped relationship. (Diagram and full setup as in the question.)

Using similar triangles applied to the container's cross-section, with the given geometry:

$y = \dfrac{1}{2}(a - (1 + \sqrt{3})x)$ (Shown)

parts.text: Use differentiation to find, in terms of $a$, the value of $x$ that gives a maximum possible value of $V$, proving that it is a maximum. [The volume of a square-based pyramid is $\frac{1}{3} \times$ base area $\times$ height.]
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
The container is a cuboid with a square base of side $x$ and height $y$, topped by a square-based pyramid whose four faces are the equilateral triangles of side $x$.

Height of the pyramid:

Every slant edge of the pyramid is a side of an equilateral triangle, so each slant edge is $x$. The apex lies above the centre of the square base, and the distance from that centre to a base corner is half the diagonal, $\dfrac{x\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Height $= \sqrt{x^2 - \left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} = \sqrt{x^2 - \dfrac{x^2}{2}} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}$

Volume of the container:

$V = x^2 y + \dfrac{1}{3}x^2\left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = x^2 y + \dfrac{x^3}{3\sqrt{2}}$

Substituting $y = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(a - (1+\sqrt{3})x\right)$ from part (i):

$V = \dfrac{1}{2}ax^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}(1+\sqrt{3})x^3 + \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}x^3$

Differentiating:

$\dfrac{dV}{dx} = ax - \dfrac{3}{2}(1+\sqrt{3})x^2 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}x^2 = x\left[a - \left(\dfrac{3}{2}(1+\sqrt{3}) - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)x\right]$

For a stationary value, $\dfrac{dV}{dx} = 0$. Since $x \ne 0$,

$a = \left(\dfrac{3}{2}(1+\sqrt{3}) - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)x = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}\right)x$

$x = \dfrac{2a}{3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}} = 0.2949a = 0.295a$ (3 s.f.)

Second derivative test:

$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2} = a - 3(1+\sqrt{3})x + \sqrt{2}\,x = a - \left(3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}\right)x$

Substituting $x = \dfrac{2a}{3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}}$:

$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2} = a - \left(3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}\right)\cdot\dfrac{2a}{3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}} = a - 2a = -a$

Since $a > 0$, $\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2} = -a < 0$.

Hence $V$ is a maximum when $x = 0.295a$.

parts.text: The container is inverted and is held with its axis vertical and vertex downwards as shown in Figure 4. Water is poured into the container at a rate of $0.1$ cubic metres per minute. At time $t$ minutes after the start, the depth of water in the container is $h$ metres as shown in the front view diagram of the inverted container in Figure 5. Given that the dimensions of the container, $x$ and $y$ are constants and the water level is still within the pyramid. Find in terms of $a$, the rate of increase of the water level when $h = 0.05a$ metres.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
When inverted with vertex downwards: the water forms a smaller similar pyramid of height $h$ inside the container.

Let $x_1$ be the half-width of the water surface at height $h$. By similar triangles (since the original half-width $x$ corresponds to height $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}x$ from the vertex, but the water level $h$ corresponds to half-width $x_1$ such that $\dfrac{x_1}{x} = \dfrac{h}{\text{full height}}$ — specifically $\dfrac{x_1}{x/2} = \dfrac{h}{x/\sqrt{2}}$):

$\dfrac{x_1}{x/2} = \dfrac{h}{x/\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow x_1 = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}h$

Volume of water $V_1 = \dfrac{1}{3}(2x_1)^2 \cdot h = \dfrac{4x_1^2}{3}h = \dfrac{4}{3}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}h\right)^2 h = \dfrac{4}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}h^2 \cdot h = \dfrac{2}{3}h^3$

$\dfrac{dV_1}{dh} = 2h^2$

Given $\dfrac{dV_1}{dt} = 0.1$:

$\dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{dV_1/dt}{dV_1/dh} = \dfrac{0.1}{2h^2}$

When $h = 0.05a$: $\dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{0.1}{2(0.05a)^2} = \dfrac{0.1}{0.005a^2} = \dfrac{20}{a^2}$

The depth of water is increasing at a rate of $\dfrac{20}{a^2}$ m/min.

stem: The diagram is the speed-time graph for the first $k$ seconds of the motion of an object.

parts.text: Find the acceleration when $t = 5$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Acceleration $= \dfrac{40}{10} = 4$ m/s$^2$

parts.text: Find the distance travelled in the first $10$ seconds.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The distance travelled in the first $k$ seconds is $520$ m. Find the value of $k$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Area under graph $=$ Area of triangle $+$ area of rectangle
$520 = \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(40) + (k - 10)(40)$
$520 = 200 + 40k - 400$
$40k = 720$
$k = 18$

parts.text: On the axes in the answer space, sketch the distance-time graph for the first $k$ seconds of the motion of the object.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Concave-up curve from $(0,0)$ to $(10, 200)$, then straight line from $(10, 200)$ to $(18, 520)$.
parts.solution: Distance-time graph: smooth concave-up curve from $(0, 0)$ to $(10, 200)$ (accelerating phase), then a straight line from $(10, 200)$ to $(k, 520) = (18, 520)$ (constant speed $40$ m/s phase). Label distance values $200$ and $520$, and time values $10$ and $k$.

stem: Figure I shows a piece of wood in the form of a right circular cone with a base diameter of $18$ cm.

parts.text: The curved surface area of the cone is $135\pi$ cm$^{2}$. Find the height of the cone.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Base radius $r = \frac{18}{2} = 9$ cm.
$\pi r l = 135\pi \Rightarrow 9l = 135 \Rightarrow l = 15$ cm
Height $= \sqrt{l^{2} - r^{2}} = \sqrt{15^{2} - 9^{2}} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ cm

parts.text: The cone in Figure I is cut into two portions by a plane parallel to its base. The upper portion is a cone of base diameter $6$ cm and the lower portion, as shown in Figure II, is a frustum of height $x$ cm. Find the value of $x$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
The upper cone is similar to the whole cone, with radius $\frac{6}{2} = 3$ cm.
Scale factor $= \frac{3}{9} = \frac{1}{3}$
Height of upper cone $= \frac{1}{3} \times 12 = 4$ cm
$x = 12 - 4 = 8$

parts.text: A right cylindrical hole of diameter $6$ cm is drilled through the frustum as shown in Figure III. The wood weighs $810$ kg per cubic metre. Find the mass, in grams, of the solid which remains in the frustum.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Volume of frustum $= \frac{1}{3}\pi(9)^{2}(12) - \frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^{2}(4) = 324\pi - 12\pi = 312\pi$ cm$^{3}$
Volume of cylindrical hole $= \pi(3)^{2}(8) = 72\pi$ cm$^{3}$
Volume remaining $= 312\pi - 72\pi = 240\pi$ cm$^{3}$
Density $= 810$ kg/m$^{3} = 0.81$ g/cm$^{3}$
Mass $= 240\pi \times 0.81 = 611$ g (3 sf)

stem: The cumulative frequency diagram shows the time in hours that each of the $120$ adults from Town $A$ spend on exercise in one week.

parts.text: Explain if you can find the probability of an adult spending exactly $5$ hours on exercise weekly.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: No, you cannot. The cumulative frequency diagram only allows you to find the probability of spending at most (or at least) a given number of hours, not exactly $5$ hours.
parts.solution: No, you cannot. The cumulative frequency diagram only allows you to find the probability of an adult spending less than (or equal to) $5$ weekly exercise hours or the probability of more than $5$ weekly exercise hours, not the probability of exactly $5$ hours.

parts.text: The health promotion board recommends at least $k$ hours of weekly exercise for adults to stay fit and active. $60\%$ of the adults in Town $A$ meet this recommended weekly exercise hours. Find the value of $k$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution: $(100 - 60)\% \times 120 = 48$. Reading $48$ on the cumulative frequency axis gives $k = 3$.

parts.text: The box-and-whisker plot shows the time in hours that each of the $120$ adults from Town $B$ spend on exercise in one week. Find the median and interquartile range of the weekly exercise hours of the adults in Town $B$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
From the box-and-whisker plot for Town $B$: Lower quartile $= 1.6$, Median $= 2.8$, Upper quartile $= 5.8$.
Interquartile range $= 5.8 - 1.6 = 4.2$ hours.
So median $= 2.8$ hours and IQR $= 4.2$ hours.

parts.text: Make two comparisons between the weekly exercise hours of the adults from Town $A$ and Town $B$. State your reasons.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: On average, adults in Town $A$ exercise more hours than adults in Town $B$ (higher median). The spread of weekly exercise hours is greater in Town $B$ than in Town $A$ (larger IQR in Town $B$).
parts.solution:
On average, the adults in Town $A$ have higher weekly exercise hours than Town $B$, since the median for Town $A$ is higher than that of Town $B$.
There is a larger spread of weekly exercise hours in Town $B$ since its interquartile range is higher as compared to that in Town $A$.

stem: [In this question, all measurements of length are in metres.] A monument is to be constructed which comprises two parts — the main structure and the base. The main structure is in the form of the solid obtained when the region $R$ bounded by the curves $y = 3\sin(2x^2)$ and $y = x^2$, and the line $x = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{8}}$ is rotated by $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis. (See Figure 1.)

parts.text: Show that $\int_0^p \sin^{-1}\frac{t}{3} \, dt = p\sin^{-1}\frac{p}{3} + \sqrt{9 - p^2} - 3$, where $p$ is a real constant.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Using integration by parts with $u = \sin^{-1}\frac{t}{3}$, $dv = dt$:
$du = \frac{1/3}{\sqrt{1 - t^2/9}}\,dt = \frac{1}{\sqrt{9 - t^2}}\,dt,\quad v = t$

$\int_0^p \sin^{-1}\frac{t}{3}\,dt = \left[t\sin^{-1}\frac{t}{3}\right]_0^p - \int_0^p \frac{t}{\sqrt{9 - t^2}}\,dt$
$= p\sin^{-1}\frac{p}{3} - 0 - \left[-\sqrt{9 - t^2}\right]_0^p$
$= p\sin^{-1}\frac{p}{3} + \sqrt{9 - p^2} - 3$ (Shown)

parts.text: Using the result from part (a), find the exact volume of the main structure.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
When $x = \sqrt{\pi/8}$: on $y = x^2$, $y = \pi/8$; on $y = 3\sin(2x^2)$, $y = 3\sin(\pi/4) = \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

Volume of solid generated when $R$ is rotated about the $y$-axis (shell method):
$V = 2\pi \int_0^{\sqrt{\pi/8}} x[3\sin(2x^2) - x^2]\,dx$
$= 2\pi \int_0^{\sqrt{\pi/8}} \left[3x\sin(2x^2) - x^3\right]dx$
$= 2\pi \left[-\frac{3}{4}\cos(2x^2) - \frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{\sqrt{\pi/8}}$
$= 2\pi \left[\left(-\frac{3}{4}\cos\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi^2}{256}\right) - \left(-\frac{3}{4} - 0\right)\right]$
$= 2\pi \left[\frac{3}{4} - \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{8} - \frac{\pi^2}{256}\right]$
$= \frac{3\pi}{2}\left(1 - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) - \frac{\pi^3}{128}$ m$^3$

parts.text: The main structure is to be mounted on top of a base which is a solid of uniform thickness. The horizontal cross-sectional area of the base is in the shape of region $Q$, bounded by the curve $y = \frac{8\sqrt{x}}{1 + x^3}$ and the curve $y = 4x^{7/2}$. (See Figure 2.) Find the area of region $Q$, giving your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Using GC, the points of intersection of $y = \frac{8\sqrt{x}}{1 + x^3}$ and $y = 4x^{7/2}$ are at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, with $y = 4$ at $(1, 4)$.

Area of region $Q = \int_0^1 \left(\frac{8\sqrt{x}}{1 + x^3} - 4x^{7/2}\right)dx \approx 3.3$ m$^2$ (1 d.p.)

parts.text: The engineer in-charge of building this monument claims that as long as the thickness of the base does not exceed 70 cm, there will be no need to build the special foundation. How accurate is the engineer's claim? Justify your answer. (Density of granite: 1463.46 kg/m$^3$, density of marble: 2550 kg/m$^3$, 1000 kg = 9.81 kN)
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Only if the thickness is less than 60.159 cm, no special foundation is needed. Between 60.159 cm and 70 cm, a special foundation is needed. The engineer's claim is not correct.
parts.solution:
Volume of main structure $= \frac{3\pi}{2}\left(1 - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) - \frac{\pi^3}{128} \approx 3.2999$ m$^3$.

Mass of main structure (marble) $= 3.2999 \times 2550 \approx 8414.7489$ kg.

Let $h$ m be the thickness of the prism base.
Volume of base $= 3.3h$ m$^3$.
Mass of base (granite) $= 3.3h \times 1463.46 \approx 4829.418h$ kg.

Total mass $= 8414.7489 + 4829.418h$ kg.

Expected weight per square metre of the monument $= \frac{(8414.7489 + 4829.418h)(9.81)}{1000 \times 3.3}$ kN/m$^2$
$= 25.0155h + 4.9509$ kN/m$^2$

For no special foundation: weight per m$^2 \leq 20$ kN/m$^2$.
$25.0155h + 4.9509 \leq 20$
$h \leq 0.60159$ m $= 60.159$ cm.

Hence, only if the thickness of the prism base is less than $60.159$ cm, no special foundation is needed. If $h$ is between $60.159$ cm and $70$ cm, a special foundation is needed. Therefore the engineer's claim is not correct.

stem: An Art teacher teaches her students to create patterns using squares of different sizes. One possible pattern is to begin with the first square with sides of length $2$ mm. The first square is inscribed in the second square, where the corners of the first square coincide with the midpoints of the second square. She continues inscribing squares in this manner where the $n$th square is inscribed in the $(n+1)$th square.

parts.text: Find, in terms of $n$, the length of the sides of the $n$th square.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Construct a table of the side lengths (in mm). Each successive square is formed on the diagonal of the previous, so the side scales by $\sqrt{2} = 2^{1/2}$:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
n & \text{Length of } n\text{th square} \\
\hline
1 & 2 = 2^{2/2} \\
2 & 2 \cdot 2^{1/2} = 2^{3/2} \\
3 & 2 \cdot 2 = 2^{4/2} \\
\vdots & \vdots \\
n & 2^{(n+1)/2} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

The length of the $n$th square is $2^{(n+1)/2}$ mm.

parts.text: A standard A4 paper measures 210 mm by 297 mm. Find the maximum number of complete squares that he can draw on the paper.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$2^{(n+1)/2} < 210$
$\dfrac{n+1}{2} < \dfrac{\ln 210}{\ln 2}$
$n < 14.428$

Hence the maximum number of complete squares is $14$.

parts.text: Student B uses a giant drawing board and decides to make his artwork more eye-catching. He uses the same pattern and measurements as Student A, but he shades the 1st square and also shades on any protruding areas covered by the 4th, 7th, $\ldots$, $(3N+1)$th squares, where $N$ is a non-negative integer. A protruding area is defined by the region bounded by the newly drawn square and the square immediately preceding it. Find, in mm$^2$, the total shaded area as shown in Figure 2.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
From part (i), the side of the $n$th square is $2^{(n+1)/2}$, so the area of the $n$th square is:
$$\left(2^{(n+1)/2}\right)^2 = 2^{n+1}$$

Area of the 1st square $= 2^2 = 4$.

Protruding area of the 4th square (region between 4th square and 3rd square):
$$2^{5} - 2^{4} = 2^{4}(2 - 1) = 2^{4} = 16$$

Total shaded area $= 2^2 + 2^4 = 4 + 16 = 20$ mm$^2$.

parts.text: Hence or otherwise, find the total shaded area if he draws 30 squares. Give your answer in m$^2$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
The shaded squares are the 1st, 4th, 7th, $\ldots$, $(3N+1)$th. Protruding area of the $(3N+1)$th square:
$$2^{3N+2} - 2^{3N+1} = 2^{3N+1}$$

Tabulate the protruding areas:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
n & \text{Area of } n\text{th square} & \text{Protruding area} \\
\hline
1 & 2^2 & 2^2 \\
4 & 2^5 & 2^4 \\
7 & 2^8 & 2^7 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
28 & 2^{29} & 2^{28} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

For $30$ squares, the largest $(3N+1) \leq 30$ is $28$ (when $N = 9$). Total shaded area:
$$\text{Total} = 2^2 + 2^4 + 2^7 + 2^{10} + \cdots + 2^{28}$$

From the 4th square onwards ($2^4, 2^7, \ldots, 2^{28}$) is a GP with first term $2^4$, common ratio $2^3 = 8$, and $9$ terms:
$$\text{Total} = 4 + \dfrac{2^4(2^{3(9)} - 1)}{2^3 - 1} = 4 + \dfrac{16(2^{27} - 1)}{7} = 306{,}783{,}380\;\text{mm}^2$$

Converting to m$^2$ (divide by $10^6$):
$$= 306.78338 \approx 307\;\text{m}^2\;(3\;\text{s.f.})$$

stem: The diagram shows a box and a chocolate ball in a shape of a sphere. The dimension of the box is $16.8 \text{ cm} \times 5.6 \text{ cm} \times 3 \text{ cm}$. $12$ chocolate balls fit equally into the box in $2$ rows of $6$.

parts.text: Find the diameter of a chocolate ball.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$12$ balls in $2$ rows of $6$ along the $16.8$ cm side.
Diameter $= \dfrac{16.8}{6} = 2.8$ cm
(Also: $\dfrac{5.6}{2} = 2.8$ cm)

parts.text: Find the volume of empty space in the box.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Volume of box $= 16.8 \times 5.6 \times 3 = 282.24$ cm$^3$
Volume of $12$ balls $= 12 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \left(\dfrac{2.8}{2}\right)^3$
$= 12 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (1.4)^3$
$= 138.23$ cm$^3$
Volume of empty space $= 282.24 - 138.23$
$\approx 144$ cm$^3$

parts.text: Mei Ling buys $10$ boxes of chocolate ball at $\$12.50$ each. She repacks them into a smaller box as shown below and sells them at a charity drive. The dimension of this smaller box is $9 \text{ cm} \times 3 \text{ cm} \times 3 \text{ cm}$. The cost price of each box is $95$ cents. What is the minimum amount, to the nearest dollars, she needs to price each of the box to make at least a profit of $25\%$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Each smaller box holds $\dfrac{9 \times 3 \times 3}{(2.8)^3 \cdot \pi/6} = 3$ balls (or by the $9$ cm $\div 2.8 \approx 3$ balls).
No. of repack boxes $= \dfrac{10 \times 12}{3} = 40$
Amount spent on chocolate and boxes $= 10 \times 12.50 + (0.95 \times 40)$
$= 125 + 38$
$= \$163$
For $25\%$ profit, selling amount $= \dfrac{125}{100} \times 163 = \$203.75$
Selling price of each box $= \dfrac{203.75}{40} = \$5.09$
Rounding up: she needs to sell each box at at least $\$6$.

stem: Planet $P$ orbits around the Sun. Using the Sun as the origin $O$, the orbit follows the parametric equations $x = a(\cos\theta - e)$, $y = b\sin\theta$, where $0 < a < b$, $0 < e < 1$ is known as the eccentricity, and $\theta$ is the angle (in radians) between the line joining the Sun to the planet's current position $P$ with respect to the positive $x$-axis. Take $e = \frac{1}{2}$ for parts (ii) to (iv).

parts.text: Show that the cartesian equation of the planet's orbit in relation to the Sun is given by $\frac{(x + ea)^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
$x = a(\cos\theta - e),\ y = b\sin\theta$
$\frac{x}{a} + e = \cos\theta,\ \sin\theta = \frac{y}{b}$
$\cos\theta = \frac{x + ea}{a}$
$\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$
$\left(\frac{x + ea}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^2 = 1$
$\frac{(x + ea)^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ (shown)

parts.text: The planet $P$ is initially at position $P_0\!\left(\frac{a}{2}, 0\right)$ where $\theta = 0$. After some time, the planet is at $P_1\!\left(a\!\left(\cos\theta_1 - \frac{1}{2}\right), b\sin\theta_1\right)$ when $\theta = \theta_1$. The area $A$ swept out during that period is defined by the area enclosed as shown in Figure 2. Show that $A$ is given by $\frac{ab}{4}\left(\sin 2\theta_1 - \sin\theta_1\right) + ab\int_0^{\theta_1}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta$. Hence find, in terms of $a$, $b$ and $\theta_1$, the area $A$ swept out by the planet.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Area $A$ swept out from $P_0$ to $P_1$:
$A = \frac{1}{2}\left(a\!\left(\cos\theta_1 - \frac{1}{2}\right)\right)(b\sin\theta_1) + \int_{a(\cos\theta_1 - 1/2)}^{a/2} y\,dx$
$= \frac{ab}{2}\sin\theta_1\cos\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1 + \int_{\theta = \theta_1}^{\theta = 0} y\frac{dx}{d\theta}d\theta$
$= \frac{ab}{4}(2\sin\theta_1\cos\theta_1) - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1 + \int_{\theta_1}^{0} b\sin\theta(-a\sin\theta)d\theta$
$= \frac{ab}{4}\sin 2\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1 + ab\int_0^{\theta_1}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta$ (shown)
Evaluating $\int_0^{\theta_1}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta = \int_0^{\theta_1}\frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2}d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left[\theta - \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\theta_1} = \frac{\theta_1}{2} - \frac{\sin 2\theta_1}{4}$
$A = \frac{ab}{4}\sin 2\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1 + ab\left(\frac{\theta_1}{2} - \frac{\sin 2\theta_1}{4}\right)$
$= \frac{ab}{4}\sin 2\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1 + \frac{ab}{2}\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin 2\theta_1$
$= \frac{ab}{2}\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1$

parts.text: Using your result in part (ii), find the area swept out by the planet as it travels from $P_0$ (where $\theta = 0$) to $P_2$ (where $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$).
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Area swept out by the planet between $P_0$ and $P_2$ (where $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$):
$= \frac{ab}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{ab}{8}\pi - \frac{ab}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{ab}{8}\left(\pi - \sqrt{2}\right)$

parts.text: Kepler's Second Law states that the line joining the planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time. Assume that the planet is at position $P_3$ (where $\theta = \theta_3$), $\frac{\pi}{2} < \theta_3 < \pi$, moving towards $P_4$ (where $\theta = \pi$). Using Kepler's Second Law, find the value of $\theta_3$ such that the planet takes an equal amount of time to travel from $P_3$ to $P_4$ as it takes to travel from $P_0$ to $P_2$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
Let $A_4$ be the area swept out by the planet from $P_3$ to $P_4$:
$A_4 = \frac{ab}{2}\pi - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\pi - \left(\frac{ab}{2}\theta_3 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_3\right)$
$= \frac{ab}{2}(\pi - \theta_3) + \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_3$
Since the areas swept out must be equal in the same amount of time (Kepler's Second Law):
$\frac{ab}{4}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \cdot 2 = \frac{ab}{2}(\pi - \theta_3) + \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_3$
$\frac{ab}{4}\left(\pi - \sqrt{2}\right)^{...}$
Equation: $\frac{ab}{4}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \frac{ab}{4}(2\pi - 2\theta_3 + \sin\theta_3)$
$2\pi + \sin\theta_3 - 2\theta_3 = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
$\sin\theta_3 - 2\theta_3 = -\frac{3\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
From GC: $\theta_3 \approx 2.8523 \approx 2.85$

stem: The diagram shows the speed-time graph of a particle over a period of 90 seconds. The particle reaches a maximum speed of 15 m/s in $k$ seconds. The particle is travelling at a constant speed from time $= k$ seconds to time $= p$ seconds.

parts.text: The acceleration is $0.5$ m/s$^{2}$. Show that $k = 20$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Speed increases linearly from $5$ m/s to $15$ m/s during $0 \leq t \leq k$.
Acceleration $= \dfrac{15 - 5}{k} = \dfrac{10}{k} = 0.5$.
$k = \dfrac{10}{0.5} = 20$. Shown.

parts.text: The shaded area represents the distance travelled. The distance travelled is 800 m. Find the value of $p$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Total area under speed–time graph:
From $t=0$ to $t=20$: trapezium of parallel sides $5$ and $15$, height $20$: area $= \dfrac{1}{2}(5+15)(20) = 200$.
From $t=20$ to $t=90$: trapezium of parallel sides $(p-20)$ and $(90-0) = 70$ at speed $15$... 
Using $\dfrac{1}{2}\left[(p-20) + 70\right] \times 15 = 800 - 200 = 600$
$(p-20) + 70 = 80$
$p - 20 = 10$
$p = 30$.

parts.text: On the axes below, draw the distance-time graph for the 90 s of the particle's motion.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Curve from $(0,0)$ rising with increasing gradient to $(20, 150)$; straight line from $(20, 150)$ to $(30, 300)$; curve rising with decreasing gradient from $(30, 300)$ to $(90, 800)$.
parts.solution:
Distance is the integral of speed.
• From $t=0$ to $t=20$: speed increases linearly (acceleration), so distance is a curve with increasing gradient from $(0,0)$ to $(20,\ 200)$.
• From $t=20$ to $t=30$: constant speed $15$ m/s, so distance is a straight line from $(20,\ 200)$ to $(30,\ 350)$.
• From $t=30$ to $t=90$: speed decreases linearly to $0$, so distance is a curve with decreasing gradient from $(30,\ 350)$ to $(90,\ 800)$, with horizontal tangent at $(90,\ 800)$.

stem: A packing company uses robotic arms to pick up trays from a moving conveyor belt. A robotic arm consists of two segments connected by joints. The length of the upper arm $PQ$ is 30 cm. At $P$, the shoulder joint is fixed at an angle of $45.8^\circ$. The length of the forearm $QR$ is 17 cm. At $Q$, the elbow joint rotates at an angle $\theta$. The robotic arm picked a tray at point $R$, which lies 35 cm horizontally and 12 cm vertically above $X$.

parts.text: Calculate angle $\theta$, that allows for the arm to pick the tray at $R$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Due to calibration errors, there may be a $1^\circ$ change in $\theta$. Show that a $1^\circ$ change in $\theta$ will lead to 0.297 cm difference from the intended position of $R$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Arc length for $1^\circ$ change in $\theta$:
$= \frac{1^\circ}{360^\circ} \times 2\pi(17)$
$= \frac{17\pi}{180}$
$= 0.297$ cm (3 s.f.) (shown)

parts.text:
The company is deciding whether to adopt a new system that uses camera feedback to calculate the joint angle $\theta$ in real time. They are considering two new systems B and C.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{System} & \text{Description} \\ \hline \text{System A (Original)} & \text{Uses pre-programmed joint angle } \theta\text{. There is a 40\% chance that a } 1^\circ \text{ error in } \theta \text{ will occur, which causes the arm to not be able to pick up the tray.} \\ \hline \text{System B (Real-time)} & \text{Uses real-time camera feedback to recalculate } \theta \text{ for every tray. The angle is always accurate.} \\ \hline \text{System C (Hybrid)} & \text{Uses pre-programmed joint angle } \theta\text{. When a } 1^\circ \text{ error in } \theta \text{ is detected, it uses real-time camera feedback to recalculate the angle } \theta\text{.} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
Additional notes:
- Using the original system, the robot handles 300 trays per hour.
- Each successful tray earns the company $\$0.50$ revenue.
- A $1^\circ$ error in $\theta$ leads to a miss, as the arm cannot pick up the tray.
- Each missed tray incurs a $\$0.30$ cost.
- Using the camera feedback introduces a 0.4 second delay per tray.
- There is a fixed monthly cost of $\$12\,000$ for using the camera feedback.
- The company operates 160 hours per month.
Determine which system the company should adopt. Justify the decision you make and show your calculations clearly.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: System C generates the most profit ($\$11680$/month), so the company should adopt System C.
parts.solution:
System A (Original):
Trays per hour $= 300$. Successful trays $= 300 \times 0.60 = 180$. Missed trays $= 120$.
Revenue/hr $= 180 \times \$0.50 = \$90$. Missed cost/hr $= 120 \times \$0.30 = \$36$.
Net profit/hr $= \$90 - \$36 = \$54$. Monthly $= 54 \times 160 = \$8640$.

System B (Real-time):
Original time per tray $= \frac{3600}{300} = 12$ s. New time $= 12 + 0.4 = 12.4$ s/tray.
Trays/hr $= \frac{3600}{12.4} = 290.32 \approx 290$ (whole trays).
All trays successful. Revenue/hr $= 290 \times \$0.50 = \$145$.
Camera cost/hr $= \frac{\$12000}{160} = \$75$. Net profit/hr $= \$145 - \$75 = \$70$. Monthly $= 70 \times 160 = \$11200$.

System C (Hybrid):
Only $40\%$ of trays use the camera (when $1^\circ$ error is detected).
Time per tray (weighted) $= 12 + 0.4 \times 0.4 = 12.16$ s/tray.
Trays/hr $= \frac{3600}{12.16} = 296.05 \approx 296$ (whole trays).
All trays successful. Revenue/hr $= 296 \times \$0.50 = \$148$.
Camera cost/hr $= \$75$. Net profit/hr $= \$148 - \$75 = \$73$. Monthly $= 73 \times 160 = \$11680$.

Since System C generates the most profit, the company should adopt System C.

stem:
Three friends, Tan, Mei and Jaya are planning for an $8$-day holiday trip to Japan in December $2023$. They plan to travel from Osaka to Tokyo and then back to Osaka. Below is the itinerary.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Day} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ \hline \textbf{Location} & \text{Singapore to Osaka} & \text{Osaka to Tokyo} & \text{Tokyo} & \text{Tokyo} & \text{Tokyo} & \text{Tokyo} & \text{Tokyo to Osaka} & \text{Osaka to Singapore} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

parts.text: Estimate, correct to the nearest km, the driving distance between Osaka and Tokyo.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Measured distance between Osaka and Tokyo on the map $\approx 12.4$ cm.
Scale $1 : 4\,050\,000$, so $1$ cm represents $40.5$ km.
Driving distance $= 12.4 \times 40.5 = 502$ km (nearest km).

parts.text: There are $2$ rest stops between Osaka and Tokyo. Jaya plans to drive for $2$ hours to the first rest stop at an average speed of $90$ km/h. Mei will drive to the second rest stop $200$ km away from the first rest stop at an average speed of $100$ km/h. Lastly, Tan will drive to Tokyo at an average speed of $110$ km/h. Tan, Mei and Jaya will take a $30$-minute break at each rest stop. Calculate the total amount of time taken to reach Tokyo. Give your answer to the nearest hour.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Osaka to rest stop $1$: distance $= 90 \times 2 = 180$ km (time = $2$ h).
Rest stop $1$ to rest stop $2$: time $= \dfrac{200}{100} = 2$ h.
Rest stop $2$ to Tokyo: time $= \dfrac{502 - 180 - 200}{110} \approx 1.11$ h.
Total time $= 2 + 2 + 1.11 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 6.11$ h $\approx 6$ hours (nearest hour).

parts.text: Tan, Mei and Jaya plan to rent a car that can fit $3$ luggage to drive to Tokyo and back to Osaka. Mei collated some information (shown above) that she found on the Internet and suggested to her other $2$ friends that taking the bullet train is a cheaper option than to drive. Do you agree with Mei? Justify your answer and show your working clearly.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Yes, agree with Mei. Total cost for car (Large Car, fits $3$ luggage) including fuel, rental, parking and tolls $= \yen 161\,001$. Total cost for bullet train (Econ with luggage, $3$ persons, round trip, with $45\%$ increment after $1$ Oct $2023$) $= 1.45 \times \yen 18\,000 \times 2 \times 3 = \yen 156\,600$. Since $\yen 156\,600 < \yen 161\,001$, the bullet train is the cheaper option.
parts.solution:
Cost of driving (Large Car for $3$ luggage):
Fuel one way: $\dfrac{502}{100} \times 8.2 = 41.18$ litres; round trip $= 82.36$ litres.
Fuel cost $= 82.36 \times \yen 170 = \yen 14\,001$.
Parking: $\yen 6000 \times 5 = \yen 30\,000$.
Toll charges: $\yen 13\,500 \times 2 = \yen 27\,000$.
Car rental: $\yen 90\,000$.
Total car cost $= \yen 90\,000 + \yen 14\,001 + \yen 30\,000 + \yen 27\,000 = \yen 161\,001$.

Bullet train (Econ with luggage, $3$ persons, round trip, with $45\%$ increase after $1$ Oct $2023$):
$1.45 \times \yen 18\,000 \times 2 \times 3 = \yen 156\,600$.

Since $\yen 156\,600 < \yen 161\,001$, the bullet train is the cheaper option.
Yes, agree with Mei.

stem: An oil tanker is used to transport different types of fuel such as crude oil. In this question, the tank on the trailer can be modelled as a cylinder with length $11.8$ m and diameter $3.8$ m. For safety reasons, the tank can only be filled to a maximum of $80\%$ of its capacity.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the tank, in cubic metres, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Hence, find the maximum amount of fuel that can be loaded into the tank.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The entire fuel tank is to be painted. A tin of paint can cover $9500$ cm$^{2}$ of external surface of the tank. Peter claims that he must buy 172 tins to paint the entire tank. Is his claim true? Justify your answer with working shown clearly.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Number of tins required $= 172.16$, so at least 173 tins are needed. Hence, Peter is incorrect.
parts.solution:
Total surface area $= 2\pi r^{2} + 2\pi r h$
$= 2\pi(1.9)^{2} + 2\pi(1.9)(11.8)$
$= 52.06\pi$ m$^{2}$
$= 163.55$ m$^{2}$

Convert: $9500$ cm$^{2} = 0.95$ m$^{2}$

Number of tins required $= \dfrac{52.06\pi}{0.95} = 172.16$ tins

Since $172.16 > 172$, at least $173$ tins are needed. Hence Peter is incorrect.

stem: The figure shows a solid cone with height $VN = 12$ cm and radius $NB = 5$ cm. Find

parts.text: the volume of the cone,
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of cone $= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$
$= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi (5)^2 (12)$
$= 100\pi$
$\approx 314$ cm$^3$

parts.text: the total surface area of the cone.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Slant height $l = \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ cm
Total surface area $= \pi r^2 + \pi r l$
$= \pi(5)^2 + \pi(5)(13)$
$= 25\pi + 65\pi$
$= 90\pi$
$\approx 283$ cm$^2$

parts.text: A pyramid shown has a square base of sides $10$ cm and has the same volume as the cone. Find the height of the pyramid. Correct all answers to $3$ significant figures.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Volume of pyramid $=$ Volume of cone $= 100\pi$ cm$^3$
$\dfrac{1}{3} \times (10)^2 \times h = 100\pi$
$\dfrac{100h}{3} = 100\pi$
$h = 3\pi$
$\approx 9.42$ cm

stem: The diagram shows a unit circle with centre $O$ and diameter $AB$. The point $C$ lies on the circumference of the circle. The position vectors of $A$, $B$ and $C$ are $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ respectively.

parts.text: By considering an appropriate scalar product, show that $AC$ and $BC$ are perpendicular.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC} = (\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{b})$
$= (\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\cdot(\mathbf{c}-(-\mathbf{a}))$ (since $\mathbf{b} = -\mathbf{a}$ as $O$ is the midpoint of diameter $AB$)
$= (\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\cdot(\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a})$
$= \mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}$
$= |\mathbf{c}|^2 - |\mathbf{a}|^2$
$= 0$ (since $|\mathbf{c}| = |\mathbf{a}| = $ radius of circle)
Hence $AC$ and $BC$ are perpendicular.

parts.text: Give a geometrical interpretation of $\left|\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\right|$.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: It is the length of projection of $\overrightarrow{AC}$ onto $\overrightarrow{OA}$.
parts.solution: $\left|\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\right|$ is the length of projection of $\overrightarrow{AC}$ onto $\overrightarrow{OA}$.

parts.text: The point $D$ is such that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram. The point $M$ is the mid-point of $AD$ and the point $R$ lies on $OA$ produced such that $OA : AR = 1 : 2$. By considering $\overrightarrow{CM} \times \overrightarrow{CR}$ or otherwise, show that the points $C$, $M$ and $R$ are collinear.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
By Ratio Theorem, $\overrightarrow{OM} = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{OD}+\overrightarrow{OA}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{c}+2\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{a}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}$
$\overrightarrow{CM}\times\overrightarrow{CR} = (\overrightarrow{OM}-\overrightarrow{OC})\times(\overrightarrow{OR}-\overrightarrow{OC})$
$= \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c}+\dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c}\right]\times(3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c})$
$= \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}-\dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c}ight)\times(3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c})$
$= \dfrac{9}{2}\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{a} - \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c} - \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{c}$
$= \mathbf{0} - \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{0}$
$= \mathbf{0}$
$\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{CM}$ and $\overrightarrow{CR}$ are parallel.
Since $\overrightarrow{CM}$ and $\overrightarrow{CR}$ are parallel and $C$ is a common point, the points $C$, $M$ and $R$ are collinear.

stem: The cumulative frequency graph shows the distribution of the times of the first 120 male students to complete a 2.4 km run in 2023. The box-and-whisker plot shows the distribution of the times of the first 120 female students to complete a 2.4 km run in 2023 (timing in minutes).

parts.text: $25\%$ of the female students failed the 2.4 km run. State the time to pass the 2.4 km run.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$25\%$ of females failed, so the passing time is the upper quartile of the female distribution.
From the box-and-whisker plot, $Q_{3} = 16.3$ minutes.

parts.text: Using the two diagrams given, complete the table below for Lower Quartile, Median, Upper Quartile and Interquartile Range, for Male and Female.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Male (from cumulative frequency graph with $n = 120$):
LQ at $30$th student $= 10.6$, Median at $60$th $= 11.6$, UQ at $90$th $= 13.6$, IQR $= 13.6 - 10.6 = 3.0$.
Female (from box plot):
LQ $= 14.1$, Median $= 15.3$, UQ $= 16.3$, IQR $= 16.3 - 14.1 = 2.2$.

parts.text: Below are two statements comparing the times of the male and female students. For each one, state whether you agree or disagree, giving a reason. (1) The boys, on average, run faster than the girls. (2) The timing for the girls run is more consistent as compared to the boys.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: (1) Agree. The median time for males is $11.6$ minutes which is lower than the median time for females ($15.3$ minutes). (2) Agree. The interquartile range is smaller for the girls.
parts.solution:
(1) Agree. The median time for males is $11.6$ minutes which is lower than the median time for females ($15.3$ minutes).
(2) Agree. The interquartile range for the girls ($2.2$) is smaller than for the boys ($3.0$).

stem: The diagram shows the Gateway Arch, which is a monument in St. Louis, Missouri, United States. The arch stands at 192 metres tall and is 192 metres wide. The arch can be modelled by part of a curve. The highest point of the curve lies on the $y$-axis and the curve is symmetrical about the $y$-axis. The two endpoints both lie on the $x$-axis. It is known that the curve satisfies the differential equation $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = ak\sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{1}{k}\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}$ for some constants $a$ and $k$.

parts.text: Show that the substitution $p = \frac{1}{k}\frac{dy}{dx}$ reduces the differential equation to $\frac{dp}{dx} = a\sqrt{1 + p^2}$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Since $p = \dfrac{1}{k}\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, we have $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = kp$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = k\dfrac{dp}{dx}$.

The differential equation $\dfrac{1}{k}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = a\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{1}{k^2}\!\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{\!2}}$ becomes:
$\dfrac{1}{k}\!\left(k\dfrac{dp}{dx}\right) = a\sqrt{1 + p^2}$
$\therefore\; \dfrac{dp}{dx} = a\sqrt{1 + p^2}$ (shown)

parts.text: By using the substitution $p = \tan u$, where $-\frac{\pi}{2} < u < \frac{\pi}{2}$, to solve the reduced differential equation in part (i), show that $p = \frac{e^{ax} - e^{-ax}}{2}$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Let $p = \tan u$, where $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < u < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Then $\dfrac{dp}{dx} = \sec^2 u\,\dfrac{du}{dx}$.

$\sec^2 u\,\dfrac{du}{dx} = a\sqrt{1 + \tan^2 u} = a\sec u$ \quad(since $\sec u > 0$)
$\sec u\,\dfrac{du}{dx} = a$
$\displaystyle\int \sec u\, du = \int a\, dx$
$\ln|\sec u + \tan u| = ax + C$

When $x = 0$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$, so $p = 0$ and $u = 0$. Hence $\ln|1| = 0 + C \;\Rightarrow\; C = 0$.

$\sec u + \tan u = e^{ax}$
$\sec u - \tan u = \dfrac{1}{\sec u + \tan u} = e^{-ax}$

Subtracting:
$2\tan u = e^{ax} - e^{-ax}$
$\therefore\; p = \tan u = \dfrac{e^{ax} - e^{-ax}}{2}$ (shown)

parts.text: Given that $a = -0.0329$ and $k = 0.701$, find $y$ in terms of $x$.
parts.label: iii

stem: Figure 1 shows a cylinder with radius $r$ cm. As shown in Figure 2, the cylinder can be inscribed in a hemisphere with fixed radius $k$ cm such that the circumference of the top surface of the cylinder is in contact with the curved surface of the hemisphere. A cross-sectional view of the cylinder and hemisphere is shown in Figure 3.

parts.text: Show that the volume of the cylinder, $V$ cm$^3$, is given by $V = \pi r^2\sqrt{k^2 - r^2}$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Height of cylinder, $h = \sqrt{k^2 - r^2}$
$V = \pi r^2 (\text{height})$
$= \pi r^2\sqrt{k^2 - r^2}$ (shown)

parts.text: Use differentiation to find, in terms of $k$, the value of $r$ which gives a maximum value of $V$, justifying that this value indeed gives a maximum $V$. Hence write down the exact maximum volume of the cylinder in terms of $k$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$\dfrac{dV}{dr} = \pi\left[r^2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}(k^2-r^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(-2r) + \sqrt{k^2-r^2}\,(2r)\right]$
$= \dfrac{\pi r\left[-r^2 + 2(k^2-r^2)\right]}{\sqrt{k^2-r^2}}$
$= \dfrac{\pi r\left[2k^2 - 3r^2\right]}{\sqrt{k^2-r^2}}$
Let $\dfrac{dV}{dr} = 0$:
$2k^2 - 3r^2 = 0$ (since $r \neq 0$)
$3r^2 = 2k^2$
$r = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}k$ (since $r > 0$)
To show maximum $V$, 1st derivative test:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline r & \left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}k\right)^- & \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}k & \left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}k\right)^+ \\ \hline \text{Sign of } \frac{dV}{dr} & +\text{ve} & 0 & -\text{ve} \\ \hline\end{array}$$
Hence $V$ is a maximum at $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}k$.
Maximum volume $= \pi \cdot \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}k^3$ cm$^3$

parts.text: Sketch the graph showing the volume of the cylinder as the radius of the cylinder varies.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution: Graph of $V$ against $r$ with maximum at $\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}k,\, \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}\pi k^3\right)$, passing through $(0,0)$ and $(k,0)$ (both excluded).

parts.text: It is given that the volume of the cylinder increases at a constant rate of $\sqrt{3}\pi k^2$ cm$^3$ per minute. Find the rate at which the radius of the cylinder is increasing when $r = 0.5k$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
$\dfrac{dr}{dt} = \dfrac{dr}{dV} \times \dfrac{dV}{dt}$
$= \dfrac{\sqrt{k^2 - (0.5k)^2}}{\pi(0.5k)\left[2k^2 - 3(0.5k)^2\right]}\left(\sqrt{3}\pi k^2\right)$
$= 2.4$ cm/min

stem: The diagram shows a regular hexagon with length of side 6 cm. The hexagon consists of six equilateral triangles.

parts.text: Find the sum of interior angles of the hexagon.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Sum of interior angles $= (6 - 2) \times 180^\circ = 720^\circ$.

parts.text: Find the value of $h$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Each of the six triangles is equilateral with side $6$ cm. Half the side $= 3$ cm.
$\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{6} \Rightarrow h = 6 \sin 60^\circ = 3\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{27}$
$h = 5.1961 \approx 5.20$ (3 s.f.)
\textbf{Alternative}: $h = \sqrt{6^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{27} \approx 5.20$.

parts.text: Find the area of the hexagon.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Area of hexagon $= 6 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times \sqrt{27}$
$= 18\sqrt{27} = 54\sqrt{3}$
$= 93.5307 \approx 93.5$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: The hexagon forms the base of a pyramid with a height of 10 cm. Find the total surface area of the pyramid.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
Slant height of a lateral face $\ell = \sqrt{h^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{27 + 100} = \sqrt{127}$
$\ell = 11.2694 \approx 11.3$ cm.
Area of one triangular face $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times \sqrt{127} = 3\sqrt{127} = 33.8082$ cm$^2$.
Total lateral area $= 6 \times 33.8082 = 202.8497$ cm$^2$.
Total surface area $= 93.5307 + 202.8497 = 296.3804$
$\approx 296$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.)

stem: A shop is having a promotion on its candles.

parts.text:
Cleo wants to buy a candle for her room and plans to place it on her bookshelf.
The bookshelf has a height of $35$ cm.
In the diagram below, two candles $P$ and $Q$ are **similar** in shape.
Candle $P$ has a radius of $3$ cm and height of $12$ cm.
Candle $Q$ has a radius of $8$ cm.

Cleo would like to buy Candle $Q$.
Determine if Candle $Q$ can fit into her bookshelf.
Show your working.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: Yes, the candle can fit into her bookshelf as its height is $32$ cm, which is less than $35$ cm.
parts.solution:
By similar candles, the ratio of corresponding lengths is constant:
$\frac{\text{radius}_P}{\text{radius}_Q} = \frac{\text{height}_P}{\text{height}_Q}$
$\frac{3}{8} = \frac{12}{h}$
$3h = 96$
$h = 32$ cm

Since $32$ cm $< 35$ cm, Candle $Q$ can fit into the bookshelf.

parts.text:
The shop owner needs to export some candles to his customers in Korea by airfreight. He has to pack the candles into the cartons. In order to lower the airfreight cost, he has to minimise the empty space left in the carton after packing the candles.

The diagram shows the two types of packing, Type $A$ and Type $B$.

The table shows the dimensions of the carton and candle, as well as the packing requirements.
$$\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Carton dimensions} & \text{Length 50 cm, Width 30 cm, Height 40 cm.} \\ \hline \text{Candle dimensions} & \text{Height 5 cm, Radius 3 cm.} \\ \hline \text{Type } A \text{ packing} & \text{Candles are placed vertically in the carton.} \\ \hline \text{Type } B \text{ packing} & \text{Candles are placed horizontally in the carton.} \\ \hline \text{Assumptions} & \text{1) Candles can be packed in as many layers as possible.} \\ & \text{2) Candles are to be packed in the same manner within} \\ & \text{the same carton in the respective type of packing.} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
parts.label: b

subparts.text:
Which type of packing could pack more candles into this carton?
Show your working.
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: Type $A$ packs more (Type $A$: $8 \times 8 \times 5 = 320$ candles; Type $B$: $8 \times 6 \times 6 = 288$ candles).
subparts.solution:
**Type $A$ (vertical packing):** candle stands up; diameter $6$ cm, height $5$ cm.
Per layer: $\lfloor 50/6 \rfloor \times \lfloor 30/6 \rfloor = 8 \times 5$ candles
Number of layers: $\lfloor 40/5 \rfloor = 8$
Total: $8 \times 5 \times 8 = 320$ candles

**Type $B$ (horizontal packing):** candle lies on its side.
$\lfloor 50/6 \rfloor \times \lfloor 30/5 \rfloor \times \lfloor 40/6 \rfloor = 8 \times 6 \times 6 = 288$ candles

subparts.text: Using your answer in part **(i)**, calculate the volume of the empty space left in the carton after packing the candles in the carton. Leave your answer to the nearest whole number.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Volume of carton $= 50 \times 30 \times 40 = 60\,000$ cm$^3$
Volume of one candle $= \pi (3)^2 (5) = 45\pi$ cm$^3$
Volume of $320$ candles $= 320 \times 45\pi = 14\,400\pi$ cm$^3$
Volume of empty space $= 60\,000 - 14\,400\pi$
$\approx 60\,000 - 45\,238.93\ldots$
$\approx 14\,761$ cm$^3$ (to the nearest whole number)
