stem: Mr Kim receives the following utility bill for his household in a particular month. The utility bill charges for the household is about the same every month. There are $3$ people in the Kim family. Each of them showers once per day. The percentage of water they use showering is the same as the percentage for a typical Singapore household. The family uses an average of $420$ litres of water per day.

parts.text: Calculate the amount of water used for showering each day by the Kim family.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: $\frac{29}{100} \times 420 = 121.8$ litres

parts.text: Each person in the Kim family reduces $5$ litres per shower each day. Assume that there are $30$ days in a month. Show that the total average amount of water used by the family in each month is $12.15\text{ m}^{3}$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Reduction per day $= 5 \times 3 = 15$ litres.
Total water used each day $= 420 - 15 = 405$ litres.
Total water used each month $= 405 \times 30 = 12150$ litres
$= \frac{12150}{1000} = 12.15$ m$^{3}$ (shown)

parts.text: Mr Kim made a claim about water savings (see image). Assume that there are $30$ days in a month. Is Mr Kim's claim correct? Justify your decision with calculations.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Total cost of water services with savings (Mr Kim's plan, monthly use $= 12.15$ m$^{3}$):
Water usage: $12.15 \times 1.2 = \$14.58$
Waterborne fee: $12.15 \times 0.9 = \$10.94$ (2 d.p.)
Water tax: $14.58 \times 50\% = \$7.29$
Total $= 14.58 + 10.94 + 7.29 = \$32.81$ (2 d.p.)

Total cost without savings (monthly use $= \frac{420 \times 30}{1000} = 12.6$ m$^{3}$):
Water usage: $12.6 \times 1.2 = \$15.12$
Waterborne fee: $12.6 \times 0.9 = \$11.34$
Water tax: $15.12 \times 50\% = \$7.56$
Total $= 15.12 + 11.34 + 7.56 = \$34.02$

Percentage of savings $= \frac{34.02 - 32.81}{34.02} \times 100\% = 3.56\%$ (3 s.f.) $> 3\%$
The savings of $3.56\%$ exceed $3\%$, so the family will save at least $3\%$ on the total cost of water services each month.
Hence, Mr Kim is correct.

stem: Figure I shows a sector $OAB$ of a circle with centre $O$ and radius 12 cm. The region $CABD$ is cut out from the sector and folded to form the frustum shown in Figure II. The small cone in Figure II has a radius of 2 cm.

parts.text: Show that the radius of the top of the frustum is 4 cm.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Arc $AB = \frac{120}{360}\times2\pi(12) = 8\pi$ cm
Circumference of frustum top $= 8\pi$ cm
$2\pi R = 8\pi$
$R = 4$ cm (shown)

parts.text: Find the volume of the frustum.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Height of large cone $H = \sqrt{12^2-4^2} = \sqrt{128}$ cm
$\frac{h}{\sqrt{128}} = \frac{2}{4}$
$h = \frac{\sqrt{128}}{2}$ cm
Volume of frustum $= \frac{1}{3}\pi(4)^2\sqrt{128} - \frac{1}{3}\pi(2)^2\left(\frac{\sqrt{128}}{2}\right)$
$= 189.5630054 - 23.69537567$
$= 165.8676297 \approx 166$ cm$^3$

parts.text: A cylinder of height 7 cm is attached to the frustum to form a vase as shown in Figure III. Water is poured into the vase at a constant rate, and it takes 10 seconds to fill up the vase. The manufacturer wants to modify the vase such that the height of the cylinder is 1.5 times of its current height. The manufacturer claims that it will take approximately 2.5 seconds more to fill up the modified vase. Assuming that the water is being filled up at the same rate as before, is the manufacturer's claim correct? Justify your answers with calculations.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: No — it takes about 1.73 s more, not 2.5 s
parts.solution:
Vol of vase $= \pi(2)^2(7) + 165.8676297 = 253.832224$ cm$^3$
Rate of water flow $= \frac{253.832224}{10} = 25.3832224$ cm$^3$/s
New height of cylinder $= 1.5\times7 = 10.5$ cm
New vol of vase $= \pi(2)^2(10.5) + 165.8676297 = 297.8145212$ cm$^3$
Time taken $= \frac{297.8145212}{25.3832224} = 11.73273103$ s
The manufacturer's claim is incorrect as it takes 1.73 s more to fill up the modified vase.

stem: The picture shows a tank trailer driven on the road to transport different kinds of fuel such as crude oil. The tank on the trailer is modelled as a cylinder with length $12$ m and diameter $4$ m.

parts.text: For safety reasons, the tank can only be filled to a maximum of $80\%$ of its capacity. Find the volume of fuel the tank should hold due to safety reasons. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of full cylindrical tank $= \pi r^{2} h = \pi (2)^{2}(12) = 48\pi \approx 150.796 \text{ m}^{3}$.
Safe volume $= 150.796 \times 0.8 = 120.6371\ldots \approx 120.64 \text{ m}^{3}$ (to 2 d.p.).

parts.text: The exterior of the tank is to be painted. The table (shown in the image) gives the price comparison between Company A and Company B. Which company would you hire to paint the exterior of the tank? Show your working clearly and explain your answer.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Cost for Company A $= \$5320$; Cost for Company B $= \$5280$. Therefore Company B is cheaper.
parts.solution:
External surface area $= 2\pi r^{2} + 2\pi r h = 2\pi(2)^{2} + 2\pi(2)(12) = 8\pi + 48\pi = 56\pi \approx 175.93 \text{ m}^{2}$.

**Company A** (charged by area band): $175.93 \text{ m}^{2}$ falls in the band $151 - 200 \text{ m}^{2}$, cost $= \$5320$.
**Company B** (charged per $\text{m}^{2}$, rounding $175.93$ to $176 \text{ m}^{2}$): cost $= 176 \times \$30 = \$5280$.

Since $\$5280 < \$5320$, **Company B** should be hired (it is cheaper).

stem: [The volume of a cone of base radius $r$ and height $h$ is given by $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$.] A disposable cup for water dispenser, in the form of a cone, is made from a circular piece of paper of radius 8 cm with negligible thickness. A sector is cut off from the piece of paper as shown in Fig. 1. The rest of the paper is then folded to form a cone with slant height 8 cm, base radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm as shown in Fig. 2.

parts.text: Find the maximum volume of the cone, giving your answer in exact form.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
$h^2 + r^2 = 8^2$
$r^2 = 64 - h^2$
$V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \frac{1}{3}\pi(64 - h^2)h = \frac{1}{3}\pi(64h - h^3)$
$\frac{dV}{dh} = \frac{1}{3}\pi(64 - 3h^2)$
At Stat point, $\frac{dV}{dh} = 0$
$64 - 3h^2 = 0$
$h^2 = \frac{64}{3}$
$h = \frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}$ (since $h > 0$)
$\frac{d^2 V}{dh^2} = -2\pi h$
When $h = \frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}$, $\frac{d^2 V}{dh^2} = -2\pi\left(\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) = -\frac{16}{3}\sqrt{3}\pi < 0$
$\therefore h = \frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}$ will give a maximum $V$
$\therefore V = \frac{1}{3}\pi\left[64\left(\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) - \left(\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)^3\right] = \pi\left(\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}\right)\left(64 - \left(\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)^2\right)$
$= \frac{1024\sqrt{3}}{27}\pi$

parts.text: Show that $r = \sqrt{2}h$ when the volume of the cone is a maximum.
parts.label: ii

parts.text: The cone with the volume found in (i) is then inverted and is held with its axis vertical and vertex downwards. Water from the dispenser flows into the cone at a rate of $3\pi$ cm$^3$ per second. At time $t$ seconds after the start, the radius of the water surface is $x$ cm as shown in Fig. 3. Find the rate of change of the height of the water in the cone after 6 seconds.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Let the height and volume of the water be $y$ cm and $V'$ cm$^3$ respectively.
By similar triangle,
$\frac{y}{x} = \frac{h}{r}$
$x = \sqrt{2} y$
$V' = \frac{1}{3}\pi x^2 y = \frac{1}{3}\pi(\sqrt{2}y)^2 y = \frac{2}{3}\pi y^3$
$\frac{dV'}{dy} = 2\pi y^2$
When $t = 6$, $V' = 18\pi$
$18\pi = \frac{2}{3}\pi y^3$
$y^3 = 27$
$y = 3$
$\frac{dV'}{dt} = \frac{dV'}{dy} \times \frac{dy}{dt}$
$3\pi = 2\pi(3)^2 \frac{dy}{dt}$
$\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{1}{6}$ cm/s

stem: A container is a prism with a triangular cross-section. The container has a height of $3h$ cm and uniform width. Water is poured into the container at a constant rate. It takes 18 seconds to fill the container.

parts.text: Find the time taken for the water level to reach a depth of $2h$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: $8$ seconds

parts.text: On the axes in the answer space, sketch the graph of the height of the water level against time.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Concave-down curve from $(0,0)$ to $(18, 3h)$; water level rises fast at first then slows because the triangular cross-section widens upward.
parts.solution: Plot points $(2, h)$, $(8, 2h)$ and $(18, 3h)$ on the axes provided. Join with a smooth increasing curve, concave down (square-root shape) passing through the origin since at $t = 0$, $h = 0$.

stem:
Yan is intending to travel from Singapore to Kuala Lumpur with his family. He is considering between three different modes of transportation: Option 1 — direct flight from Singapore to Kuala Lumpur; Option 2 — direct drive from Singapore to Kuala Lumpur; Option 3 — trains from Singapore (Woodlands) $\to$ JB Sentral $\to$ Gemas $\to$ KL Sentral.
$$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Mode} & \text{Plane} & \text{Train (Woodlands-JB)} & \text{Train (JB-Gemas)} & \text{Train (Gemas-KL)} & \text{Car} \\ \hline \text{Passenger capacity} & 300 & 320 & 150 & 125 & 5 \\ \hline \text{Travel duration} & 60\text{-}65 \text{ min} & 5 \text{ min} & 4\text{h }45\text{m} & 2\text{h }35\text{m} & 6\text{-}7 \text{ h} \\ \hline \text{Distance (km)} & 310 & 5 & 205 & 130 & 370 \\ \hline \text{Fuel} & & 6 \text{ gal} & 200 \text{ gal} & 130 \text{ gal} & 45 \text{ L} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
Fuel efficiency is the distance a vehicle can travel per unit of fuel (measured in litres per kilometre). $1$ gallon $= 3.785$ litres.

parts.text: The pie charts show the breakdown of total fuel consumption for a flight. The amount of fuel needed for cruising during any flight is $5760/1000$ km. In case of emergencies, it is mandatory for all flights to carry an additional $20\%$ of the total fuel needed to complete the flight. Find the amount of fuel, in litres, required for the plane to fly from Singapore to Kuala Lumpur.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Total % for non-cruising phase $= 15\% + 7\% + 2\% = 24\%$, so cruising $= 76\%$.
Amount of fuel for cruising $= \dfrac{5760}{1000} \times 310 = 1785.6$ l
Total fuel needed $= 1785.6 \div 76\% \times 120\% = 2819.37$ l $\approx 2820$ l (3 s.f.)

parts.text: Yan is looking to travel using the mode that is the most fuel efficient per passenger. Suggest a suitable mode of transport for Yan and his family to travel to Kuala Lumpur. Justify the decision you made and show your calculations clearly.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Fuel efficiency per passenger (L/km): Car $= \dfrac{45}{370 \times 5} \approx 0.02432$; Plane $= \dfrac{2819.37}{310 \times 300} \approx 0.03032$; Average train $= \dfrac{0.01419 + 0.02462 + 0.03028}{3} \approx 0.02303$. The train has the smallest fuel consumption per passenger-kilometre, so Yan should choose the train.
parts.solution:
Fuel efficiency per passenger (l/km):
Car: $\dfrac{45}{370 \times 5} = 0.024324$
Plane: $\dfrac{2819.37}{310 \times 300} = 0.030316$
Train Singapore to JB: $\dfrac{6 \times 3.785}{5 \times 320} = 0.014194$
Train JB to Gemas: $\dfrac{200 \times 3.785}{205 \times 150} = 0.024618$
Train Gemas to KL: $\dfrac{130 \times 3.785}{130 \times 125} = 0.03028$
Average fuel efficiency for train $= \dfrac{0.014194 + 0.024618 + 0.03028}{3} = 0.023031$
Yan should choose the train as it is the most fuel efficient per passenger.

parts.text: State one assumption you have made in the above calculations.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: The vehicles are at full passenger capacity.
parts.solution: The vehicles are at full passenger capacity (e.g. the car carries 5 passengers, the plane 300, etc.).

stem: A circle with fixed radius $r$ cm is inscribed in an isosceles triangle $ABC$ where $\angle ABC=\theta$ radians and $AB=BC$. The circle touches all three sides at $D$, $E$ and $F$, as shown in Fig. 1.

parts.text: Show that the length $BD$ can be expressed as $r\cot\dfrac{\theta}{2}$ cm.
parts.label: i
parts.solution: $BD$ is the tangent length from $B$; with the incentre $O$, $\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}=\dfrac{r}{BD}$, so $BD=r\cot\dfrac{\theta}{2}$ (shown).

parts.text: By finding the length $AD$ in terms of $r$ and $\theta$, show that the perimeter of triangle $ABC$ can be expressed as $4r\cot\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\theta}{4}\right)+2r\cot\dfrac{\theta}{2}$ cm.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$\angle BAC=\dfrac{\pi-\theta}{2}$, so $\angle DAO=\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\theta}{4}$ and $AD=r\cot\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\theta}{4}\right)$.
Tangent lengths: $AD=AF=CE=CF=r\cot\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\theta}{4}\right)$, $BD=BE=r\cot\dfrac{\theta}{2}$.
Perimeter $=4r\cot\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\theta}{4}\right)+2r\cot\dfrac{\theta}{2}$ (shown).

parts.text: Using differentiation, find the exact value of $\theta$ such that the perimeter of triangle $ABC$ is minimum. Find the minimum perimeter, leaving your answer in the form $a\sqrt{b}\,r$ cm, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers to be determined.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
$\dfrac{dP}{d\theta}=r\,\mathrm{cosec}^2\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\theta}{4}\right)-r\,\mathrm{cosec}^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}=0$.
This gives $2\sin^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}+\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}-1=0\Rightarrow\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}=\dfrac12$ (rejecting $-1$).
$\dfrac{\theta}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\Rightarrow\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ (in $0<\theta<\tfrac{\pi}{2}$).
$P=4r\cot\dfrac{\pi}{6}+2r\cot\dfrac{\pi}{6}=6r\sqrt3=6\sqrt3\,r$ cm.

parts.text: Fig. 2 shows a sphere of fixed radius inscribed in an inverted right circular cone with base radius $R$ cm and slant height $2R$ cm; the sphere touches the slopes and the base. Fluorescent liquid leaks into the bottom of the inverted cone at a rate of $2$ cm$^3$ per minute. Assuming the leaked liquid does not reach the exterior of the sphere, find the exact rate of increase of the depth of the leaked liquid when its volume is $24$ cm$^3$. Express your answer in terms of $\pi$. [Volume of a cone of base radius $r$ and height $h$ is $\tfrac13\pi r^2 h$.]
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
Cone semi-vertical angle: $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{R}{2R}=\dfrac12\Rightarrow\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
Leaked liquid forms a small cone (apex angle the same), radius $\rho=h\tan\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt3}$.
$V=\dfrac13\pi\rho^2 h=\dfrac13\pi\cdot\dfrac{h^2}{3}\cdot h=\dfrac{\pi h^3}{9}$, so $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=\dfrac{\pi h^2}{3}$.
When $V=24$: $h^3=\dfrac{216}{\pi}\Rightarrow h^2=\dfrac{36}{\pi^{2/3}}$.
$\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{dV/dt}{dV/dh}=\dfrac{2}{\pi h^2/3}=\dfrac{6}{\pi h^2}=\dfrac{6\pi^{2/3}}{36\pi}=\dfrac{1}{6\sqrt[3]{\pi}}$ cm/min.

stem: The Penang Hill funicular railway which climbs the Penang Hill was built in 1923. The diagram shows a schematic drawing of the railway. During the journey from the start (foot of the hill) to the end point (top of the hill), the passenger carriage makes a vertical gain of $691.4$ m. The horizontal distance between $M$ and $N$ is $1810$ m.

parts.text: Calculate the angle of elevation, $\theta$, of the Penang Hill funicular railway.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the length of the railway track.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The railway is built on supporting structures in the form of arches which can withstand an overall maximum load of 140 tonnes. The information table shows some technical parameters of the Penang Hill funicular railway. ($1$ tonne $= 1000$ kg.) Some further details of the Penang Hill funicular railway are as follows: Operating hours are from 0900 till 1900. Ticket for the 2-way ride (up and down the hill) costs $\$45$ per person. Rides up and down the hill are scheduled every hour, with each ride taking 30 minutes non-stop. Only 1 passenger carriage is used for the rides up and down the hill. The government of Penang claims that the Penang Hill funicular railway receives a daily estimated total of at least $\$80000$ from the sale of tickets for the rides. Assuming the average weight of a passenger is 75 kg, justify with calculations, if the claim made by the government of Penang is true.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Cross-sectional area of I-beam $= (150 \cdot 15) + (75 \cdot 15) + (270 \cdot 15) = 7425$ mm$^{2}$. Mass of track $= 7425 \times 10^{-4}$ m$^{2} \times 1937.59$ m $\times 8030$ kg/m$^{3} \approx 115524$ kg. Max allowable passengers weight $= 140000 - 115524 - 14500 = 9976$ kg, so max passengers per ride $= 9976 / 75 \approx 133$. Rides per day (10 hr / 1 hr per round) $= 10$ two-way rides. Max passengers/day $= 133 \times 10 = 1330$. Max daily revenue $= 1330 \times \$45 = \$59850 < \$80000$, so the claim is false.
parts.solution:
Maximum load for the supporting arches $= 140 \times 1000 = 140000$ kg.
Cross-sectional area of track $= (150 \times 15) + (75 \times 15) + (270 \times 15) = 7425\ \text{mm}^{2}$.
Mass of track $= \dfrac{7425}{100} \times 1937.585712 \times 100 \times 8.03 = 115524.1885$ kg.
(Total fixed mass) $= 115524.1885 + 14500 = 130024.1885$ kg.
Maximum allowable weight of passengers $= 140000 - 130024.1885 = 9975.8115$ kg.
No.\ of passengers carriage can carry on each ride $= \dfrac{9975.8115}{75} \approx 133.01 \to 133$.
Maximum no.\ of single-rides in one day $= \dfrac{10 \times 60}{30} = 20 \Rightarrow$ maximum no.\ of two-way rides in one day $= 10$.
Maximum no.\ of passengers taking the rides each day $= 133 \times 10 = 1330$.
Maximum money received from ticket sales each day $= 1330 \times 45 = \$59850\ (< \$80000)$.

Hence, \textbf{the claim is false} as the maximum revenue from ticket sales is less than the stated $\$80000$.

stem: A game has two sets of eight icons. One icon from each set is randomly chosen to be displayed on each turn, starting with set $1$. The icons for each set are shown in the diagram. For example, if an icon is chosen from set $2$, the display would be as shown.

parts.text: Find the probability that, on one turn,
parts.label: a

subparts.text: $00$ is displayed,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Set 1 has $4$ circle icons out of $8$; Set 2 has $2$ circle icons out of $8$.
$P(\text{circle and circle}) = \frac{4}{8} \times \frac{2}{8} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{8}$

subparts.text: at least one icon is displayed,
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$P(\text{at least one circle}) = 1 - P(\text{no circle from either set})$
$= 1 - \frac{4}{8} \times \frac{6}{8}$
$= 1 - \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3}{4}$
$= 1 - \frac{3}{8} = \frac{5}{8}$

parts.text: The game is now programmed such that no two same icons will appear in the display. Draw a tree diagram to show the probabilities of all the possible outcomes.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Tree diagram with branches from set $1$ and set $2$ showing conditional probabilities (no repeats of identical icons).
parts.solution:
Set 1 (chosen first): circle $\frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2}$, junk $\frac{1}{8}$, rocket $\frac{2}{8} = \frac{1}{4}$, graduate $\frac{1}{8}$.
For Set 2 the icon type already chosen is removed, then one of the remaining icons is chosen:
After circle (2 circles removed, 6 left): junk $\frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$, rocket $\frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$, graduate $\frac{1}{6}$.
After junk (2 junks removed, 6 left): circle $\frac{1}{3}$, rocket $\frac{1}{2}$, graduate $\frac{1}{6}$.
After rocket (3 rockets removed, 5 left): circle $\frac{2}{5}$, junk $\frac{2}{5}$, graduate $\frac{1}{5}$.
After graduate (1 graduate removed, 7 left): circle $\frac{2}{7}$, junk $\frac{2}{7}$, rocket $\frac{3}{7}$.

stem: Diagram I shows a box of dimensions 100 cm by 64 cm by 75 cm.

parts.text: Find the volume of the box.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Volume $= 100 \times 64 \times 75 = 480\,000\text{ cm}^{3}$

parts.text: Diagram II shows a rectangular packet of cornflakes of dimensions 10 cm by 8 cm by 5 cm. The packet is to have a label wrapped round it which exactly covers the vertical surface area. Calculate the area of the label.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
The packet stands on a $5$ cm by $8$ cm base with a height of $10$ cm.
Perimeter of base $= 2(5 + 8) = 26$ cm
Area of label $= $ perimeter of base $\times$ height $= 26 \times 10 = 260\text{ cm}^{2}$

parts.text: Mr Wong packed the rectangular packets of cornflakes into the box, as shown in the diagram below. How many packets of cornflakes are required to fill the box completely?
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Along the $75$ cm edge: $\dfrac{75}{5} = 15$ packets
Along the $64$ cm edge: $\dfrac{64}{8} = 8$ packets
Along the $100$ cm height: $\dfrac{100}{10} = 10$ packets
Number of packets $= 15 \times 8 \times 10 = 1200$

parts.text: Mr Wong planned to sell the packets of cornflakes in the box at $\$0.75$ per packet. He managed to sell half of them at this price. The rest were sold at 12% discount. Calculate the total amount he received from selling all the cornflakes.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
Half of the packets $= \dfrac{1200}{2} = 600$
Amount from the first half $= 600 \times \$0.75 = \$450$
Discounted price $= \$0.75 \times \dfrac{88}{100} = \$0.66$
Amount from the second half $= 600 \times \$0.66 = \$396$
Total amount received $= 450 + 396 = \$846$

A curved arch that supports a bridge can be modelled by a quadratic function $y = -\dfrac{1}{5}x^{2} + \dfrac{11}{5}x$, where $x$ m is the horizontal distance from $O$ and $y$ m is the height of the arch above the surface of the water. The arch is $11$ m wide at its base. The table below shows some values of $x$ and the corresponding values of $y$.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & 2 & 4 & 5 & 7 & 8 & 10 & 11 \\ \hline y & 0 & 3.6 & 5.6 & 6 & 5.6 & p & 2 & 0 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

parts.text: Calculate the value of $p$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: On the grid provided, draw the graph of $y = -\dfrac{1}{5}x^{2} + \dfrac{11}{5}x$ for $0 \leq x \leq 11$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Plot the 8 points $(0, 0)$, $(2, 3.6)$, $(4, 5.6)$, $(5, 6)$, $(7, 5.6)$, $(8, 4.8)$, $(10, 2)$, $(11, 0)$ on the grid.
Draw a smooth curve passing through all the points.

parts.text: Use your graph to determine the maximum height of the arch above the surface of the water.

parts.text: A point on the arch is $4$ m vertically from the surface of water. Using your graph, determine the width of the arch at this height.

parts.solution:

parts.text: Find the ratio of the revenue in Year 3 to the revenue in Year 1.

stem:
The following are the information about a soda can.
Height ($h$): 11.4 cm
Outer Diameter ($d_1$): 6.4 cm
Inner Diameter ($d_2$): 5.0 cm
Density of soda $= 1.2$ g/cm$^3$
Safety information: The soda can is to be filled to a maximum of 95% of its total volume.
The soda can (above) can be modelled as a cylinder with an inner hemisphere that is hollowed inwards (concave) at the base of the can.

subparts.text: Find the base area, in square centimetres, of the soda can.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Base area $=$ (Area of big circle $-$ Area of small circle) $+$ curved surface area of hemisphere
$= \left[\pi\left(\frac{6.4}{2}\right)^2 - \pi\left(\frac{5.0}{2}\right)^2\right] + 2\pi(2.5)^2$
$= (32.169908 - 19.63495) + 39.269908$
$= 51.8048$
$= 51.8$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.)

subparts.text: Find the total volume, in cubic centimetres, of the soda can.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Total volume $=$ Volume of cylinder $-$ Volume of hemisphere
$= \pi\left(\frac{6.4}{2}\right)^2(11.4) - \frac{2}{3}\pi\left(\frac{5.0}{2}\right)^3$
$= 366.7369 - 32.72492$
$= 334.0119$
$= 334$ cm$^3$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: The material used to make the wall of the soda can must be carefully chosen such that the total mass of each filled soda can is less than 620 g. The manufacture manager of the soda can proposed to use an alloy which has a mass of 0.8 g for every 1 cm$^2$ to make the can. If the thickness of the soda can is negligible, will you accept his proposal? Justify your answer with suitable calculations.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: No — total mass $\approx 631.3$ g $> 620$ g, so the proposal is not acceptable
parts.solution:
Volume of soda in can $= \frac{95}{100}(334.0119) = 317.3113$ cm$^3$
Mass of soda $=$ Density $\times$ Volume $= 1.2 \times 317.3113 = 380.77356$ g
Area of material used $=$ Curved SA $+$ Base area $+$ Area of top circle
$= 2\pi(3.2)(11.4) + 51.8048 + \pi(3.2)^2$
$= 229.2106 + 51.8048 + 32.1699$
$= 313.1853$ cm$^2$
Mass of material used $= 313.1853 \times 0.8 = 250.54824$ g
Total mass $= 380.77356 + 250.54824 = 631.3218$ g
Since total mass $631.3218$ g $> 620$ g, therefore the proposal is not acceptable.

stem: The diagram shows a cone with a height of 30 cm and a smaller cone with a height of 22 cm. The volume of the bigger cone is $600$ cm$^{3}$. The small cone is removed from the top of the bigger cone. The diagram shows the solid remaining with a remaining slant height of $x$ cm.

parts.text: By using similar triangles, express the slant height of the smaller cone in terms of $x$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Let the slant height of the small cone be $l_{s}$ cm.
By similar triangles, $\dfrac{l_{s}}{l_{s} + x} = \dfrac{22}{30} = \dfrac{11}{15}$.
$15 l_{s} = 11 l_{s} + 11x$
$4 l_{s} = 11x$
$l_{s} = \dfrac{11}{4} x$.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the remaining solid.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let the volume of the small cone be $V_{s}$ cm$^{3}$.
Similar solids: $\dfrac{V_{s}}{600\pi} = \left(\dfrac{11}{15}\right)^{3}$
$V_{s} = \left(\dfrac{11}{15}\right)^{3} \times 600\pi = 743.37$ cm$^{3}$.
Volume required $= 600\pi - 743.37 = 1141.59 \approx 1140$ cm$^{3}$ (3 s.f.).

stem: It is given that the volume of a circular cone with base radius $r$ and vertical height $H$ is $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 H$. Figure 1 shows an IV fluid bag modelled by a cylindrical and a conical section. The radius is 4 cm, cylindrical height 20 cm, conical height 4 cm. The height from the apex of the cone to the fluid level is $h$ cm.

parts.text: Fluid is delivered at a rate of 50 cm$^3$/hour. Find $h$ and the volume when $h$ is decreasing at 1.21 cm/hour.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
The liquid level could be in the cylindrical or conical section. Assume cylindrical section of height $L$ and constant cross-sectional area $16\pi$:
$V = \pi r^2 L = 16\pi L$
$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 16\pi \dfrac{dL}{dt}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{dL}{dt} = \dfrac{-50}{16\pi} = -0.99472$ cm/h for $h \geq 4$.
Since $\dfrac{dL}{dt} = -0.99472 \neq -1.21$, liquid level is in the conical section, so $h < 4$.

Let $r$ be the radius of the water surface in the conical section. From similar triangles, $r = h$.
$V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi h^3$
$\dfrac{dV}{dh} = \pi h^2$
$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{dV}{dh} \cdot \dfrac{dh}{dt}$
$-50 = \pi h^2 (-1.21)$
$h^2 = \dfrac{50}{1.21\pi}$
$h = 3.6267 \approx 3.63$ cm (3 sf)

$V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi (3.6267)^3 = 49.9552 \approx 50.0$ cm$^3$ (3 sf)

parts.text:
Once the IV fluid enters the body, it is mixed with the blood and circulated through the blood vascular system (arteries, capillaries and veins). Due to the viscous nature of blood and friction with the blood vessel walls, resistance to blood flow is generated. To measure this resistance, the blood vessel is modelled as a cylinder with length $L$ and radius $r$. The resistance $R$ is given by the equation
$$R = \mu\left(\frac{L}{r^4}\right)$$
where $\mu$ is a positive constant determined by the viscosity of the blood in the body.

Figure 2 shows a main blood vessel with radius $r_1$, branching at an acute angle of $\theta$ into a smaller blood vessel with radius $r_2$. The length $AD$ is given as $m$ while the length $CD$ is given as $k$. The total resistance, $R_T$, of the path $ABC$ is the sum of the resistance of the path $AB$ (with radius $r_1$) and the resistance of the path $BC$ (with radius $r_2$).

Show that $R_T = \mu\left(\frac{m - k\cot\theta}{r_1^4} + \frac{k\csc\theta}{r_2^4}\right)$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
From the diagram (right-angled triangles in branching):
$\dfrac{k}{BD} = \tan\theta \Rightarrow BD = k\cot\theta$
$AB = m - k\cot\theta$
$R_{AB} = \mu\left(\dfrac{m - k\cot\theta}{r_1^4}\right)$

$\dfrac{k}{BC} = \sin\theta \Rightarrow BC = k\csc\theta$
$R_{BC} = \mu\left(\dfrac{k\csc\theta}{r_2^4}\right)$

$\therefore R_T = R_{AB} + R_{BC} = \mu\left(\dfrac{m - k\cot\theta}{r_1^4} + \dfrac{k\csc\theta}{r_2^4}\right)$ (shown)

parts.text: Show that $\cos\theta = \frac{r_2^4}{r_1^4}$ gives a stationary value of $R_T$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
$\dfrac{dR_T}{d\theta} = \mu\left[-\dfrac{k(-\csc^2\theta)}{r_1^4} + \dfrac{k(-\csc\theta\cot\theta)}{r_2^4}\right]$
$= \mu k\left(\dfrac{\csc^2\theta}{r_1^4} - \dfrac{\csc\theta\cot\theta}{r_2^4}\right)$
$= \mu k\left(\dfrac{\csc^2\theta}{r_1^4} - \dfrac{\csc^2\theta\cos\theta}{r_2^4}\right)$
$= \mu k\csc^2\theta\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1^4} - \dfrac{\cos\theta}{r_2^4}\right)$

When $\dfrac{dR_T}{d\theta} = 0$:
$\csc\theta = 0$ (no solution) or $\dfrac{1}{r_1^4} - \dfrac{\cos\theta}{r_2^4} = 0$
$\therefore \cos\theta = \dfrac{r_2^4}{r_1^4}$ (shown)

parts.text: Explain why this gives the least resistance.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
Using the first derivative test:
$\dfrac{dR_T}{d\theta} = \dfrac{\mu k \csc^2\theta}{r_2^4}\left(\dfrac{r_2^4}{r_1^4} - \cos\theta\right)$

For acute $\theta$, $\cos\theta$ is decreasing.
- When $\theta < \theta_0$ (i.e. $\cos\theta > \dfrac{r_2^4}{r_1^4}$): $\dfrac{dR_T}{d\theta} < 0$
- When $\theta = \theta_0$ (i.e. $\cos\theta = \dfrac{r_2^4}{r_1^4}$): $\dfrac{dR_T}{d\theta} = 0$
- When $\theta > \theta_0$ (i.e. $\cos\theta < \dfrac{r_2^4}{r_1^4}$): $\dfrac{dR_T}{d\theta} > 0$

Hence the stationary value is a minimum, giving the least total resistance.

stem:
Martin is trying to build a small dam at a river. In the event of heavy rain, the dam restricts the flow of the water to prevent a flood. Figure 1 shows a map of the river, drawn to scale. He hopes to build the dam at the narrowest part of the river. To better design the dam, Martin measured the depth of the river at 10 different locations during a rainy day. The data obtained is presented in Figure 2. One possible prototype of the dam is shown in Figure 3. The base of the dam is designed to be thicker to account for the greater pressure exerted by the water. The dam has height $h$ m and a length $l$ m and the inclined part of the dam makes an angle of $\theta^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. The width of the dam, $w$ m, should cover the width of the river completely.
Design specifications:
- The height of the dam, $h$ m, should be $10\%$ greater than the depth of the water at the location it is built.
- The length of the dam, $l$ m, should be as small as possible and satisfy the inequality $\min(2h,\ w) \leq l \leq 3$. [The minimum function $\min$ gives the smaller value of the two numbers. For e.g., $\min(2, 5) = 2$.]
- The total volume of the dam should exceed $1.5$ m$^{3}$ for the dam to be operating safely.

parts.text: Figures 1 and 2 show a scale map and a depth profile of the river.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: Find the actual width of the narrowest part of the river.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: Measure $w = 1.4$ cm $\pm 0.05$ cm on the scale map. Actual width $= 1.4 \times \dfrac{200}{100} = 2.8$ m (accept $2.7$ m, $2.8$ m or $2.9$ m).

subparts.text: Calculate a suitable value of $\theta$, leaving your answers corrected to 4 decimal places.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Decide on depth $\approx 0.59$ m (the maximum depth, so the dam will not overflow even with $10\%$ greater height).
$h = \dfrac{110}{100} \times 0.59 = 0.649$ m.
$\min(0.649 \times 2,\ 2.8) = \min(1.298,\ 2.8) = 1.298$ m, so a suitable $l = 1.298$ m.
$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{0.649}{1.298 - 0.8}\right) = 52.49973^{\circ} = 52.4997^{\circ}$ (to 4 d.p.).

parts.text:
Two holes of radius $r$ are drilled through the length of the dam to allow some water to flow through the dam. The hollowed part resembles a truncated cylinder with circular base as shown in Figure 4. For a truncated cylinder, the volume is given by $V = \dfrac{1}{2}(h_{1} + h_{2})\pi r^{2}$. Information about the radii of the holes and their corresponding dimensions is shown in the table below.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline r\ (\text{cm}) & h_{1}\ (\text{cm}) & h_{2}\ (\text{cm}) \\ \hline 10 & 97 & 113 \\ \hline 15 & 93 & 116 \\ \hline 20 & 90 & 120 \\ \hline 25 & 86 & 124 \\ \hline 30 & 82 & 128 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
To ensure a certain rate of water flow, the shaded base area of each hole should be between $700$ cm$^{2}$ to $1000$ cm$^{2}$. Suggest a suitable radius for the holes to be drilled such that the dam can be operated safely according to all the specifications provided. Justify your decision and show your calculations clearly.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Choose $r = 15$ cm. Base area $A = \pi(15)^{2} = 706.86$ cm$^{2}$ (within $700 - 1000$ cm$^{2}$). Volume of dam prism (before drilling) $= \tfrac{1}{2}(0.8 + 1.298)(0.649)(2.8) = 1.9062$ m$^{3}$. Volume of one truncated cylinder hole $= \tfrac{1}{2}(0.93 + 1.16)\pi(0.15)^{2} = 0.073867$ m$^{3}$. Total volume remaining $= 1.9062 - 2(0.073867) = 1.76$ m$^{3} > 1.5$ m$^{3}$. So $r = 15$ cm is suitable.
parts.solution:
Volume of prism (before drilling) $= \dfrac{1}{2}(0.8 + l) \times h \times w = \dfrac{1}{2}(0.8 + 1.298) \times 0.649 \times 2.8 = 1.9062$ m$^{3}$ (to 5 s.f.).

Choose $r = 15$ cm. Then $A = \pi(15)^{2} = 706.86$ cm$^{2}$ (within $700 - 1000$ cm$^{2}$); $r = 20$ gives $A = 1256.6$ cm$^{2}$ (reject).

Volume of one truncated cylinder hole $= \dfrac{1}{2}(h_{1} + h_{2}) \pi r^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}(0.93 + 1.16) \pi (0.15)^{2} = 0.073867$ m$^{3}$.

Total volume $= 1.9062 - 2 \times 0.073867 = 1.76$ m$^{3}$ (to 3 s.f.).

Since $1.76$ m$^{3} > 1.5$ m$^{3}$, the prototype can be operated safely when $r = 15$ cm.

stem: Tower cranes are used at major construction sites to lift building materials such as steel, concrete and large tools for example, generators. The load is lifted when the jib is rotated in the vertical plane about the turntable. The turntable also allows the load being lifted to be rotated horizontally. The tower crane standing on level ground can be modelled by the diagram below. It is represented by a tower $AB$ and a jib $BC$. A vertical cable hangs from $C$ and is attached to a load on the ground at the point $L$. The jib is inclined at an angle of $x^{\circ}$ to the horizontal line $BD$.

parts.text: Calculate the angle of inclination of the jib if the vertical cable attached to the load is taut at $32$ m from the ground.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
When vertical cable $= 32$ m, $CD = 32 - 24$
$= 8$ m
$\sin x^\circ = \dfrac{8}{16}$
$x^\circ = \sin^{-1}\dfrac{8}{16}$
$= 30^\circ$
$\therefore$ Angle of inclination $= 30^\circ$

parts.text: The load is lifted from $L$ as the jib is rotated in a vertical plane about $B$. When the jib is in the position $BC$, the length of the vertical cable is increased. The load is now on the ground at the point $L'$, $10$ m from $A$. Calculate the length of the vertical cable, $C'L'$ from the tip of the jib to the ground.
parts.label: b

parts.text:
The two diagrams below show the top view (diagram 1) and the side view (diagram 2) of the maximum swing radius of the tower crane. To ensure safety, all working personnel must stay outside of the maximum swing radius of $4$ m from the load being lifted (shown as the shaded area in diagram 1). The main person-in-charge at a particular construction site is deciding if this model of tower crane is suitable for use. All the following criteria must be met for a tower crane to be used at this site:
- The maximum swing area cannot exceed $1280$ m$^{2}$.
- The tip of the tower crane's jib must be able to reach a height of $40$ m.
Useful information: The maximum swing area of a crane is the area of the circle, using the outer maximum swing radius (away from the crane tower), the load lifted might reach.
Is this tower crane suitable for use at this particular construction site? Justify your answer with calculations.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Maximum swing area $= \pi(16 + 4)^{2} = 1256.63$ m$^{2} < 1280$ m$^{2}$ (criterion met). Maximum height $= 16\sin 60^{\circ} + 24 = 37.86$ m $< 40$ m (criterion not met). Not suitable for use as the tip of the jib cannot reach a height of $40$ m.
parts.solution:
Maximum swing area happens when jib is horizontal, $AL = BC = 16$ m.
Maximum swing area $= \pi(16 + 4)^{2}$
$= 1256.63\ldots$ m$^{2} < 1280$ m$^{2}$
$\Rightarrow$ Max. swing area did not exceed $1280$ m$^{2}$.
Maximum height the tip of the tower crane's jib can reach happens when $x^\circ = 60^\circ$.
$\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{CD}{16}$
$CD = 16 \sin 60^\circ$
$= 13.8564\ldots$ m
Maximum height $= 13.8564\ldots + 24$
$= 37.8564\ldots$ m $< 40$ m
$\Rightarrow$ Tip of tower crane's jib cannot reach $40$ m.
$\therefore$ This tower crane is not suitable for use at this particular construction site as the tip of the crane's jib cannot reach a height of $40$ m.

stem: $ABCD$ is a rectangle in which $AB = 8$ cm and $BC = 6$ cm. A circular piece of wire, centre $O$, passes through the vertices of the rectangle as shown in Diagram I.

parts.text: Show that the radius of the circular wire is 5 cm.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
By Pythagoras' theorem, diagonal $= \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10$ cm.
Radius $= \frac{10}{2} = 5$ cm

parts.text: Show that angle $AOB = 106.3^\circ$, correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$\tan(\angle BOE) = \frac{4}{3}$, where $E$ is the midpoint of $AB$.
$\angle AOB = 2\angle BOE = 2\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) = 106.26^\circ = 106.3^\circ$

parts.text: Calculate the area of the shaded segment.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Area of segment $=$ area of sector $OAB -$ area of triangle $OAB$
$= \frac{106.26^\circ}{360^\circ} \times \pi(5)^2 - \frac{1}{2}(5)(5)\sin 106.26^\circ$
$= 11.2$ cm$^2$

parts.text: The circular wire is cut at $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, and four pieces joined to form the shape shown in Diagram II. Calculate the area enclosed by the wires in Diagram II.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
Angle $AOD = \frac{360^\circ - 106.26^\circ - 106.26^\circ}{2} = 73.74^\circ$
Area of segment $B = \frac{73.74^\circ}{360^\circ} \times \pi(5)^2 - \frac{1}{2}(5)(5)\sin 73.74^\circ = 4.08755$
Area enclosed $=$ rectangle $- (2A + 2B)$
$= (8 \times 6) - [2 \times 11.182 + 2 \times 4.08755]$
$= 17.5$ cm$^2$

stem:
Ryan has set up a home theatre system in one of his rooms, which is in the shape of a cuboid with dimensions 4 m by 3.6 m by 3 m.

**Figure 1** shows the three-dimensional layout of the room, where a television is mounted on the front wall $QRWV$, and two speakers are mounted on the back wall $PSWT$, at $F$ and $T$ respectively.
{{IMG:question_images/48f5d8e5-4aa9-4ccd-8e59-de61f4953dd3.png}}
Ryan is planning to put an armchair along $MN$, which is a straight path that cuts across the centre of the room from the back to the front.

**Figure 2** shows the cross-sectional view of him sitting in the armchair, where his eye level at $X$, is 1.24 m directly above the ground and $d$ m away from the front wall. The centre of the television at $Y$, is 1.6 m directly above $N$.

parts.text: Find the angle of elevation from $X$ to $Y$ when $d = 1.2$ m.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Horizontal distance $X$ to $N = d = 1.2$ m; vertical rise $= 1.6 - 1.24 = 0.36$ m. Angle of elevation $= \tan^{-1}\frac{0.36}{1.2} = 16.7^\circ$.

parts.text:
Ryan found out that:
- To have an optimal view of the television, the angle of elevation from $X$ to $Y$ should be less than $15^\circ$.
- To have an optimal audio experience, the position of the two speakers and $X$ should form an equilateral triangle.

Suggest a suitable value for $d$ such that the position of the armchair will provide Ryan with the best possible user experience.
Justify the decisions you make and show your calculations clearly.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Elevation $< 15^\circ$: $\tan^{-1}\frac{0.36}{d} < 15^\circ \Rightarrow d > 1.34$ m.
Equilateral triangle (speakers at the two back-wall top corners, $3.6$ m apart; $X$ on the centre line): $XP^2 = 1.8^2 + (4-d)^2 + (3-1.24)^2 = 3.6^2 \Rightarrow (4-d)^2 = 6.62 \Rightarrow d = 1.43$ m.
Since $1.43 > 1.34$, elevation $= \tan^{-1}\frac{0.36}{1.43} = 14.1^\circ < 15^\circ$ too. Suitable $d \approx 1.43$ m.

stem: An ice-cream mould is in the shape of a prism. The thickness of the mould is $1.5\text{ cm}$ and it has a height of $9\text{ cm}$. The cross-section of the ice-cream mould consists of a trapezium $ABCD$ and a segment $CED$. In the trapezium, $AB = 5\text{ cm}$ and the perpendicular distance between $AB$ and $DC$ is $8\text{ cm}$. Segment $CED$ is part of a circle with radius $2\text{ cm}$ and centre $O$.

parts.text: Show that $\angle COD = \dfrac{2}{3}\pi$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Total height of the cross-section $= 9$ cm (the height of the mould).
Height of the trapezium ($AB$ to $DC$) $= 8$ cm, so the depth of the segment below $DC = 9 - 8 = 1$ cm.
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $DC$. With $OE = 2$ cm (radius), $OM = OE - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1$ cm.
$\cos \angle DOM = \dfrac{OM}{OD} = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \angle DOM = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$
$\angle COD = 2 \angle DOM = \dfrac{2}{3}\pi$

parts.text: Calculate the area of segment $CDE$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution: Area of segment $= \dfrac{1}{2} r^2 (\theta - \sin\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2}(2^2)\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 2.46$ cm$^2$

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the ice-cream mould.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
$DC = 2 \times 2\sin 60^\circ = 2\sqrt{3} = 3.464$ cm
Area of trapezium $= \dfrac{1}{2}(AB + DC) \times 8 = \dfrac{1}{2}(5 + 3.464)(8) = 33.86$ cm$^2$
Cross-sectional area $= 33.86 + 2.46 = 36.31$ cm$^2$
Volume $= 36.31 \times 1.5 = 54.5$ cm$^3$

$P(\text{one } < 320 \text{ and other } > 360) = \dfrac{14}{160} \times \dfrac{56}{159} \times 2 \approx 0.0616$ (values depend on graph readings).

I disagree. The median mass of apples from tree $A$ is approximately the same as that from tree $B$, so on average apples from both trees weigh the same.

parts.text: Sketch scatter diagrams that might be expected when $x$ and $y$ are related approximately as given in cases (A) $y = ax^2 + b$ (where $a$ is negative, $b$ is positive) and (B) $y = c\ln x + d$ (where $c$ is negative, $d$ is positive). Each diagram should include 6 points in the first quadrant.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
(A) For $y = ax^2 + b$ with $a < 0$, $b > 0$: a downward-opening parabolic arc — $y$ decreases at an increasing rate.
(B) For $y = c\ln x + d$ with $c < 0$, $d > 0$: $y$ decreases at a decreasing rate.
[See diagrams in solution image]

parts.text: Draw a scatter diagram for the given data. Use your diagram to explain whether a linear model is appropriate.
parts.label: ii
parts.answer: A linear model is not appropriate as the points do not lie close to a straight line.
parts.solution:
[Scatter diagram of given $(t, W)$ data in solution image.]
As the points do not lie close to a straight line, a linear model is not appropriate. (Alternatively: $W$ decreases at a decreasing rate, so linear is not appropriate.)

parts.text: Find, correct to 4 decimal places, the product moment correlation coefficient between (a) $t$ and $W$, (b) $t^2$ and $W$, (c) $\ln t$ and $W$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
From a graphing calculator:
(a) $r$-value for $t$ and $W$: $-0.8675$ (4 d.p.).
(b) $r$-value for $t^2$ and $W$: $-0.7294$ (4 d.p.).
(c) $r$-value for $\ln t$ and $W$: $-0.9822$ (4 d.p.).

parts.text: Using your answers to parts (i), (ii) and (iii), explain which of $W = at + b$, $W = ct^2 + d$ or $W = e\ln t + f$ is the most appropriate model. Find the equation of a suitable regression line.
parts.label: iv
parts.answer: $W = e\ln t + f$ is most appropriate since $|r|$ is closest to 1. $W = -1.73\ln t + 16.9$
parts.solution:
From part (ii), the scatter pattern for $W$ against $t$ resembles case (B) — $W$ decreases at a decreasing rate. From part (iii), $|r|$ is closest to 1 for $\ln t$ vs $W$.
Hence the most appropriate model is $W = e\ln t + f$.
Regression line of $W$ on $\ln t$: $W = -1.7295\ln t + 16.929$, or $W = -1.73\ln t + 16.9$ (3 s.f.).

parts.text: Use your equation to estimate the time taken to reduce the temperature of water in the pot-in-pot cooler to $16^\circ$C and explain whether your estimate is reliable.
parts.label: v
parts.answer: $t = 1.71$ hours. The estimate is reliable since $W = 16$ lies within the given data range and $|r|$ is close to 1.
parts.solution:
When $W = 16$:
$$16 = -1.7295\ln t + 16.929 \Rightarrow \ln t = \frac{0.929}{1.7295} \Rightarrow t = e^{0.5371} \approx 1.7111$$
$t = 1.71$ hours (3 s.f.).
Since $W = 16$ lies within the given data range and $|r|$ is close to 1, the estimate is reliable.

stem: A curve $D$ has parametric equations $x = t + \frac{1}{t} + 4$, $y = t - \frac{1}{t} + 1$, $t \leq -1$. A curve $E$ has equation $y = x - 2 - \frac{1}{x - 3}$, $x \leq 2$.

parts.text: Show that curve $D$ and $E$ intersect only once at $t = -1$ and hence find the coordinates of the point of intersection.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Substitute $x = t + \tfrac{1}{t} + 4$, $y = t - \tfrac{1}{t} + 1$ into $y = x - 2 - \dfrac{1}{x - 3}$:
$$t - \frac{1}{t} + 1 = \left(t + \frac{1}{t} + 4\right) - 2 - \frac{1}{\left(t + \tfrac{1}{t} + 4\right) - 3}$$
$$t - \frac{1}{t} + 1 = t + \frac{1}{t} + 2 - \frac{1}{t + \tfrac{1}{t} + 1}$$
$$-\frac{2}{t} - 1 = -\frac{t}{t^2 + t + 1} \Rightarrow \frac{2}{t} + 1 = \frac{t}{t^2 + t + 1}$$
Multiplying out gives $t^3 + 2t^2 + 3t + 2 = 0$.
Factorise: $(t + 1)(t^2 + t + 2) = 0$.
Since $t^2 + t + 2 = 0$ has discriminant $1 - 8 < 0$, no real solution.
Hence the only real root is $t = -1$, so $D$ and $E$ intersect only once at $t = -1$.
When $t = -1$: $x = -1 - 1 + 4 = 2$, $y = -1 + 1 + 1 = 1$.
The point of intersection is $(2, 1)$.

parts.text: Sketch the graph of curve $D$, indicating clearly the point of intersection found in part (i).
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Sketch of curve $D$ (point of intersection at $(2, 1)$ indicated):
[See diagram in solution image]

parts.text: Using $x = t + 3$, parameterise the equation of $E$. Sketch the graph of $E$ on the same diagram in part (ii).
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
With $x = t + 3$:
$$y = (t + 3) - 2 - \frac{1}{(t + 3) - 3} = t + 1 - \frac{1}{t}$$
Since the point of intersection has $x = 2$, we require $x \le 2 \Rightarrow t + 3 \le 2 \Rightarrow t \le -1$.
Curve $E$: $x = t + 3$, $y = t + 1 - \dfrac{1}{t}$, $t \le -1$.
[Sketch on the same diagram as part (ii)]

parts.text: Given that $D$ intersects the $y$-axis at $t = -\sqrt{3} - 2$, find the area of the finite region bounded by $D$, $E$ and the $y$-axis, giving your answer correct to four decimal places.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
For curve $D$: $x = t + \tfrac{1}{t} + 4 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{t^2}$.
At $x = 0$: $t = -\sqrt{3} - 2$ (given). At $x = 2$: $t = -1$.
For curve $E$: $x = t + 3 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 1$.
At $x = 0$: $t = -3$. At $x = 2$: $t = -1$.
Using the $y$-axis (curve $D$ on the right, curve $E$ on the left):
$$\text{Area} = \int_{-\sqrt{3} - 2}^{-1} \left(t - \frac{1}{t} + 1\right)\left(1 - \frac{1}{t^2}\right) dt - \int_{-3}^{-1} \left(t + 1 - \frac{1}{t}\right)(1)\,dt$$
$$= 1.3929\ \text{square units (4 d.p.)}$$

stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f: x \mapsto \frac{1}{1 + x^2}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $0 < x \leq k$ where $k$ is a real constant.

parts.text: Show that $f$ has an inverse.
parts.label: i
parts.solution: Every horizontal line $y = k$ cuts the graph of $y = f(x)$ at most once. Hence $f$ is one-one and the inverse of $f$ exists.

parts.text: Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state the domain of $f^{-1}$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$y = f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}$
$\frac{1}{y} = 1 + x^2$
$x^2 = \frac{1}{y} - 1$
$x = \sqrt{\frac{1}{y} - 1}$ (reject $-\sqrt{\frac{1}{y}-1}$ since $x > 0$)
$f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{x} - 1}$
Domain of $f^{-1} = \left[\frac{1}{1+k^2}, 1\right)$

parts.text: It is further given that $k < \frac{1}{1+k^2}$. Sketch the graph of $y = f^{-1}(x)$. Your sketch should indicate the position of the graph in relation to the line $y = x$.
parts.label: iii
parts.answer: Graph of $y = f^{-1}(x)$ lies entirely above the line $y = x$.
parts.solution: See diagram.

parts.text: Deduce the number of solutions of the equation $f(x) = f^{-1}(x)$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
Since $y = f^{-1}(x)$ does not intersect the line $y = x$, it will not intersect $y = f(x)$ either. Hence there are no solutions for $f(x) = f^{-1}(x)$.

Alternative:
Since the domains of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are different, there is no solution for $f(x) = f^{-1}(x)$.

stem: Each diagram shows a container and axes for the graph of depth $d$ cm against time $t$ seconds.

parts.text: Liquid is flowing out of the full cylindrical container at a constant rate. After $t$ seconds, the depth of water in the container is $d$ cm. Sketch the graph of $d$ against $t$.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: Straight line sloping downwards from maximum depth on the $d$-axis to 0.
parts.solution:
The container is a cylinder (uniform cross-section) and liquid flows out at a constant rate, so the depth decreases at a constant rate.
Graph: straight line starting at the full depth on the $d$-axis, sloping down with constant gradient to meet the $t$-axis.

parts.text: Liquid is poured into the empty inverted-cone container at a constant rate. After $t$ seconds, the depth of water in the container is $d$ cm. Sketch the graph of $d$ against $t$.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Curve increasing steeply at first then levelling off (concave down), from O up to the maximum depth.
parts.solution:
The cone is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top, so at a constant inflow rate the depth rises quickly at first, then more and more slowly.
Graph: increasing curve through the origin, steep initially and becoming less steep (concave downwards), approaching the full depth.

stem: Janet has been a home-baker since the Covid-19 period. She bakes macarons, which take the estimated shape of a cylinder. The diameter of her macaron is $3.5$ cm and its thickness is $2.4$ cm.

parts.text: Calculate the estimated volume of each macaron.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Janet sells her macarons in boxes of $6$. Every $6$ macarons are packed in an opened top six-pocketed thermoformed pockets, with a thickness of $0.4$ cm to separate one macaron from another as shown in the diagram below. Each of these pockets in the six-pocketed thermoformed pockets was created to fit in the macarons of dimensions stated above. Find the volume occupied by air in each single row of $6$ macarons packed in the six-pocketed thermoformed pockets.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Volume of $1$ pocket $= 3.5 \times 2.4 \times 3.5 = 29.4$ cm$^3$
Volume of total air $= 6(29.4 - 23.0907) = 37.8558 = 37.9$ cm$^3$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text:
Janet also custom-makes boxes and paper bags to pack the macarons from the same supplier that creates the thermoformed pockets. The prices quoted by the supplier are as shown.
$$\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Items} & \text{Pricing} \\ \hline \text{six-pocketed thermoformed pockets} & \$2.80 \text{ each} \\ \hline \text{box for } 6 \text{ macarons} & \$1.65 \text{ per box} \\ \hline \text{paper bag} & \$0.40 \text{ each} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
In her recipe, every $12$ macarons require the following amount of ingredients.
$$\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Ingredients} & \text{Mass required (in grams)} \\ \hline \text{almond flour} & 65 \\ \hline \text{powdered sugar} & 65 \\ \hline \text{castor sugar} & 45 \\ \hline \text{egg whites} & 60 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
Each egg is estimated to contain an average of $30$ grams of egg white. The price list of a store she purchases her baking ingredients from is shown below.
$$\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Items} & \text{Pricing} \\ \hline 1\text{kg of almond flour} & \$30 \\ \hline 1\text{kg of powdered sugar} & \$2.50 \\ \hline 800 \text{ g of castor sugar} & \$2.60 \\ \hline \text{a dozen of eggs} & \$2.50 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
Janet provides delivery to her customers with the delivery costs shown below.
$$\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Purchase Amount} & \text{Delivery cost} \\ \hline \text{below } \$50 & \$15 \\ \hline \text{above } \$50 & \$10 \\ \hline \text{for bulk orders, above } \$200 & \text{Free} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
parts.label: c

subparts.text: What is Janet's cost price of making and packing one box of macarons?
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
For $12$ macarons:
cost of almond flour $= \dfrac{30}{1000} \times 65 = \$1.95$
cost of powdered sugar $= \dfrac{2.5}{1000} \times 65 = \$0.1625$
cost of castor sugar $= \dfrac{2.6}{800} \times 45 = \$0.14625$
cost of egg whites $= \dfrac{2.5}{12} \times 2 = \$0.4167$
Total cost of ingredients for $6$ macarons $= \dfrac{1}{2}(1.95 + 0.1625 + 0.14625 + 0.4167) = \$1.3377$
Total cost price (with packing) $= 1.3377 + 2.80 + 1.65 + 0.40 = \$6.1877 = \$6.19$ (nearest cent)

subparts.text: How much should Janet charge a customer who orders $72$ macarons should she want to make a profit of $30\%$? Round off your answer to the nearest dollar.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$\dfrac{72}{6} = 12$ boxes
Total cost price with delivery $= \$6.1877 \times 12 + \$10 = \$84.2524$
Selling price $= \$84.2524 \times 130\% = \$109.528 = \$110$ (nearest dollar)

Mr Aziz is planning a housewarming party from $11$ am to $5$ pm for $30$ of his friends and family. He will be using disposable cups as seen in Diagram 1. The cup can be modelled as a frustum with dimensions as shown in Diagram 2.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the cup.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of cup $= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times (3.6)^{2} \times 11.1 - \dfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times (2.4)^{2} \times 7.4$
$= 106.0099$
$= 106$ cm$^3$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: The hot drink dispenser is made using a cylinder of radius $7$ cm and height $30$ cm as shown in Diagram 3. Calculate the number of cups that can be filled with one hot drink dispenser.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Volume of the cylinder $= \pi \times 7^{2} \times 30 = 4618.1412$ cm$^3$
Total number of cups possible $= 4618.1412 \div 106.0099 = 43.56 \approx 43$ cups

parts.text:
Mr Aziz plans to serve tea during the party. Hot drink dispensers are usually rented out when batches of tea are sold. Three companies are selling each batch of tea as follow, with prices inclusive of GST.
$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|} \hline  & \textbf{The Tea Bros} & \textbf{Tarik King} & \textbf{Miss Teh Tarik} \\ \hline \textbf{Cost of the tea} & \$57\text{ per order} & \$46\text{ per order} & \$52\text{ per order} \\ \hline \textbf{Dispenser rental} & \$2\text{ per hour} & \$3\text{ per hour} & \$2\text{ per hour} \\ \hline \textbf{Islandwide delivery charges} & \$12 & \$10 & \$12 \\ \hline \textbf{Promotion} & 10\%\text{ discount on all purchase} & - & \text{Free delivery with 2 or more orders} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
Suggest a sensible amount of budget for Mr Aziz to host his party. State one assumption that you have made.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: A sensible budget is around $\$130$ (e.g. Tarik King with 2 batches: $\$124.20$). Assumption: Mr Aziz orders 2 batches of Tarik King; each guest takes 3 cups; tea filled to brim; each guest dispense tea into their cups to the brim; no spillage.
parts.solution:
Assuming Mr Aziz orders 2 batches of tea for 11 am to 5 pm (6 hours):
Total number of filled cups $= 43.56 \times 2 = 87$ cups, so most guests may drink about 3 cups each.
Cost of 2 batches:
The Tea Bros: $(\$57 + \$57 + \$2 \times 6 + \$12) \times 0.9 = \$124.20$
Tarik King: $\$46 + \$46 + \$3 \times 6 + \$10 = \$120$
Miss Teh Tarik: $\$52 + \$52 + \$2 \times 6 = \$116$
A sensible budget is $\$130$ as this will cover the cost of tea from all companies.
Assumption: Mr Aziz orders 2 batches of Teh Tarik.

stem: Here are some statistics about COVID-19 on the 5$^{\text{th}}$ of July 2021 in StarShine Island. Below is a news article about COVID-19 vaccination on the 5$^{\text{th}}$ of July 2021 in StarShine Island.

parts.text: From the 7$^{\text{th}}$ of June 2021 to the 4$^{\text{th}}$ of July 2021, when was the highest number of COVID-19 cases reported?
parts.label: a
parts.solution: The highest number of COVID-19 cases was reported on $17^{\text{th}}$ June 2021.

parts.text: As at 5$^{\text{th}}$ of July 2021, StarShine Island had 295 **active** COVID-19 cases. The following information was extracted from the Ministry of Health (MOH) of StarShine Island's official website: Active cases = In Community Facilities* + In Hospitals. *Patients who are clinically well but still test positive for COVID-19 are isolated and cared for at community facilities. Calculate the total number of cases in the community facilities as at 5$^{\text{th}}$ July 2021.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Active cases $=$ community facilities $+$ hospitals
Community facilities $= 295 - 103 = 192$

parts.text: Calculate the number of deaths due to COVID-19 as a percentage of the total number of COVID-19 cases as at 5$^{\text{th}}$ of July 2021.
parts.label: c
parts.solution: Percentage of deaths $= \dfrac{36}{62617} \times 100\% = 0.05749\% \approx 0.0575\%$

parts.text: As at 5$^{\text{th}}$ July 2021, calculate the average number of people being vaccinated per day. Give your answer correct to the nearest integer.
parts.label: d
parts.solution: Average vaccinated per day $= \dfrac{2156751}{187} = 11533.42... \approx 11533$

parts.text: The total estimated population in StarShine Island is 5.9 million. StarShine Island aims to vaccinate two-thirds of its population by the 9th of August, which is 35 days away from the 5$^{\text{th}}$ of July. Assuming that the rate of vaccination is increased by 5 times, will StarShine Island be able to achieve its aim to vaccinate two-thirds of its population by the 9$^{\text{th}}$ of August? Show your workings clearly.
parts.label: e
parts.answer: Target = $\frac{2}{3} \times 5.9 = 3.933$ million. Already vaccinated $\approx 2.2$ million. Still needed: $1.733$ million. New rate = $5 \times 11\,533 = 57\,665$ per day. Number of people that can be vaccinated in 35 days $= 57\,665 \times 35 = 2\,018\,275 > 1\,733\,300$. Yes, StarShine Island will be able to achieve its aim.
parts.solution:
Target $= \dfrac{2}{3} \times 5.9 = 3.9333$ million
Still needed $= 3.933 - 2.2 = 1.733$ million
New rate ($\times 5$): $187$ days $\to 11$ million
Time for $1.733$ million $= \dfrac{1.733}{11} \times 187 = 29.41 \approx 30$ days
Since $30$ days $< 35$ days, yes, StarShine Island will be able to achieve its aim.

stem:
Mr Robert stays in a semi-detached house and is concerned about the rising electricity costs. After reading about solar power from the newspaper, he is thinking of installing solar panels to reduce his family's electricity bills. The cost of electricity per kilowatt hour (kWh) is known as the electricity tariff rate, which is revised every quarter by SP Power. Information about the electricity tariff rates (chart shown in the figure; price before 7% GST) and monthly electricity consumptions by domestic customers are provided below.
$$\begin{array}{|l|c|} \hline \text{Type of Premise} & \text{Average Monthly Consumption (kWh)} \\ \hline \text{Apartment} & 573.27 \\ \hline \text{Terrace} & 872.82 \\ \hline \text{Semi-Detached} & 1195.87 \\ \hline \text{Bungalow} & 2364.58 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

parts.text: The electricity tariff rate for Oct$-$Dec 22 is expected to increase by 8% from Jul$-$Sep 22 due to geopolitical reasons and shortage of resources. Calculate the electricity tariff rate for Oct$-$Dec 22 to 2 decimal places.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Electricity tariff rate for Oct$-$Dec 22 $= 1.08 \times 30.17 = 32.58$ cents/kWh

parts.text: Mr Robert is currently with Best Power on a 12 month plan that offers a 6% discount off the electricity tariff rate. Estimate Mr Robert's amount paid for his family's electricity consumption in Oct 2022 after GST.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Amount paid before GST $= 1195.87 \times \$0.3258 \times 0.94 = \$366.24$
Amount paid after GST $= 1.07 \times \$366.24 = \$391.87$

parts.text: Mr Robert decides to consult another electricity provider to enquire about solar energy and solar panel installation. After an assessment is done on his house, he received an information sheet (Table 2). Roof area for installation is 9 m by 4 m; each solar panel is 1.65 m by 1 m; cost of installing every 10 solar panels is $\$6250$; average amount of electricity produced by 1 solar panel is 19 kWh per month; lifespan of solar panels is 20 years. Suggest whether Mr Robert should go ahead with installing solar panels for his house. Justify any decision you make and show your calculations clearly.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Yes, he should install. Number of panels $= 5 \times 4 = 20$; monthly generation $= 20 \times 19 = 380$ kWh; new monthly bill $\approx \$267.35$ on electricity $+ \$52.08$ panel cost/month $= \$319.43 < \$391.87$. Since the amount paid after installing the solar panels is less than currently, he should proceed.
parts.solution:
Number of solar panels: $9 \div 1.65 \approx 5$ (length) and $4 \div 1 = 4$ (width), so $5 \times 4 = 20$ panels.
Average electricity produced per month $= 20 \times 19 = 380$ kWh
Average cost per month after solar savings $= (1195.87 - 380) \times \$0.3258 \times 0.94 \times 1.07 = \$267.35$
Average cost of installing panels per month $= \dfrac{2 \times \$6250}{20 \times 12} = \$52.08$
Total average amount paid per month $= \$267.35 + \$52.08 = \$319.43$
Since the amount paid after installing the solar panels ($\$319.43$) is less than the current amount ($\$391.87$), Mr Robert should proceed with the installation.

It takes $8$ minutes to fill the container. After $t$ minutes the depth of the water is $d$ cm. Find the value of $t$ when $d = 6$ cm.

parts.text: The diagram shows a pyramid with rectangular base $ABCD$ and vertex $E$. $AB = 16$ cm, $BC = 12$ cm, $AE = BE = CE = DE$ and the height of the pyramid is $24$ cm.

subparts.text: A smaller, similar pyramid of volume $24$ cm$^3$ is removed from the top of the original pyramid. The diagram shows the solid remaining. Find the total surface area of the remaining solid.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
Volume of original pyramid $= \frac{1}{3} \times 16 \times 12 \times 24 = 1536$
$\left(\frac{l_1}{l_2}\right)^3 = \frac{24}{1536}$
$\frac{l_1}{l_2} = \frac{1}{4}$
Perpendicular height of face $AEB = \sqrt{26^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{612}$
Perpendicular height of face $BEC = \sqrt{26^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{640}$
Area of 4 triangular faces of original pyramid $= 2 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 16 \times \sqrt{612} + 2 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 12 \times \sqrt{640}$
Area of 4 triangular faces of smaller pyramid $= \frac{1}{16} \times$ (area of 4 triangular faces of original pyramid)
Area of 4 trapeziums $= \frac{15}{16} \times$ (area of 4 triangular faces of original pyramid)
Total surface area $= \frac{15}{16}\left(2 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 16 \times \sqrt{612} + 2 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 12 \times \sqrt{640}\right) + 4 \times 3 + 16 \times 12$
$= 860\text{ cm}^2$

stem: [The surface area of a sphere with radius $r$ is $4\pi r^2$, and the curved surface area of a cylinder with radius $r$ and height $h$ is $2\pi rh$.]

parts.text: A container of negligible thickness is in the shape of a cylinder with a hollow hemi-spherical cover. The base radius of the cylinder and the cover is $r$ cm, and the height of the cylinder is $h$ cm. The volume of the cylinder is fixed at $120\pi$ cm$^3$. Given that the costs of making the cover and the cylinder are $\$0.10$ per cm$^2$ and $\$0.03$ per cm$^2$ respectively, show that the total cost, $\$C$, to manufacture the container is given by $C = \pi\left(0.23r^2 + \frac{7.2}{r}\right)$. Use differentiation to find the exact value of $\frac{r}{h}$ that gives the minimum value of $C$ as $r$ varies.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$C = (\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh)(0.03) + (2\pi r^2)(0.10)$
$\pi r^2 h = 120\pi \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{120}{r^2}$
$C = \left(\pi r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\dfrac{120}{r^2}\right)\right)(0.03) + (2\pi r^2)(0.10)$
$= \pi\left(0.23 r^2 + \dfrac{7.2}{r}\right)$
$\dfrac{dC}{dr} = \pi\left(0.46 r - \dfrac{7.2}{r^2}\right) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 0.46 r - \dfrac{7.2}{r^2} = 0$
$\Rightarrow r^3 = \dfrac{7.2}{0.46} = \dfrac{360}{23}$, i.e. $r = 2.50$ (3 s.f.).
$\dfrac{d^2C}{dr^2} = \pi\left(0.46 + \dfrac{14.4}{r^3}\right)$
At $r = 2.50$: $\dfrac{d^2C}{dr^2} = 1.38\pi = 4.34 > 0$.
Hence $C$ is a minimum when $r^3 = \dfrac{360}{23}$.
$\dfrac{r}{h} = \dfrac{r}{\frac{120}{r^2}} = \dfrac{r^3}{120} = \dfrac{360/23}{120} = \dfrac{3}{23}$.

parts.text: A manufacturer constructs one such container with radius 4 cm such that the curved surface of the cylinder is decorated with a curve. The diagram below shows the curved surface, flattened out, with the bottom left corner as the origin and the $x$- and $y$-axes as indicated. The curve has equation $y = 2\cos\frac{x}{4} + 5.5$. A point $P$ with $x$-coordinate $p$ moves along the curve such that $p$ increases at a constant rate of 0.1 cm per second. The point $Q$ is vertically below $P$ on the $x$-axis. Find the exact rate of change of the area of triangle $OPQ$ when $P$ is at the lowest point of the curve.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Coordinates of $P$ are $\left(x, 2\cos\dfrac{x}{4} + 5.5\right)$.
Area of triangle $OPQ$, $A = \dfrac{1}{2}x\left(2\cos\dfrac{x}{4} + 5.5\right) = x\cos\dfrac{x}{4} + \dfrac{11}{4}x$
$\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{dA}{dx}\times\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}x\sin\dfrac{x}{4} + \cos\dfrac{x}{4} + \dfrac{11}{4}\right)\dfrac{dx}{dt}$
At the lowest point of the curve, $x = 4\pi$ and $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 0.1$:
$\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{4}\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{4} + \cos\dfrac{4\pi}{4} + \dfrac{11}{4}\right)(0.1) = \left(-\pi\sin\pi + \cos\pi + \dfrac{11}{4}\right)(0.1)$
$= \left(0 - 1 + \dfrac{11}{4}\right)(0.1) = 0.175 \text{ cm}^2\text{/s}$.

stem: An art student wants to create an art installation \"Glimpse of Hope\" on the wall. The installation consists of a drawing modelled by the curve $y = 2x^{2}e^{(2 - x)}$ and the line $y = 2ex$. The two graphs intersect at the origin and touch at the point $(1, 2e)$. The student intends to fit lightbulbs into the region $R$.

parts.text: Find the exact area of region $R$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Each light bulb consists of part of an empty sphere of radius $6$ cm and a solid cylinder of radius $2\sqrt{5}$ cm and height $3$ cm. The bottom of the sphere is sliced off so that its edge touches the top edge of the cylinder. The sphere is modelled by rotating part of the curve $x^{2} + (y - 6)^{2} = 36$ about the $y$-axis.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Assuming the filament takes up negligible space and the light bulb is of negligible thickness, calculate the exact volume of the spherical part of the light bulb that needs to be filled with inert gas.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
$x^{2} + (y - 6)^{2} = 36 \Rightarrow x^{2} = 36 - (y - 6)^{2}$.
When $x = 2\sqrt{5}$: $20 + (y - 6)^{2} = 36$, so $(y - 6)^{2} = 16$, giving $y = 2$ or $y = 10$ (reject); the sphere is sliced at $y = 2$.
Volume of the spherical part $= \pi\int_{2}^{12} x^{2}\,dy = \pi\int_{2}^{12}\left(36 - (y - 6)^{2}\right)dy$
$= \pi\left[36y - \frac{(y - 6)^{3}}{3}\right]_{2}^{12}$
$= \frac{800}{3}\pi$ cm$^{3}$.

subparts.text: It is given that the area of a surface of revolution formed by revolving the graph of $x = f(y)$ about the $y$-axis over the interval from $y = a$ to $y = b$ is $\int_{a}^{b} 2\pi f(y)\sqrt{1 + \left(f'(y)\right)^{2}}\,dy.$ Find the numerical value of the surface area of the spherical part of the light bulb.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text: Each light bulb can effectively light up a circular area of $0.5\text{ m}^2$. Using the formula $\text{Number of light bulbs} = \frac{\text{Area of Region } R}{0.5}$, and given that 1 unit on the installation represents $100$ m, determine the number of light bulbs the art student would acquire. Suggest why this number may not be accurate.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.answer: $6897.514 \approx 6898$. The formula assumes the circular lit areas tile the region $R$ exactly with no overlaps or gaps, which is not physically possible, so the true number needed differs.
subparts.solution:
Since 1 unit represents $100$ m, $1$ unit$^{2}$ represents $10\,000$ m$^{2}$.
Area of region $R = (11e - 4e^{2}) \times 10\,000 = 3448.76$ m$^{2}$.
Number of light bulbs $= \frac{3448.76}{0.5} = 6897.5 \approx 6898$.
This may not be accurate because the formula assumes the circular lit regions cover $R$ exactly with no gaps or overlaps, which is impossible for an irregular region, so the actual number needed differs.

stem: The cumulative frequency diagram shows the times taken by $200$ girls from school $A$ running a $2.4$ km test. The box-and-whisker plot shows the times for another group of girls from school $B$.

parts.text: $75\%$ of the girls in school $B$ failed the test. Find the number of girls who passed in school $A$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
From school $B$, the lower quartile $Q_1 = 14$ minutes is the passing time (the fastest 25% passed).
Number of girls in school $A$ who passed the test $= 60$ (read from the cumulative frequency curve at $t = 14$ minutes).

parts.text: $30\%$ of the girls in school $A$ took longer than $t$ minutes. Find $t$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$30\%$ of the girls $= \dfrac{30}{100} \times 200 = 60$, so $200 - 60 = 140$ girls took $t$ minutes or less.
From the curve, a cumulative frequency of 140 corresponds to $t = 16$.

parts.text: Find the proportion of girls in school $A$ who took between $14.5$ minutes and $17$ minutes to complete the run.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
At $t = 14.5$, cumulative frequency $= 80$.
At $t = 17$, cumulative frequency $= 177$.
Proportion of girls $= \dfrac{177 - 80}{200} \times 100\% = 48.5\%$

stem: The figure shows the sector $AOB$ of a circle. The length of its arc $AB$ is $8\pi$ cm and angle $AOB$ is $120^\circ$.

parts.text: Show that the radius $AO$ is 12 cm.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$\frac{120^\circ}{360^\circ}(2\pi)(AO) = 8\pi$
$\frac{2\pi}{3}(AO) = 8\pi$
$AO = 12 \text{ cm}$

parts.text: The sector is folded so that the straight edges meet and form a cone. Calculate the radius of the base of the cone.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let the radius of the base of the cone be $r$.
$8\pi = 2\pi r$
$r = \frac{8\pi}{2\pi} = 4 \text{ cm}$

parts.text: It is given that the slant height of the cone is 6.4 cm and the height of the cone is 5 cm. Calculate the curved surface area of the cone.
parts.label: c
parts.solution: Curved surface area of the cone $= \pi(4)(6.4) = 80.42477 = 80.4 \text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.)

stem: Mr Lim is a 35 year old employee who earns a gross (before CPF contribution) monthly salary of $\$3700$ and credits his salary (after CPF contribution) to a DBS Multiplier account. He has $\$40\,000$ of savings and spends between $\$100$ to $\$300$ on his DBS credit card each month. Mr Lim does not insure or invest with any banks. Information on CPF contribution, DBS Multiplier, OCBC 360 and UOB One accounts is given in the images below.

parts.text: How much salary will be credited to his bank account after deduction for his CPF contribution?
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Salary credited $= 0.8 \times 3700 = \$2960$ (after $20\%$ CPF contribution).

parts.text: Calculate the annual interest that Mr Lim's savings of $\$40\,000$ alone will earn through his DBS Multiplier account.
parts.label: b
parts.solution: DBS Multiplier interest on the savings $= \frac{0.4}{100} \times 40\,000 = \$160.$

parts.text: Mr Lim was promoted and his new gross monthly salary is $\$4500$. Because of the pay rise, Mr Lim decided that he will spend between $\$500$ to $\$700$ on his credit card each month. Suggest if Mr Lim should change to an OCBC 360 or UOB One account to maximise the interest earned for his $\$40\,000$ savings alone. Justify your decision and show any calculations you made clearly.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: DBS Multiplier: salary $\$3600$ + transactions $\$4100$–$\$4300$, interest $= 0.4\% \times 40\,000 = \$160$. OCBC 360: $1.2\% + 0.3\% + 0.05\% = 1.55\%$, interest $= \$620$. UOB One: tiered $0.5\%/0.55\%/0.65\%$ giving $75 + 82.50 + 65 = \$222.50$. Mr Lim should change to the OCBC 360 account as it pays the highest interest on his $\$40\,000$ savings.
parts.solution:
DBS Multiplier: salary credited $= 0.8 \times 4500 = \$3600$ with transactions $\$4100$–$\$4300$, giving interest $= \frac{0.4}{100} \times 40\,000 = \$160$.
OCBC 360: $1.2\% + 0.3\% + 0.05\% = 1.55\%$, interest $= \frac{1.55}{100} \times 40\,000 = \$620$.
UOB One: first $\$15\,000$ at $0.5\% = \$75$; next $\$15\,000$ at $0.55\% = \$82.50$; next $\$10\,000$ at $0.65\% = \$65$; total $= \$222.50$.
Mr Lim should change to the OCBC 360 account, as it pays the highest interest ($\$620$) on his $\$40\,000$ savings.

stem: A hot water tank is made by joining a hemisphere of radius 30 cm to a cylinder of radius 30 cm and height 70 cm.

parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the water tank.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Total surface area
$= \frac{1}{2} \times 4\pi \times 30^2 + 2\pi \times 30 \times 70 + \pi \times 30^2$
$= 1800\pi + 4200\pi + 900\pi$
$= 6900\pi$
$= 21676.989$
$= 21700$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: The tank is filled with water completely.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Calculate the number of litres of water in the tank.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Volume of water
$= \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{3}\pi \times 30^3 + \pi \times 30^2 \times 70$
$= 18000\pi + 63000\pi$
$= 81000\pi$ cm$^3$
$= 81000\pi \div 1000$ litres (1 litre $= 1000$ cm$^3$)
$= 81\pi$ litres
$= 254.469$
$= 254$ litres (3 s.f.)

subparts.text: The water drains from the tank at a rate of 3 litres per second. Calculate the time, in minutes and seconds, taken to empty the tank.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Time taken $= 81\pi \div 3$ seconds
$= 84.823$ seconds
$= 1$ minute 25 seconds

subparts.text: All the water from the tank fills a bath completely. The bath is a prism whose cross-section is a trapezium. The lengths of the parallel sides of the trapezium are 0.4 m and 0.6 m. The depth of the bath is 0.3 m. Calculate, in metres, the length of the bath.
subparts.label: iii

stem: The amount of mass loss in kilograms of 200 members was recorded by Amazing Fitness. The cumulative frequency curve shows the distribution of the results. Use the curve to estimate

parts.text: In order to encourage members to be active in their mass loss, Amazing is waiving a one month membership fee for members who managed to lose at least $x$ kg in a year. Given that 10% of the members managed to qualify for the waiver, find the value of $x$.

parts.text: This box-and-whisker plot represents the distribution of the mass loss of 200 members of another fitness centre, Supreme Fitness Centre. Make two comments comparing the mass loss of the members in the two fitness centres.
parts.label: d

stem: Two groups of students were surveyed on their weekly screen time in hours. The results are shown in the table.

parts.text: $20\%$ of students in Group 2 recorded a screen time of at least $x$ hours. Find $x$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$20\%$ of $10$ students $= \dfrac{20}{100} \times 10 = 2$ students.
The two highest screen times in Group 2 are $45$ and $90$, so "at least $x$ hours" corresponds to $x = 45$ hours.

parts.text:
Complete the table below.
$$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|} \hline & \text{Group 1} & \text{Group 2} \\ \hline \text{Median} & 34 & \\ \hline \text{Interquartile Range} & & 19 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Median of Group 2 $= 29$; Interquartile Range of Group 1 $= 32$.
parts.solution:
Median of Group 2 (mean of the middle two of $10$ ordered values) $= \dfrac{29 + 29}{2} = 29$.
Interquartile range of Group 1 $= Q_3 - Q_1 = 55 - 23 = 32$.

parts.text: Make a comparison between the screen times of the students in these two groups.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Group 2 students have shorter screen time on average since their median ($29$ h) is less than Group 1's median ($34$ h). Alternatively, Group 2 screen times are less spread out than Group 1's (IQR $19$ h vs $32$ h).
parts.solution: Group 2 students have a shorter average screen time, since their median ($29$ h) is less than Group 1's median ($34$ h). Group 2's screen times are also less spread out, since their interquartile range ($19$ h) is smaller than Group 1's ($32$ h).

parts.text: Explain why median is a better measure for average screen time for the two groups of students compared to the mean.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: There are extreme values (such as $90$) present in the data, which would affect the calculation of the mean but not the median.
parts.solution: There are extreme values (such as $90$) in the data. These affect the calculation of the mean but not the median, so the median is a better measure of the average.

subparts.text: The box-and-whisker plot for the distribution of screen time for students in Group 2 is drawn in the grid below. Write down the values for $Q_{1}$, $Q_{2}$ and $Q_{3}$.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: Due to a recording error, the recorded amount of screen time for Group 1 is $1$ hour more than the actual screen time. State how the median and standard deviation of the screen times have been affected by this error.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: The actual median will decrease by $1$ hour from $34$ h to $33$ h. The standard deviation remains the same.
